### Mock 7: "We can't think gender without thinking 'race'" (Hill Collins). Using the matrix of domination and Crenshaw's intersectionality, assess what Black feminist thought adds to the analysis of woman-as-other.

The lecturer's "Black feminist thought" slide quotes Hill Collins twice, gives the matrix of domination, and concludes with the sharp formulation "we can't think gender without thinking 'race'". The next slide defines Crenshaw's intersectionality as the notion that "different types of discrimination intersect and often compound experiences of exclusion and social subjugation". I argue that Black feminist thought adds three things to the woman-as-other analysis: a plural standpoint to replace the singular, a matrix architecture to replace single-axis diagnosis, and a political agency to replace pure victimhood. The result is a sharper, not diluted, feminism.

Start with Beauvoir as the position being supplemented. "Humanity is male and man defines woman not in herself but as relative to him… He is the Subject, he is the Absolute; she is the Other" (de Beauvoir, 1949: 6) is a structural diagnosis of othering. The lecturer's critique of Beauvoir is direct: "Does de Beauvoir try to 'universalize' her argument/situation? Is her account historically and socially limited (she is a middle class, white, European intellectual)? Can she really describe and account for the way in which ALL women have been oppressed all over the world, in every age?" The honest answer is no. The "woman" of *The Second Sex* is a particular woman, generalised. This is the universalising charge the lecture lays against pre-1980s feminism, alongside essentialising and ahistoricism.

Hill Collins formulates the alternative. "Black feminist thought consists of ideas produced by Black women that clarify a standpoint of and for Black women" (Hill Collins, 1986: 70). The standpoint is named, not assumed. The matrix of domination follows: "structural, disciplinary, hegemonic, and interpersonal domains of power reappear across quite different forms of oppression". Power is not a single axis but a four-domain architecture, and the architecture recurs across different oppressions. The lecturer's gloss is decisive: "Gender does not exist 'on its own'… 'Race' (or the idea of race) is equally important, if not more important, than 'gender'. Indeed, we can't think gender without thinking 'race'."

Crenshaw's intersectionality is the diagnostic tool. The lecture defines it as "the notion that different types of discrimination intersect and often compound experiences of exclusion and social subjugation". A Black woman is not Beauvoir's other in single-axis form; she is othered by race and gender simultaneously, and the compound is its own analytic object, not the sum of two parts. The Lean In versus Black/intersectional contrast is the contemporary political register: a corporate feminism premised on white middle-class professional women cannot register the harms Crenshaw names.

What does this add to woman-as-other? Three contributions.

First, the standpoint becomes plural. Hartsock's "women's lives differ structurally from those of men" (Hartsock, 1983: 284) is correct but needs differentiation. The Black domestic worker and her white employer occupy structurally different positions on the gender axis itself, because their gendering is racially mediated. Hill Collins's standpoint claim "of and for Black women" is the methodological consequence. The L8 lineage matters: Du Bois's "double consciousness", "always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity" (Du Bois, 1903: 5), is the structural form Hill Collins inherits and pluralises into the matrix. Gilroy's Black Atlantic shows modernity from the standpoint of those it enslaved; Black feminism extends this to gender.

Second, the architecture becomes matricial rather than linear. Beauvoir's other is othered along one axis; the matrix shows that othering operates simultaneously through structural (laws, formal institutions), disciplinary (bureaucratic enforcement), hegemonic (culture, common sense), and interpersonal (face-to-face encounters) domains. Adichie's parking-attendant episode runs all four: structural (Igbo inheritance rules), disciplinary (restaurant routines), hegemonic (the assumption that "Louis is a man" suffices to redirect thanks), interpersonal (the gift exchange). The matrix names the architecture; intersectionality names how axes co-produce experience.

Third, agency becomes intrinsic. Beauvoir's woman is described as object, not subject. hooks insists: "the 'gaze' has always been political in my life… There is power in looking" (hooks, 1992: 115). The othered subject is also capable of looking back; resistance is not added later but lived in the same moment as the othering. hooks adds, against second-wave universalism, that home for Black women is also refuge from racial terror, not only constraint. The L10 vision work connects this: Mulvey's male gaze names a structural pattern, hooks's oppositional gaze names the practice of refusing it. The othered subject of Beauvoir becomes the looking subject of hooks.

Two qualifications. Mohanty (L9) warns that Western feminism produces "the third world woman" as "ignorant, poor, uneducated, tradition-bound, domestic, family-oriented, victimized" (Mohanty, 1984: 261); Black feminist thought must not be flattened into a single Black standpoint either. Harding's synthesis applies: "There is no single, ideal woman's life from which standpoint theories recommend that thought start" (Harding, 2004: 131). And Butler's destabilisation runs alongside: "the category of 'women,' the subject of feminism, is produced and restrained by the very structures of power through which emancipation is sought" (Butler, 1990: 2). The matrix must be read as itself reflexively constructed.

The political register is alive. Black Lives Matter and post-Roe America are intelligible together only through intersectional categories; restrictions on reproductive control fall hardest where the matrix predicts. The cost-of-living crisis intensifies the same pattern: low-paid care work is gendered, racialised and classed at once.

So Black feminist thought does not refute woman-as-other; it makes the diagnosis precise. Beauvoir's pattern survives; the diagnostic apparatus gets sharper. We cannot think gender without thinking race because the othering of women is racially co-produced, and a feminism that ignores this reproduces the colonial gaze it claims to dismantle. (Word count: 745.)

### Mock 8: "The personal is political." Discuss with reference to Hall and Walby on the public/private split.

I argue that the second-wave slogan "the personal is political" remains one of feminism's most analytically powerful tools. It does not claim that private life is identical with the political; it claims that the boundary between personal and political is itself politically produced, and therefore contestable. Hall (1980) and Walby (1986) historicise that boundary; Hartsock translates the historicisation into epistemology; Adichie and Criado-Perez document its present effects.

Recall the provenance. Second-wave consciousness-raising discovered that experiences each woman had treated as her own (housework, marital sex, harassment, reproductive anxiety) were systemically patterned. The lecture's reading of the split gives the historical move: with the rise of capitalism, "the production of goods shifted from the small-scale domestic level to the large-scale, anonymous level… you go out to work. In factories." The home is reinvented as private and feminised; "Women's role becomes the inconspicuous work of making the work of the (male) wage-worker possible… The domestic sphere becomes invisible" (Hall, 1980; Walby, 1986). The slogan repoliticises this newly invented private.

Hartsock translates this epistemologically: women have been given "the responsibility for certain areas of production and reproduction such as childbirth and child-rearing… 'women's lives differ structurally from those of men'" (Hartsock, 1983: 284). The personal (childbirth, childrearing, domestic labour) is precisely what has been politically allocated; calling this allocation "private" is the political move the slogan exposes. The cost-of-living crisis and the present squeeze on care work make the slogan operationally relevant: housework and care are still privatised, and still gendered.

Apply the slogan to Adichie's cases. The parking attendant says "Thank you, sah!" to Louis after Adichie tips him, because "Louis is a man". The Nsukka class-monitor episode: Adichie scored highest but "my teacher said the monitor had to be a boy". The Igbo extended-family meetings from which Adichie is excluded "because I am female" show the split reproduced in non-European institutional forms. Each personal moment is a political pattern.

Three objections must be met.

First, the slogan is too broad: if everything is political, nothing is. This misreads. The slogan claims the *boundary* is a political artefact, not that all private life is uniformly political. Recognising this opens specific questions: who benefits from this boundary being drawn here? Whose labour is privatised? Whose violence?

Second, the slogan flattens difference. This was Black feminism's legitimate concern. The slogan needs to be read plurally: which personal is whose political? hooks's revision, "the 'gaze' has always been political in my life… There is power in looking" (hooks, 1992: 115), uses it while pluralising. Hill Collins and hooks "questioned second-wave understandings of the home as a site of repression and subjugation"; for Black women under racial terror, the home was also refuge.

Third, the slogan is dated. Against this I set Criado-Perez's gender data gap, the slogan in 21st-century empirical clothes. Crash-test dummies modelled on the "reference man" leave women "47% more likely to be seriously injured" in a comparable crash. Office thermostats run "five degrees too cold for women". Apple Health launched without a period tracker. Each looks personal (my cold office) and is in fact a political arrangement of who counts as default. #MeToo and Black Lives Matter scale the slogan: individual testimony becomes structural diagnosis.

Butler radicalises further. "Feminist critique ought also to understand how the category of 'women,' the subject of feminism, is produced and restrained by the very structures of power through which emancipation is sought" (Butler, 1990: 2). The personal/political distinction is not only redrawn; the subject who inhabits "the personal" is itself a political production. The L4 work on language extends the same diagnosis into the medium through which the personal is named: Spender argues English is "man-made", structured around male-as-norm so that female is "minus male" (Spender, 1980), and Beauvoir notes "a man would never set out to write a book on the peculiar situation of the human male" (de Beauvoir, 1988: 15). The very vocabulary in which intimate experience is described is therefore already political, which is why consciousness-raising had to invent new terms.

The slogan, read through intersectional revision, remains one of feminism's most powerful tools. Adichie's parking attendant, Criado-Perez's reference man, Hartsock's standpoint and the historicisation of the public/private split are its current vindications. (Word count: 720.)

### Mock 9: Critically assess hooks's argument that home can function as a site of resistance.

"Collins and bell hooks both questioned second-wave understandings of the home as a site of repression and subjugation"; for Black women, home can be a refuge as well as a constraint. I assess this argument as broadly correct, sharper than mainstream second-wave framing, and necessary to any feminism that does not collapse into Beauvoir's universalising mistake.

The standard second-wave reading, drawing on Hall (1980) and Walby (1986), treats the home as the seat of women's invisibility under capitalism. "Women's role becomes the inconspicuous work of making the work of the (male) wage-worker possible through the provision of sustenance (material and emotional) in the home… The domestic sphere becomes invisible." Women are denied subjecthood, their labour unwaged, made "other". Beauvoir gives the phenomenology; "humanity is male and man defines woman not in herself but as relative to him" (de Beauvoir, 1949: 6); the home is the architectural form.

hooks's correction. For Black women under racial terror, the home is also a refuge from the violence of the white public sphere. The "oppositional gaze" extends the point: "When thinking about black female spectators, I remember being punished as a child for staring, for those hard intense direct looks children would give grown-ups, looks that were seen as confrontational, as gestures of resistance, challenges to authority. The 'gaze' has always been political in my life… There is power in looking" (hooks, 1992: 115). Resistance is forged in the home, in the family, in the practices of looking that the public sphere punishes. Black Lives Matter draws on this lineage: the household as a base for resistance.

Why this matters analytically.

First, second-wave universalisation. Mainstream analysis implicitly analysed the white middle-class suburban home. Hill Collins's matrix shows the same architectural form functions differently across racial and class positions: "structural, disciplinary, hegemonic, and interpersonal domains of power reappear across quite different forms of oppression" (Hill Collins). Meaning varies by position.

Second, the standpoint move. The home, on Hartsock's account, is the site of social reproduction: "women have been given the responsibility for certain areas of production and reproduction such as childbirth and child-rearing" (Hartsock, 1983: 284). hooks complicates this: the standpoint is achieved differently depending on whether the home is also a barrier to racial terror. Standpoint privilege is plural.

Third, the intersectional refinement. The home is gendered, racialised and classed at once; it is not the same institution for the Black domestic worker and her white employer.

Adichie adds a non-Black-American case. Igbo family life is both her socialisation and her exclusion: "only the male members of the extended family can attend the meetings where major family decisions are taken… I cannot have a formal say. Because I am female." Yet it is also the site of her formation: her great-grandmother "ran away from the house of the man she did not want to marry… She did not know that word *feminist*. But it doesn't mean she wasn't one." The same home that excludes her transmits the genealogy of resistance.

The argument has limits. hooks does not abolish the home's repressive function; she adds a resistance function. The two coexist. A feminism reading hooks as simply liberatory would lose Hall, Walby and Hartsock. A feminism ignoring hooks would repeat second-wave universalisation. The synthesis is the matrix reading. The cost-of-living crisis sharpens this: the home is both an intensified site of unpaid care work and a contested refuge.

Criado-Perez is the contemporary cousin. The home is where the thermostat is *not* set to a male resting metabolic rate, and yet the office is where women find themselves "five degrees too cold". The public/private split keeps shifting; the home's resistance functions keep needing to be defended. The L10 vision material situates hooks's argument more sharply: Mulvey's male gaze (1975) makes women "passive objects of a heterosexual male spectator's pleasure and control" in cinema, and hooks's reply, "Not only will I stare. I want my look to change reality" (hooks, 1992: 116), is forged in the home, where Black children were "punished for staring". The home is a resistance site partly because it is the one space where the disciplinary public gaze is suspended long enough to learn to look back.

So hooks is right: the home can be a site of resistance, particularly where the public sphere is racially hostile. The right reading holds repression and resistance together in Hill Collins's matrix. (Word count: 720.)

### Mock 10: What does de Beauvoir mean by "one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman", and why does she treat lived experience as central?

The sentence contains two of the most consequential moves in twentieth-century feminist theory: an anti-essentialist account of gender, and a methodological commitment to lived experience as the ground of philosophical knowledge. Together they make *The Second Sex* (1949) the hinge between liberal first-wave feminism and the second-wave, standpoint and post-structuralist traditions that follow.

Begin with the sentence. Beauvoir's claim is not that biological sex is irrelevant but that "woman" (the social, psychological, juridical, aesthetic category) is constituted through a process: socialisation, mythology, institutional positioning, interpersonal recognition. The category is historical and contingent, not natural. This is the conceptual seed of what Butler later theorises as performativity: gender as constituted through repeated acts that present themselves as if always already there.

The structural finding grounding the claim is woman-as-other. "Humanity is male and man defines woman not in herself but as relative to him; she is not regarded as an autonomous being... She is the incidental, the inessential as opposed to the absolute. He is the Subject, he is the Absolute; she is the Other" (de Beauvoir, 1949: 6). Because man is taken as the universal human, woman becomes the marked term. To become a woman is to be inserted into this asymmetric structure and to learn it as nature.

Why does Beauvoir treat lived experience as central? Three reasons.

First, the existentialist apparatus demands it. Human beings are not essences but projects, freedoms exercised within concrete situations. To know what it is to be a woman one must investigate the lived situation, not legislate from outside.

Second, experience is the ground on which the woman-as-other diagnosis becomes available. The second-wave slogan "the personal is political" is already implicit, and Hartsock's "women's lives differ structurally from those of men" (Hartsock, 1983: 284) extends Beauvoir into a full theory of situated knowledge.

Third, the work has to do double duty: persuade women that patterns they read as personal failings are systemic, and persuade philosophy that "women" is a question. Adichie's *We Should All Be Feminists* uses the same method: autobiographical episodes (the Lagos parking attendant thanking her through Louis, hotel staff assuming her to be a sex worker) generating the diagnosis.

The anti-essentialism is the most enduring contribution. If becoming a woman is a process, it can be done differently: by raising daughters and sons differently (Adichie's prescription), or by destabilising the binary (Butler). The same move underwrites trans-feminist interventions and the current trans-rights debates: if "woman" is constituted rather than given, there is no metaphysical bar to its being constituted otherwise. Beauvoir's parallel argument in L4 makes the linguistic dimension visible: "a man would never set out to write a book on the peculiar situation of the human male. But if I wish to define myself, I must first of all say: 'I am a woman'" (de Beauvoir, 1988: 15). One is not born a "woman writer"; one becomes one because language pre-marks femininity. Spender's "man-made language" (1980) generalises the point structurally.

The centrality of lived experience must be qualified. Beauvoir is herself a middle-class, white, European intellectual writing in 1949, and the experience she describes is in important respects her own. Hill Collins, Crenshaw and hooks supply the corrective: many lived experiences, structured by the matrix of domination across race, class, sexuality and ability. Harding makes the point explicitly: "There is no single, ideal woman's life from which standpoint theories recommend that thought start. Instead, one must turn to all of the lives that are marginalized in different ways" (Harding, 2004: 131). Black Lives Matter and #MeToo are contemporary instances: shared lived experience becoming structural diagnosis.

Concrete examples reinforce why the move matters. Criado-Perez's gender data gap is Beauvoir restated empirically: when the world is engineered around the "reference man", women's lived experience (freezing offices, ill-fitting stab vests) registers the asymmetry materially. Adichie's class-monitor episode is Beauvoir in autobiographical miniature: a girl who scores highest is told "the monitor had to be a boy". One is not born a "woman who cannot be class monitor"; one is made one.

So the sentence means: woman is a process, not an essence; and one must read that process from inside the lives it shapes. That is why Beauvoir puts lived experience at the centre, and why the move still organises feminist thought seventy-five years on. (Word count: 720.)

### Mock 11: Compare Hartsock's feminist standpoint with Hill Collins's matrix of domination.

Hartsock and Hill Collins are doing related but distinct work, and the most defensible contemporary feminist sociology requires both. Hartsock supplies an epistemology: a theory of how knowledge is produced from structurally located lives. Hill Collins supplies an ontology of power: a theory of how oppression is organised across domains and axes. Each completes what the other leaves under-theorised.

Begin with Hartsock. Her 1983 essay adapts Marx's standpoint move from the proletariat to women. "Women's lives differ structurally from those of men" (Hartsock, 1983: 284), and that difference (women's location in social reproduction) generates a critical vantage dominant-group thinkers cannot easily reach. Women are insiders (essential to social reproduction) and outsiders (denied power). "Just as Marx's understanding of the world from the standpoint of the proletariat enabled him to go beneath bourgeois ideology, so a feminist standpoint can allow us to understand patriarchal institutions and ideologies as perverse inversions of more human social relations" (Hartsock, 1983: 142). The standpoint is achieved through political and theoretical work, not given by anatomy.

Now Hill Collins. *Black Feminist Thought* (1990) and "Learning from the Outsider Within" (Hill Collins, 1986) develop the matrix of domination. Collins identifies four interlocking domains: structural (laws, formal institutions), disciplinary (bureaucratic application through schools, prisons, welfare offices, HR), hegemonic (culture, ideology, common sense), and interpersonal (face-to-face encounters, everyday microaggressions). Any system of oppression operates through all four simultaneously. Collins also insists on a Black feminist standpoint: "Black feminist thought consists of ideas produced by Black women that clarify a standpoint of and for Black women" (Hill Collins, 1986: 70).

The comparison yields four contrasts and three convergences.

First contrast: scope. Hartsock writes about women's structural location in social reproduction as singular. Collins plurialises: many standpoints, many positions in the matrix. A Black domestic worker and a white middle-class housewife differ; Hartsock's singular standpoint elides this, Collins's matrix centres it.

Second contrast: object. Hartsock's primary object is knowledge: how do we know what we know, and why does location matter? Collins's primary object is power: how is domination structured, and why does it recur across oppressions?

Third contrast: genealogy. Hartsock works in a Marxist register, extending the proletarian standpoint. Collins works in a Black feminist register.

Fourth contrast: method. Hartsock theorises top-down from structural location to epistemic consequence. Collins theorises bottom-up from Black women's lived practices to analytic categories.

The convergences. Both reject the "God-trick" of disembodied universal knowledge. Both insist location matters for knowledge. Both treat standpoint as achieved.

Three illustrations clarify the complementarity.

Adichie's parking-attendant episode. Hartsock explains why women generate the analysis: women occupy the position of the one whose money is taken and whose recognition is rerouted to the nearest man. Collins explains why the misrecognition operates across domains: structural (Igbo inheritance and meeting rules), disciplinary (restaurant routines), hegemonic (the assumption that "Louis is a man" suffices to redirect thanks), interpersonal (the moment of the gift).

Criado-Perez's gender data gap. Hartsock explains why an engineering community without women produced defective car safety: crash-test dummies modelled on the "reference man", leaving women "47% more likely to be seriously injured" and "17% more likely to die". Collins explains why the gap is not symmetric across race: the male face-shape used for dust, hazard and eye masks doesn't fit most women "as well as a lot of black and minority ethnic men". Black Lives Matter and the Lean In / Black-intersectional contrast are the contemporary political register: a singular gender harm produced through differently positioned matrices.

The public/private split. Hartsock's standpoint reading names the epistemic privilege. Collins's matrix reading explains why the split is reproduced across radically different cultural settings, from Hall and Walby's industrial-capitalism case to Adichie's Igbo extended-family meetings.

So which is more useful? Neither alone. For epistemic and methodological questions, Hartsock is sharper. For structural-architectural questions about how power is organised, Collins is sharper. The right contemporary sociology reads them together, as Harding's strong objectivity already implicitly does, and as the broader L6 standpoint tradition systematises: "standpoint theorists themselves all explicitly argue that marginal lives that are not their own provide better grounds for certain kinds of knowledge" (Harding, 2004: 129). Hartsock supplies the epistemic principle, Hill Collins its intersectional architecture, Harding the methodological apparatus that makes both rigorous. (Word count: 730.)

### Mock 12: How does Crenshaw's intersectionality refine Beauvoir's account of woman-as-other?

Crenshaw's intersectionality is best read as a refinement, not a refutation, of Beauvoir's woman-as-other. Beauvoir names the structural asymmetry in which "humanity is male and man defines woman not in herself but as relative to him" (de Beauvoir, 1949: 6); Crenshaw shows the asymmetry is not single-axis. Read together, they deliver a sharper analytic apparatus than either alone.

Recall Beauvoir. *The Second Sex* (1949) diagnoses the structural condition of "woman": "He is the Subject, he is the Absolute; she is the Other" (de Beauvoir, 1949: 6). Her anti-essentialism, "one is not born but rather one becomes a woman", makes the othering social and historical.

The limits of Beauvoir, as the lecture asks: "Does de Beauvoir try to 'universalize' her argument/situation? Is her account historically and socially limited (she is a middle class, white, European intellectual)? Can she really describe and account for the way in which ALL women have been oppressed all over the world, in every age?" The answer is no. The "woman" of *The Second Sex* is a middle-class white European.

Crenshaw refines. Intersectionality is "the notion that different types of discrimination intersect and often compound experiences of exclusion and social subjugation." The othering Beauvoir describes is itself differentiated. A Black woman is not simply Beauvoir's other; she is othered by race and gender simultaneously, and the compound is its own analytic object. The contrast between Lean In feminism and Black/intersectional feminism is the contemporary live form of this critique.

Hill Collins's matrix of domination is the systemic counterpart. "Structural, disciplinary, hegemonic, and interpersonal domains of power reappear across quite different forms of oppression… Gender does not exist 'on its own'… 'Race'… is equally important, if not more important, than 'gender'… we can't think gender without thinking 'race'" (Hill Collins). The matrix is the architecture; intersectionality is the diagnostic.

How this refines Beauvoir. Four moves.

First, the universalising critique. Beauvoir's woman-as-other is, on Crenshaw's reading, a particular position mistakenly generalised. The refinement: locate the position. Which woman, othered by which combination of axes?

Second, the experience critique. Beauvoir centres lived experience; Hartsock translates this into standpoint epistemology. Crenshaw plurialises the experiential ground: "Black feminist thought consists of ideas produced by Black women that clarify a standpoint of and for Black women" (Hill Collins, 1986: 70). Black Lives Matter operationalises the same insight.

Third, the home critique. Beauvoir reads the home as the site of female othering by generalising a particular case. Hill Collins and hooks "both questioned second-wave understandings of the home as a site of repression and subjugation". For Black women, the home is also refuge. "Home" is one architectural form whose function varies by position.

Fourth, the colonial critique. The lecture identifies "how white women have benefited from colonialism" as one of the histories pre-1980s feminism ignored. Beauvoir's woman-as-other was, in some respects, also a coloniser; intersectionality theorises this.

hooks's oppositional gaze is the active counterpart. "The 'gaze' has always been political in my life… There is power in looking" (hooks, 1992: 115). The othered subject is also capable of looking back; the othering is not total. The L8 lineage is decisive here: Du Bois's "double consciousness", "always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity" (Du Bois, 1903: 5), pre-figures both Beauvoir's woman-as-other and Crenshaw's compound othering. Intersectionality is not simply added to Beauvoir; it grafts the Black radical analysis of doubled vision onto her structural diagnosis.

Adichie supplies a non-Black-American case. Her Lagos hotel experience, her class-monitor episode, her exclusion from Igbo extended-family meetings: each is a Beauvoirian othering and each is also intersectional (gender, ethnicity, region, class, age).

Butler radicalises further. "The category of 'women,' the subject of feminism, is produced and restrained by the very structures of power through which emancipation is sought" (Butler, 1990: 2). Beauvoir's "woman" is not pre-political; the othering produces the category.

Criado-Perez confirms the structural diagnosis materially while requiring the intersectional refinement: women are "47% more likely to be seriously injured" in a comparable crash, and the male face-shape used for dust and eye masks fits neither most women nor "a lot of black and minority ethnic men". Same structural pattern, intersectionally differentiated.

So Crenshaw refines Beauvoir by plurialising the othered subject without abandoning the structural diagnosis. The diagnosis stands; the diagnostic apparatus gets sharper. (Word count: 720.)

### Mock 13: Is queer theory a vindication or a refutation of feminist standpoint theory?

Against the disjunction, queer theory is best read as a *modification* of feminist standpoint theory: neither vindication nor refutation, but a critical extension that exposes a flaw in the original formulation while preserving its core epistemic claim. Harding's reformulation integrates the queer-theoretical correction without abandoning standpoint epistemology.

Begin with the two positions.

Standpoint theory, in Hartsock's 1983 formulation, holds that women's structural location, particularly in social reproduction, produces a critical vantage on patriarchy. "Women's lives differ structurally from those of men" (Hartsock, 1983: 284); that difference, theorised reflexively, generates situated knowledge. Standpoint privilege is achieved, not given. The empirical pay-off is the Criado-Perez gender data gap: starting from women's bodies and lives would have produced better engineering, medicine and policy than the engineering from the reference man.

Queer theory, in Butler's *Gender Trouble* (1990), destabilises the category "woman". "Feminist critique ought also to understand how the category of 'women,' the subject of feminism, is produced and restrained by the very structures of power through which emancipation is sought" (Butler, 1990: 2). Gender is performative. The heterosexual matrix produces "woman" as one of two stable categories; anything not fitting (intersex bodies, trans subjectivities) is rendered unintelligible. Current trans-rights debates are the live register.

Why might queer theory look like a refutation? Because if "woman" is unstable, the structural location from which the standpoint is supposed to be generated is itself politically constructed. Hartsock's grounding in social reproduction looks suspect: women are not simply "in" social reproduction; women are constituted as those who belong there. The standpoint is, on this reading, an artefact of the very gender system feminism aims to dismantle.

The refutation reading has force but overstates. Three reasons.

First, Hartsock and Harding already insisted the standpoint is achieved. Standpoint privilege does not depend on a metaphysically prior "woman" but on the work that turns a structural location into analytic vantage. Butler's destabilisation deepens this, not undermines it.

Second, the empirical pay-off does not depend on metaphysical stability. When Criado-Perez shows crash-test dummies modelled on the reference man leave women 47% more likely to be seriously injured, "women" is doing material-statistical work, not metaphysical work. Butler insists the category be used reflexively, not abandoned. Standpoint theory can, and Harding does, accept the reflexive use.

Third, queer theory's own critical purchase requires something like a standpoint move. To name compulsory heterosexuality as a structure of power requires starting from lives that the structure renders unintelligible. This is standpoint method in queer-theoretical clothes.

So queer theory is best read as a vindication-through-modification. It vindicates the core claim (knowledge is socially situated; marginalised locations generate critical resources) while modifying it in three ways.

First, the relevant locations are plural. Not one standpoint of "woman" but many standpoints of differently positioned subjects. This is also Hill Collins's correction: "ideas produced by Black women that clarify a standpoint of and for Black women" (Hill Collins, 1986: 70). Black Lives Matter and Black/intersectional feminism are the live political registers.

Second, the locations are themselves constructed. Standpoint analysis must include analysis of how the location was produced. Harding's strong objectivity, "Strong objectivity requires that the subject of knowledge be placed on the same critical, causal plane as the objects of knowledge", handles this.

Third, the standpoint is mobilised strategically. We use "woman" when the structural pattern (the gender data gap, the public/private split, the woman-as-other diagnosis) needs naming; we destabilise it when its use threatens to exclude. Post-Roe America illustrates: "women" is needed to name the harm, even as the harm differentiates by race, class and trans status. The L6 epistemic principle holds across the modification: "the subject of knowledge must be considered as part of the object of knowledge" (Harding, 2004: 136). Queer theory's contribution is to ensure that the gendered subject of feminist knowledge is itself analysed, not assumed. That is reflexivity, not refutation.

Concrete examples. Adichie uses the category "woman" openly while attending to its constructedness. Her response to being told feminism was "un-African", that her great-grandmother "did not know that word *feminist*. But it doesn't mean she wasn't one", uses "feminist" as a strategic category applied retrospectively. #MeToo did the same at scale.

So the answer is neither pure vindication nor pure refutation. The corrected standpoint theory (Harding's strong objectivity, plurialised through Hill Collins, made reflexive through Butler) is stronger than either parent position alone. (Word count: 720.)

### Mock 14: Does Harding's strong objectivity rescue or replace standpoint theory?

Harding's strong objectivity rescues standpoint theory rather than replacing it. The core claim, that knowledge is produced from socially located lives and that marginalised locations generate privileged resources, is preserved. Harding adds a methodological apparatus that defends the claim against charges of ethnocentrism, relativism, and unique-abilities-of-the-oppressed essentialism.

Recall Hartsock. "Women's lives differ structurally from those of men" (Hartsock, 1983: 284); women are insiders (essential to social reproduction) and outsiders (denied power); this duality generates a privileged vantage. The Marxist analogy: "just as Marx's understanding of the world from the standpoint of the proletariat enabled him to go beneath bourgeois ideology, so a feminist standpoint can allow us to understand patriarchal institutions and ideologies as perverse inversions of more human social relations" (Hartsock, 1983: 142).

The charges. Three classical objections, all addressed by Harding.

First, the God-trick. Critics suggest standpoint theory just substitutes one privileged viewpoint for another. Harding: "Standpoint knowledge projects do not claim to originate in purportedly universal human problematics; they do not claim to perform the 'God-trick.'… All thought by humans starts off from socially determinate lives" (Harding, 2004: 128).

Second, ethnocentrism. Critics suggest standpoint theory treats the holder's culture as superior. Harding: "standpoint theorists themselves all explicitly argue that marginal lives that are not their own provide better grounds for certain kinds of knowledge" (Harding, 2004: 129); the universalising claim is itself the ethnocentric one.

Third, relativism. "Judgmental (or epistemological) relativism is anathema to any scientific project" (Harding, 2004: 131). "It is not equally true as its denial that women's uteruses wander around in their bodies when they take math courses, that only Man the Hunter made important contributions to distinctively human history" (Harding, 2004: 131–132). Some locations are scientifically better starting points; this is substantive, not relativist.

Harding's positive synthesis. "Strong objectivity requires that the subject of knowledge be placed on the same critical, causal plane as the objects of knowledge. Thus, strong objectivity requires what we can think of as 'strong reflexivity'" (Harding, 2004: 136). Standard "objectivism" is "not rigorous or objectifying enough"; it eliminates only values differing within the existing community, leaving culturewide assumptions intact. Strong objectivity makes the subject part of the object, and expands the community of inquiry.

Subjects of knowledge are "embodied and visible… multiple, heterogeneous, and contradictory" (Harding, 2004: 132-134). "Men, too, must contribute distinctive forms of specifically feminist knowledge from their particular social situation" (Harding, 2004: 135). Feminism is not the property of women.

Why this rescues. Three points.

First, the standpoint claim is preserved. Marginalised locations still generate privileged resources. Harding embeds the claim in a framework that handles objections.

Second, pluralism is enhanced. Hill Collins's Black feminist standpoint, hooks's oppositional gaze, and Crenshaw's intersectionality are absorbed: "There is no single, ideal woman's life from which standpoint theories recommend that thought start. Instead, one must turn to all of the lives that are marginalized in different ways… The different feminisms inform each other" (Harding, 2004: 131). Black Lives Matter and the Lean In / intersectional contrast are political instances.

Third, Butler's destabilisation is accommodated. Reflexivity turns the subject of knowledge into part of the object; this is Butler's move. "The category of 'women,' the subject of feminism, is produced and restrained by the very structures of power through which emancipation is sought" (Butler, 1990: 2). Strong objectivity is the methodological form of the critical injunction.

Criado-Perez is the empirical verification. The reference man (a Caucasian male, 25-30, around 70kg) is the unreflexive subject of engineering. Crash-test dummies, stab vests, office thermostats, smartphones, Google voice recognition, Apple Health's missing period tracker: each a case where strong objectivity would have produced more accurate engineering. The cost-of-living crisis is a sociological extension: starting from carers (disproportionately women) generates a more accurate policy diagnosis than starting from the reference worker. The L6 broader standpoint apparatus shows the move is not specific to feminism: Haraway's "situated knowledges" and refusal of "the 'God-trick' of speaking authoritatively about everything in the world from no particular location" (Harding, 2004: 4) generalise the principle across post-positivist sociology of science.

So Harding rescues. Standpoint theory was vulnerable in its raw form; strong objectivity defends it. The lecture's framing, that "different standpoints/perspectives" matter and that there is a "duality to experience", is preserved and made operational. (Word count: 720.)

### Mock 15: How does Criado-Perez's account of the gender data gap illustrate Harding's strong objectivity?

Criado-Perez's *Guardian* extract is an extended empirical illustration of exactly what Harding's strong objectivity demands. The reference man is the unreflexive subject of modern engineering; the gender data gap is what strong objectivity, had it been practised, would have prevented. Together the texts give the most operational current statement of standpoint epistemology.

Recall Harding. "Strong objectivity requires that the subject of knowledge be placed on the same critical, causal plane as the objects of knowledge. Thus, strong objectivity requires what we can think of as 'strong reflexivity'" (Harding, 2004: 136). Standard objectivism identifies and eliminates only values that "differ among the researchers and critics who are regarded by the scientific community as competent to make such judgments". Culturewide assumptions are left untouched. Strong objectivity expands the community of inquiry and makes the researcher's standpoint an object of analysis.

Criado-Perez's central claim is that science, engineering and policy operate from an unreflexive male default: "Reference Man… Caucasian men aged 25 to 30, who weigh 70kg. This is 'Reference Man' and his superpower is being able to represent humanity as a whole. Of course, he does not." This is Harding's "God-trick" in engineering clothes.

The empirical specifications.

Crash-test dummies. Until 2011 the US used a 50th-percentile male dummy (1.77m, 76kg). The EU still does not require an anthropometrically female dummy; the "female" dummy used in some tests is "just a scaled-down male dummy". Women are "47% more likely to be seriously injured" and "17% more likely to die" in a comparable crash.

PPE. Body armour and stab vests sized to male bodies. "In 1997, a British female police officer was stabbed and killed" after removing armour to use a hydraulic ram. Another had breast-reduction surgery because of the vest. Dust and eye masks based on a US male face shape do not fit most women, "as well as a lot of black and minority ethnic men".

Office temperature. A 1960s formula calibrated to the male resting metabolic rate "may overestimate female metabolic rate by as much as 35%".

Technology. Smartphones at the upper limit of male hand size. Google speech recognition "70% more likely to accurately recognise male speech". Apple Health launched in 2014 without a period tracker. Siri could find prostitutes and Viagra suppliers but not abortion providers.

Toilets. "50/50 division of floor space has even been formalised in plumbing codes"; women need more time and trips, so formal equality is substantive inequality. Sandi Toksvig's anthropology professor names the conceptual move. Shown an antler bone with 28 markings, a male reading gives "man's first attempt at a calendar"; the female professor reads it as a woman tracking her cycle. Same data, different subjects of knowledge.

Why this is Harding's strong objectivity in action.

First, the reference man is exactly the unreflexive universal subject Harding identifies. He is "embodied and visible" but treated as if "culturally and historically disembodied or invisible" (Harding, 2004: 132). Strong objectivity makes the subject part of the object: once we name Reference Man, the male default becomes analysable.

Second, the corrective is to "start off research from women's lives" (Harding, 2004: 6). A crash-test programme that began from female bodies would have produced cars in which women did not die at 17% higher rates.

Third, the multiplicity Harding requires is present. The dust-mask issue affects "black and minority ethnic men" too; Hill Collins's matrix is implicit. There is no single "reference woman" to substitute; the corrective is plural. Black Lives Matter and the Lean In / Black-intersectional contrast are the political registers of this plural correction.

Fourth, political engagement is met. Harding insists "political engagement, rather than dispassionate neutrality, was necessary" (Harding, 2004: 6). Criado-Perez's work is openly feminist and openly polemical; it produces more accurate findings precisely because politically engaged. #MeToo and post-Roe America are the cultural-political instances where engaged starting points generate better diagnosis.

Hartsock's standpoint is the underlying epistemology, and the L6 standpoint tradition generalises the move: "women's lives differ structurally from those of men" (Hartsock, 1983: 284), and any "marginal lives… provide better grounds for certain kinds of knowledge" (Harding, 2004: 129). Adichie's "I am a feminist" is the political stance; Criado-Perez's data is the empirical pay-off.

So the gender data gap is Harding's strong objectivity made flesh, or rather made bone, dummy, vest, thermostat, smartphone and antler. To start from women's lives is to design better. (Word count: 720.)

### Mock 16: How convincing do you find Butler's argument that "woman" is not a stable category?

Butler's argument is convincing in its core claim (that the category "woman" is produced and restrained by the very structures of power feminism aims to dismantle) but requires reading in a modified form that integrates standpoint and intersectional critique. The destabilisation of "woman" is not an argument against using the category but for using it reflexively.

Recall the argument. *Gender Trouble* (1990) opens: "It is not enough to inquire into how women might become more fully represented in language and politics. Feminist critique ought also to understand how the category of 'women,' the subject of feminism, is produced and restrained by the very structures of power through which emancipation is sought" (Butler, 1990: 2). Gender is performative: constituted through repeated acts that present themselves as always already there. The heterosexual matrix produces "woman" as one of two stable categories; anything not fitting (intersex bodies, trans subjectivities, non-binary identities) is rendered unintelligible. Feminism taking "woman" as a self-evident pre-political subject reproduces the system it claims to challenge.

How convincing? Very, on three counts.

First, the politics of exclusion. Pre-Butler feminism repeatedly failed lesbian, working-class, non-white, trans and intersex women by assuming a default "woman" who was straight, middle-class, white and cis. Black feminism had made the analogous point about race and class (Hill Collins's matrix, Crenshaw's intersectionality). Butler completes the move for gender identity and sexuality. The current trans-rights debates within feminism turn precisely on whether "woman" is a self-evident category. Butler's intervention is the conceptual reason to refuse that move.

Second, the deeper logic of Beauvoir. Beauvoir saw that "humanity is male and man defines woman not in herself but as relative to him" (de Beauvoir, 1949: 6). Butler radicalises: the very binary that produces both is an effect of power. Beauvoir's "one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman" is the seed; Butler's performativity is the full flowering.

Third, the empirical record. First-wave "woman" excluded Black, working-class and colonised women. Second-wave "woman" centred reproductive labour and partly excluded lesbian and child-free women. Butler's argument is the systematic reason why interrogation is permanent.

But the argument faces serious objections.

First, political. If "woman" is unstable, who is the subject of feminist politics? A wholly destabilised category makes the political "we" hard to construct. Adichie's defence of the *word* feminist points the other way: dropping it for "human rights" "would be a way of pretending that it was not women who have, for centuries, been excluded." #MeToo and post-Roe America are political moments where "women" as a category did indispensable work.

Second, epistemological. Standpoint theory requires some description of where the standpoint is located. Hartsock locates women in social reproduction; if "woman" is wholly destabilised, this becomes harder. Harding's synthesis: hold "woman" as strategic, plural, historically located while recognising its constructedness. Strong objectivity is the apparatus.

Third, empirical. Criado-Perez's gender data gap shows the category has hard material effects: women "17% more likely to die" in a comparable crash because of male-default engineering (the reference man); offices freezing because of a 1960s HVAC formula; Apple Health launching without a period tracker. The category is necessary to name these facts. Butler does not deny this; she insists on reflexive use.

Fourth, intersectional. Hill Collins and Crenshaw had already plurialised "woman" in another idiom; Butler converges with them. The Lean In versus Black/intersectional contrast is the political form.

Concrete examples sharpen the assessment. Adichie handles the tension productively. Her dictionary definition is universalising, but her examples (Igbo extended-family meetings, the parking attendant who thanks Louis, the hotel staff who read a woman alone as a sex worker) implicitly hold the category open. The class-monitor case is performativity in the schoolroom: a girl learns that being "female" is what disqualifies her from the role, and the disqualification is the act through which the gendered subject is produced. The L4 work on language gives the linguistic counterpart: Spender's "man-made language" (1980) shows English structured around male-as-norm so that "female" is "minus male"; the instability Butler theorises is therefore not abstract but embedded in everyday speech. "Culture does not make people. People make culture": Butler at the level of practical pedagogy.

So my assessment: very convincing in core, requiring modification at the edges. Butler is best read with Hill Collins's matrix, Crenshaw's intersectionality and Harding's strong objectivity. Together they deliver a defensible contemporary feminism none alone can. (Word count: 720.)

### Mock 17: "Women's labour is essential but their power within society is not" (Hartsock). Discuss with reference to Adichie's *We Should All Be Feminists*.

Hartsock's epigram remains the sharpest one-sentence statement of patriarchy's structural form, and Adichie's *We Should All Be Feminists* (2014), despite its register of personal narrative, is a sustained empirical illustration of exactly the asymmetry Hartsock names. Read together they do the analytic work neither does alone.

Begin with Hartsock. The 1983 essay theorises women's position as dual: essential to the reproduction of social life (care, domestic labour, emotional work, biological reproduction) and yet structurally excluded from the power and recognition that flows from that contribution. "Women's lives differ structurally from those of men" (Hartsock, 1983: 284) is the empirical proposition; the analytic move is that this difference generates standpoint epistemology, a critical vantage unavailable to dominant-group thinkers. The Marxist origin is explicit: as the proletariat's location generated Marx's critique, women's location in social reproduction generates the critique of patriarchal ideology.

Adichie's *We Should All Be Feminists* builds from autobiographical episodes; each is a case study in Hartsock's asymmetry.

The parking-attendant story. Adichie tips a Lagos parking attendant; he says "thank you" to her male friend Louis, not to her, "because Louis is a man". The labour (paid attention, money) comes from Adichie; the recognition flows to Louis. Women's contribution is essential to the social transaction; the register of power runs through the man.

The class-monitor story. Adichie's teacher promised the highest-scoring student would be class monitor; Adichie scored highest but the role went to a boy. "If we do something over and over, it becomes normal", Adichie says: performativity in early form, and a description of how Hartsock's asymmetry is reproduced across generations.

The hotel-lobby story. Adichie enters a Lagos hotel alone; the staff assume she is a sex worker. A single woman in public is legible only through the script of commercial sexual availability. The labour (professional travel) is invisible; the projected meaning is what registers. Beauvoir's woman-as-other (de Beauvoir, 1949: 6) is the structural diagnosis; Adichie supplies the lived datum.

The Igbo extended-family meetings where Adichie cannot have a formal say "because I am female" repeat the pattern. Labour is essential, power is not.

Adichie generalises: "We teach girls to shrink themselves, to make themselves smaller." Socialisation produces a feminine subject essential to social reproduction but trained away from asserting power within it. "Culture does not make people. People make culture": the asymmetry is contingent and contestable.

Criado-Perez is the macro counterpart. Women's bodies and labour are essential to the economy (medical reception, education, retail, care, cleaning, food production, all disproportionately female) but the engineering and policy that shape their working conditions are calibrated to the reference man. Crash-test dummies, stab vests, office thermostats, smartphones, Apple Health's missing period tracker: contribution taken for granted, needs not registered. The cost-of-living crisis sharpens the point: the squeeze on care work, mostly female, is the structural asymmetry intensified.

Three intersectional refinements are needed.

First, the asymmetry is not the same for all women. Hill Collins's matrix of domination shows race, class and other axes intersect. The Black domestic worker's labour is essential to the white professional household; the migrant nanny's to the destination economy. The Black Lives Matter / Lean In contrast captures the political form.

Second, the asymmetry is reproduced across cultural settings. Hall (1980) and Walby (1986) trace its origin to industrial capitalism. Adichie's Lagos episodes show the same asymmetry in postcolonial Nigerian urban life. The L9 postcolonial work cautions against reading Adichie through a Western frame: Mohanty warns that Western feminism produces "the third world woman" as "ignorant, poor, uneducated, tradition-bound, domestic, family-oriented, victimized" (Mohanty, 1984: 261), and Adichie's great-grandmother who "ran away from the house of the man she did not want to marry" is precisely the kind of agent Mohanty's "third world woman" image erases. Hartsock's asymmetry is real; the cultural form is local.

Third, Butler's destabilisation must be folded in. The category "woman" through which Hartsock's epigram operates is itself produced by power; "the category of 'women,' the subject of feminism, is produced and restrained by the very structures of power through which emancipation is sought" (Butler, 1990: 2).

Adichie's defence of the word "feminist" articulates the political stake of Hartsock's epigram. The asymmetry is real and specific to women as a structural category, even as the category is plural. Adichie is the autobiographical proof; Hartsock the analytic theorem; the gender data gap the empirical verification. (Word count: 730.)

---

### Mock 18: Using the work of at least two authors, explain why universalist feminism fails Black women.

Using Hill Collins, Crenshaw and hooks, I argue universalist feminism fails Black women in three connected ways: it misdescribes their experience, mishandles their exclusion from rights regimes, and misidentifies the targets of political action. The corrective is not adding Black voices to an unchanged universalism but starting analysis from a different ground.

"Universalist feminism" takes "woman" as a unified pre-political category whose experiences can be theorised in the singular. The strand is detectable in Wollstonecraft (1792), in much of Beauvoir (1949), and in classic second-wave consciousness-raising. The lecture is explicit that pre-1980s feminism universalised, essentialised, and was ahistorical (neglecting "how white women have benefited from colonialism"). Contemporary "Lean In" feminism is the corporate descendant; the contrast with Black/intersectional feminism is the live political register.

The first failure is descriptive. Hill Collins formulates the alternative: "Black feminist thought consists of ideas produced by Black women that clarify a standpoint of and for Black women" (Hill Collins, 1986: 70). The matrix of domination shows gender does not exist on its own; it is produced through race, class, sexuality and other axes across "structural, disciplinary, hegemonic, and interpersonal domains of power" (Hill Collins). The "woman" of universalist feminism is implicitly white, middle-class, partnered and straight.

The second failure is structural. Crenshaw's intersectionality is "the notion that different types of discrimination intersect and often compound experiences of exclusion and social subjugation." The single-axis frame cannot register compound harms. Black Lives Matter is the contemporary articulation: Black women's harm is intelligible only through the intersection.

The third failure is political. Hill Collins and hooks "both questioned second-wave understandings of the home as a site of repression and subjugation". For Black women under racial terror, the home was also a site of refuge, family, organisation and resistance. The mainstream programme (escape the domestic, enter the public) presupposed the universalist case. hooks's oppositional gaze, "There is power in looking" (hooks, 1992: 115), is the political consequence: Black women looking back.

The convergence is illuminating. Hill Collins gives the architecture (the matrix), Crenshaw the diagnostic (intersectionality), hooks the political indictment. All three propose starting from Black women's lives as methodologically privileged ground. The L8 lineage is decisive: Du Bois's "double consciousness", "this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity" (Du Bois, 1903: 5), is the conceptual ancestor of Hill Collins's "outsider within". Universalist feminism's failure is not just that it omits Black women but that it omits the older Black radical tradition without which the matrix cannot be theorised.

Concrete examples sharpen the argument.

Beauvoir's universalising slide is canonical. "Humanity is male and man defines woman not in herself but as relative to him" (de Beauvoir, 1949: 6) is a real diagnosis, but the "woman" defined is a middle-class white European. "Can she really describe and account for the way in which ALL women have been oppressed all over the world, in every age?" The Black feminist answer is no.

Adichie supplies a non-Black-American case. Her great-grandmother who "ran away from the house of the man she did not want to marry" was a feminist without the word; the academic who told her feminism was "un-African" used a universalising frame to deny her standing.

Criado-Perez. The male face-shape used for dust, hazard and eye masks doesn't fit most women "as well as a lot of black and minority ethnic men". The universalist frame catches part of the harm; the matrix catches the rest.

Post-Roe America makes the political point empirically: restrictions on reproductive control fall hardest on poor Black women, where intersectional analysis predicts. Social media activism around Black Lives Matter has done the corrective work universalist feminism missed.

Harding's directive, "There is no single, ideal woman's life from which standpoint theories recommend that thought start. Instead, one must turn to all of the lives that are marginalized in different ways" (Harding, 2004: 131), is the methodological synthesis. Universalist feminism cannot meet this without ceasing to be universalist.

So universalist feminism fails Black women descriptively, structurally and politically. The corrective, supplied by Hill Collins, Crenshaw and hooks together, is a feminism that begins from Black women's lives and treats the matrix of domination as the architectural truth of how power operates. (Word count: 720.)

---

### Mock 19: Can feminism survive without a universal subject?

Feminism can survive, and must, without a universal subject in the metaphysical sense, while retaining "woman" as a strategic, plural, operational category. The death of the universal subject of pre-1980s feminism is not the death of feminism but its maturation. Harding's strong objectivity supplies the synthesis; Hill Collins, Crenshaw, hooks, Butler and Adichie converge on it from different directions.

Begin with what is dead. The universal subject of first-wave and early second-wave feminism has been progressively dismantled. Hill Collins's matrix of domination shows gender is always co-produced with race and class ("'Race'… is equally important, if not more important, than 'gender'… we can't think gender without thinking 'race'"). Crenshaw's intersectionality formalises the diagnostic. hooks rewrites the home as a site of resistance. Butler destabilises "woman": "the category of 'women,' the subject of feminism, is produced and restrained by the very structures of power through which emancipation is sought" (Butler, 1990: 2). The universal subject in the strong sense is gone.

Does feminism die with it? Three positions.

One: pure pluralism. No "feminism", only feminisms. Strength: descriptive accuracy. Weakness: political. If "woman" is wholly destabilised, the subject of any structural diagnosis disappears. Criado-Perez's claim that women are "47% more likely to be seriously injured" in a comparable crash presupposes a working category "women".

Two: tactical universalism. Retain "woman" strategically, knowing it is constructed. Butler holds something like this. Adichie's defence: dropping "feminist" for "human rights" "would be a way of pretending that it was not women who have, for centuries, been excluded."

Three: Harding's synthesis. "There is no single, ideal woman's life from which standpoint theories recommend that thought start. Instead, one must turn to all of the lives that are marginalized in different ways… The different feminisms inform each other" (Harding, 2004: 131). The unity is in the *practice*, not in a prior subject. This is the position I defend.

Five reasons feminism survives.

First, structural patterns persist and require naming. Criado-Perez: crash-test dummies leave women "47% more likely to be seriously injured"; office thermostats "five degrees too cold"; Apple Health launched without a period tracker. These facts hold for women as such across race and class.

Second, the political "we" can be operational without being metaphysical. Adichie's "I am a feminist" and "All of us, women and men, must do better" use the category as a tool. #MeToo, Black Lives Matter, post-Roe America and the Iran women-life-freedom protests all use the singular to coordinate plural standpoints.

Third, the analytic categories survive without the subject. Patriarchy, the public/private split (Hall, 1980; Walby, 1986), the matrix of domination, intersectionality, performativity, the personal is political, the reference man, the oppositional gaze: none requires a unified prior subject. The L10 vision material confirms this: Mulvey's male gaze (1975) and hooks's oppositional gaze (hooks, 1992: 116) name structural relations of looking that operate regardless of whether "woman" is metaphysically stable. The structures are there to be analysed; the subject is plural in practice.

Fourth, the descriptive plural strengthens the political singular. Hill Collins's "ideas produced by Black women that clarify a standpoint of and for Black women" (Hill Collins, 1986: 70) is a Black feminist standpoint *and* a contribution to feminism in the singular. The contrast between Lean In feminism and Black/intersectional feminism is the productive form of this dialectic.

Fifth, Butler's own continued use of "feminism" demonstrates the position's coherence. The most-cited destabiliser of the unified subject continues to write feminist theory under that name.

Concrete examples. Adichie mobilises "feminist" openly while attending to Igbo specificity. Her brother Kene is "the best feminist I know", illustrating Harding's point: "Men, too, must contribute distinctive forms of specifically feminist knowledge from their particular social situation" (Harding, 2004: 135). The great-grandmother who "did not know that word *feminist*. But it doesn't mean she wasn't one" applies the strategic singular retrospectively.

A critic might object that strategic universalism is universalism in retreat. The reply: strategic is reflexive (held under interrogation), plural (accommodating different positions), and revisable. Universalism had none of these.

So: yes, feminism can survive, and is flourishing, without a universal subject in the metaphysical sense. The condition is Harding's synthesis: unity in practice rather than in subject, plurality of standpoints, strategic use of "woman" as a category whose construction is part of feminism's object. The death of the metaphysical universal subject is the maturation of feminism. (Word count: 720.)
