These techniques generalise across institutional sites and produce the closure named on Slide 17: "If power shouted at us all the time we would notice it. Rather, it invites and incites us to behave in certain ways. We discipline ourselves! We self-regulate!" The disciplinary apparatus is most efficient when it is invisible, when the subject monitors herself against norms she experiences as her own.

Bordo extends the productive thesis at the level of gendered embodiment. The slender, well-toned body is not coerced; it is produced through the magazine, the mirror, the gym, the fitness tracker, and the social media feed. Bordo's clinching formulation gives the contemporary scene: "the chasm that produces bodies habituated to self-monitoring and self-normalization" (Bordo, 1992: 202-3). The City of London worker at the gym, working out to "show you mean business" (Slide 28), is the productive thesis enacted as personal aspiration.

Counter-argument and conclusion. The productive thesis can be pushed too far. If everything is produced by power, the analysis risks losing the distinction between produced and coerced, between disciplined and dominated. Slide 8's Damiens execution reminds us that sovereign power has not vanished, and L8's analyses of stop-and-search and immigration enforcement show that the visibly coercive register persists. The right reading: the productive thesis names what is distinctive about modern power without exhausting all of contemporary power. What disciplinary power produces is the docile, self-regulating subject of contemporary capitalism. The bourgeoisie may not have entirely won, but the apparatus the lecture names is the political form in which contemporary life is lived.

[~736 words]

### M4: Is the panopticon a model of modernity? Discuss with reference to hierarchical observation, the formation of the conscience of the inmate, and the link between power, visibility, vision and knowledge.

The question is the title of Slide 15, and the lecture answers it in three connected moves: the panopticon is an ideal of a prison; it is also a diagram that generalises across institutions; and it makes power, visibility, and knowledge inseparable in a way that defines modernity. My thesis: yes, the panopticon is a model of modernity, but a particular kind, a diagram rather than a literal architecture, and reading it as a diagram lets us see how disciplinary surveillance has migrated from the cell to the schoolroom, the clinic, the gym, and the algorithmic feed.

The original setting first. Bentham designed the panopticon as an ideal prison: a central watchtower with a light shining out into back-lit cells (Slide 14). Inmates are continuously visible to the supervisor but cannot see into the tower. The architecture produces asymmetric visibility: "in the peripheric ring, one is totally seen, without ever seeing; in the central tower, one sees everything without ever being seen" (Foucault, 1977: 316 in Calhoun reader). Because the inmate cannot verify when she is being watched, she behaves as if continuously observed. The tower can be empty; the apparatus still works.

Slide 15 names the productive effect. "The panopticon encourages the prisoner to behave as if they are continually under surveillance. They begin to inspect or monitor their own behaviour. This opens up an interiority into which both the prison guard and the inmate can look. The Panopticon is where the exercise of power produces the formation of the conscience of the inmate." This is the lecture's strongest formulation of the productive thesis at the level of subjectivity. The panopticon does not just observe a pre-existing conscience; it forms the conscience the inmate then experiences as her own. Power is linked to visibility, to vision, and to knowledge in a single apparatus.

Why does this make the panopticon a model of modernity rather than a model of prisons? Because the diagram travels. The same cellular logic, Foucault notes, can house "a madman, a patient, a condemned man, a worker or a schoolboy" (Foucault, 1977: 314 in Calhoun reader). Slide 10's school is the paradigmatic case without an architectural tower. The "registers, progress reports, school photos, records of achievement, testing, key stages" produce the same panoptic effect through a distributed apparatus of paperwork. Lynch's transcript, "this will go on your permanent record," compresses the diagram into a single sentence (Lynch, 2011: 13-14). The hospital ward, the factory floor, and the barracks all instantiate the diagram. Foucault calls this "an indefinitely generalizable mechanism of panopticism" (Foucault, 1977: 316 in Calhoun reader).

Contemporary scenes update the diagram without abandoning its structure. CCTV networks in public spaces, facial recognition at airports, social media follower counts, fitness tracker dashboards, and HR performance reviews all produce asymmetric visibility, unverifiability, and internalisation. The Instagram filter is panoptic without a literal tower: the camera produces a self that knows it might be watched and behaves accordingly. Bordo's analysis (Slides 25-32) shows the bathroom mirror functioning as the tower, with the woman becoming both watcher and watched, and the slender norm supplying the unverifiable standard. A *Black Mirror* episode in which everyone rates everyone else makes the diagram cultural.

A cross-link with L10's analyses of vision sharpens the point. Berger's claim that "men look at women; women watch themselves being looked at" (Berger, 1972: 47) and Mulvey's male gaze (Mulvey, 1975: 11) describe panoptic structures of vision before Foucault named them. The same disciplinary diagram organises both the prison cell and the cinema screen. Visibility is not neutral; it is organised by relations of power, and those relations produce subjects who watch themselves in the act of being watched.

Counter-argument and conclusion. The panopticon is not the only diagram of modern power. Biopolitical injunctions (Slide 24's salt, 5-a-day, anti-obesity policy) target the population statistically, not the individual cell, and the panoptic figure is the wrong tool for the population aggregate. Sovereign power still operates (Slide 8) where the state visibly seizes bodies. Lynch warns that theory should not "answer everything" (Lynch, 2011: 15). Yet within its proper scope, the panopticon is the right diagram for the disciplinary mode of modernity. Where asymmetric visibility, unverifiability, and self-regulating internalisation are in play (the school, the body, the clinic, the algorithmic feed), the panopticon names the contemporary apparatus precisely. As a diagram, not as a building, it remains a model of modernity.

[~732 words]

### M5: "Am I different from the rest? Is everyone like me?" How does normalising judgement combine with hierarchical observation and the examination to produce the three aspects of discipline?

The questions on Slide 21 sit at the heart of the lecture's analysis of contemporary subjectivity. "Am I different from the rest? Is everyone like me? Am I a good friend?" The lecturer notes that this is why questionnaires are everywhere. My thesis is that these are not innocent questions but the operating noises of normalising judgement, the third and decisive aspect of disciplinary power, and that read with hierarchical observation and the examination they describe the complete mechanism through which disciplinary society produces the self-regulating subject.

The three aspects of discipline are introduced across Slides 19 and 21. Hierarchical observation comes first. Observers "inspect from a distance and are themselves unobserved and are not judged" (Slide 19). The asymmetry is the point: I can be watched without being able to verify when, and the watcher remains invisible to me. The examination comes second: "where we are tested, where we are checked to see how we fit in with the rest. To see how far we fit in with or deviate from the Norm." Normalising judgement is third and most important. Slide 21 makes the historical claim sharply: "Previous forms of discipline simply stated what was forbidden and what was allowed. The revolution in the development of disciplinary society is that it introduces the idea of what is normal."

This is why Slide 22 asks the polemical question: "Is the concept of the normal one of the most insidious of all concepts of modernity?" The lecturer's answer is yes, and the reason is the double effect Slide 21 describes. Disciplinary society "operates both by making us homogenized, we must all conform to norms, to the normal," and by "making us take on responsibility as individuals for matching up to norms." The norm is not just an external standard; we are made responsible for our own conformity to it. The chasm Bordo names is exactly this gap: "media images of self-containment and self-mastery and the reality of constant everyday stress" produce "bodies habituated to self-monitoring and self-normalization" (Bordo, 1992: 202-3).

The three aspects fit together as a single machine. Hierarchical observation produces visibility; normalising judgement produces a standard against which the visible can be evaluated; the examination produces a documented combination of the two. The school is the lecture's paradigm. Registers monitor attendance, progress reports measure against age-appropriate norms, school photos and records of achievement document the combination, key-stage testing examines under controlled conditions (Slide 10). Each instrument simultaneously knows the child and disciplines her. The pupil is observed, judged against the normal, and examined in documents that follow her through life.

Slide 21's questionnaires extend the mechanism into adult life. "Am I different from the rest?" is the self-administered version of the examination. "Is everyone like me?" is the self-administered hierarchical observation. "Am I a good friend?" is the self-administered normalising judgement. The questionnaire is the disciplinary apparatus internalised. Today's BuzzFeed personality quizzes, mental-health self-screening apps, ADHD checklists, and social media self-presentation extend the form. We measure ourselves against invented standards we experience as our own.

Bordo's body norms make the mechanism concrete. Hierarchical observation: the magazine, the mirror, the peer, the City colleague (Slide 28). Normalising judgement: the slender, well-toned body as the standard against which deviation registers as failure ("being fat is equated with being lazy. Of not caring. Of being a failure", Slide 28). Examination: the bathroom scale, the calorie count, the dressing-room verdict, the weekly step total. The mirror reads the self into the norm; the scale documents the result. Slide 32 names the productive closure: "we have to produce ourselves as normal individuals, in control of ourselves."

Counter-argument and conclusion. Two qualifications. First, the three aspects do not exhaust all power. Biopolitical norms target the population through statistical aggregates (Slide 24), and sovereign power still seizes bodies visibly (Slide 8). Second, normalising judgement is contested. Bordo's diachronic move (Slide 25) shows that today's slender norm is no more natural than 1880's plump norm, and Lynch insists that "power relations can always be altered" (Lynch, 2011: 25). Body-positivity movements and contestations of ADHD diagnosis demonstrate contemporary resistance. Yet on balance, the three aspects of discipline name the contemporary apparatus precisely. The questionnaire's questions are not innocent; they are the everyday voice of normalising judgement, and asking them is how we participate in our own discipline.

[~719 words]

### M6: "It is our duty to keep ourselves healthy." What power mechanisms help support such a statement, and how does the consumer-culture imperative that we "produce ourselves as normal individuals, in control of ourselves" extend Foucault's analysis from disciplinary to biopolitical power?

Slide 24 poses the lecture's sharpest question about the biopolitical register. "It is our duty to keep ourselves healthy. This may seem obvious but what power mechanisms help support such a statement?" The lecturer gives three examples: "it is the duty of government to make us reduce our salt level"; "we feel bad if we do not eat 5 portions of fruit/veg per day"; "the government must stop obese children." My thesis is that this duty looks obvious only because we live inside a biopolitical regime that produces it, that the consumer-culture imperative on Slide 32 extends the disciplinary individual body into the biopolitical population, and that reading Slides 24 and 32 together gives us the lecture's clearest diagnosis of contemporary self-government.

The duty unpacked first. None of Slide 24's mechanisms target an individual through coercion. The salt-reduction target acts on the population's aggregate sodium intake; the 5-a-day campaign moralises a dietary norm whose felt failure registers as personal moral failure; the anti-childhood-obesity policy targets a cohort. This is biopower in the sense Lynch describes: power that "does not directly address particular individuals, but rather groups of people and populations as a whole" (Lynch, 2011: 14). Its rationality is "to save lives" by acting on aggregates. The modern police force, Slide 37 reminds us, was instituted not only for law and order but "for assuring urban supplies, hygiene, health" (Foucault, 1982: 215). The biopolitical genealogy is as old as modern urban government.

What is distinctive about contemporary biopolitical injunctions is that they reach into individual conduct as duties. "It is our duty to keep ourselves healthy" frames a population-level rationality as personal moral obligation. We are not coerced into eating five portions of fruit and vegetables; we feel bad if we do not. The felt failure is the apparatus. Government salt-reduction targets work not principally through compulsion of manufacturers but through self-monitoring of consumers who read labels and adjust their intake. Pandemic contact-tracing apps, COVID-era mask mandates, and vaccination drives extend the same logic: population-level rationalities are taken up as personal duties.

Slide 32 completes the picture. "We live in a consumer society, one which runs on us drinking coffee, eating cakes, take-away food etc. But we have to produce ourselves as normal individuals, in control of ourselves, and this means being in control of our bodies." The biopolitical regime sits inside a consumer culture that incites consumption and demands self-mastery simultaneously. The injunction is contradictory: eat the cake and stay slender. Bordo's chasm names exactly this gap. "Self-management in consumer culture becomes more elusive as it becomes more pressing... lies the chasm that produces bodies habituated to self-monitoring and self-normalization" (Bordo, 1992: 202-3). The duty is biopolitical (acting on the population's health) and disciplinary (acting on individual bodies) at once.

Fitness trackers, calorie-counting apps, and smartwatch step-counters automate the regime. They individualise the biopolitical norm: the population-level recommendation to walk 10,000 steps per day becomes the individual's daily target on her wrist. The cohort recommendation to consume less sugar becomes the individual's pre-meal app entry. The disciplinary individual body and the biopolitical population are governed through the same digital apparatus. Where the public-health director once acted on the population, the individual now self-administers the same rationality.

A cross-link with L8 sharpens the point. Race is one of biopower's paradigmatic objects, and pandemic-era disparities in COVID outcomes by ethnicity show biopolitical injunctions falling unevenly on differently positioned populations. Du Bois's "double consciousness" (Du Bois, 1903: 8) names the embodied experience of being folded into the population as both managed object and excluded interiority. Biopolitics is racial from its origins.

Counter-argument and conclusion. The risk is over-generalisation: if everything is biopolitical, the concept loses discriminating power. Lynch warns against using theory to "answer everything" (Lynch, 2011: 15). Sovereign power persists (Slide 8 the Damiens trace), disciplinary power on individual bodies operates alongside biopolitical norms (the school combines registers and 5-a-day), and biopolitical injunctions are resisted (anti-vaccine politics, fat-acceptance movements). Yet on balance, the duty Slide 24 names is biopolitical in form and disciplinary in execution. The salt label is the biopolitical state speaking to the disciplinary subject through the consumer aisle. The duty is real because it has been produced.

[~699 words]

### M7: How does Bordo's analysis of the slender body and Butler's account of power forming the subject together extend Foucault's notion of disciplinary power?

Slide 32 closes the lecture's body sequence with the lecturer's clearest invitation to read Bordo with Foucault. "Power operates more subtly but more closely in the regulation of women's bodies with regard to normalising judgements. Foucault's work on power can help us understand this situation better." Slide 12 supplies the parallel invitation for Butler: power is "what we depend on for our existence and what we harbour and preserve in the beings that we are" (Butler, 1997: 1-2). My thesis: Bordo gives Foucault the gendered specification he did not develop, Butler radicalises the productive thesis at the level of subject formation, and reading them together is reading Foucault at full strength.

Bordo first. Slides 25-32 trace her argument in three moves. The diachronic move (Slide 25) historicises body norms: in the late nineteenth century, plumpness signalled male success, muscle signalled working-class status, and pale skin signalled women's exemption from fieldwork. The norms have inverted, but the form persists. Slide 27 tracks the contemporary scene: "30 years ago we were concerned with weight... encouraged to diet, fight the flab. Nowadays, we have to be slender. Adverts talk of being in trim, well-toned, well-defined." Body parts are framed "in revolt", thighs, stomach, upper arms, calves. The gendered specification (Slide 28): "more demands are made on women than men in terms of producing themselves as normal." The self-regulatory closure (Slide 29): "the chasm that produces bodies habituated to self-monitoring and self-normalization" (Bordo, 1992: 202-3).

What does Bordo add to Foucault? Foucault's three aspects of discipline (Slides 19, 21) were relatively gender-neutral. Bordo applies them to bodies with feminist precision. Hierarchical observation: the magazine, the mirror, the advertising image, the peer group, the Instagram feed. Normalising judgement: the slender, well-toned norm as the standard against which deviation registers as moral failing. The examination: the scale, the calorie count, the dressing-room verdict, the gym-mirror appraisal. Foucault's apparatus is filled in with the gendered content the lecture endorses. As Slide 32 puts it, Foucault's work helps "us understand this situation better/more accurately."

Butler second. Slide 12 cites *The Psychic Life of Power*: "We are used to thinking of power as what presses on the subject from the outside... But if we understand power as *forming* the subject as well as providing the very condition of its existence... then power is not simply what we oppose, but also, in a strong sense, what we depend on for our existence and what we harbour and preserve in the beings that we are" (Butler, 1997: 1-2). Foucault on Slide 18 says power "makes individuals subjects" (Foucault, 1982: 212); Butler radicalises the claim. There is no pre-power subject who resists disciplinary normalisation; the subject is itself a product of the apparatus.

What does Butler add to Foucault? She makes resistance immanent. If power forms the subject, the subject of feminist resistance is itself produced by power, and resistance cannot stand on an authentic pre-disciplinary self. This complicates the politics: there is no return to an untouched body or untouched gender. But it opens a more honest politics of immanent contestation. Bordo's diachronic historicisation is exactly this: showing that today's slender norm is no more natural than 1880's plump one denaturalises the present without claiming an outside.

Reading them together. The contemporary scene is both Bordoian and Butlerian. The Instagram filter is Bordoian (disciplinary observation against a norm) and Butlerian (constitution of the photographed self through filtering). The fitness tracker is Bordoian (self-monitoring against a daily target) and Butlerian (formation of the kind of person whose worth is tracked numerically). A cross-link with L5 sharpens the point: Butler's earlier *Gender Trouble* describes gender as a "stylized repetition of acts" (Butler, 1990: 25), so the disciplinary norms Bordo describes do not regulate a pre-existing gender but constitute it through citational performance.

Counter-argument and conclusion. The risk of pushing the productive thesis is that agency disappears. If power forms the subject, what grounds resistance? Lynch's reading helps: "to understand subjectivity as constituted (in part) through power relations is not to deny that subjects can act intentionally" (Lynch, 2011: 24). Bordo's historicisation and Butler's immanent contestation are agency at the disciplinary scale. Verdict: reading Foucault without Bordo loses the gendered specification; reading Foucault without Butler loses the radical productive thesis. Together they give the lecture's most powerful contemporary diagnosis: the disciplinary subject is produced through gendered norms she experiences as her own.

[~728 words]

### M8 (was Mock Q1, quote-driven): "Visibility is a trap." Discuss with reference to Foucault.

"Visibility is a trap" (Foucault, 1977: 315 in Calhoun reader) appears as Foucault unpacks Bentham's panopticon. The trap is not that the inmate is seen (sovereign power saw bodies too, in the spectacle of the scaffold) but that the inmate is visible while the watcher is invisible, so the inmate behaves as if continuously observed even when no one is in the tower. The line is a compressed theory of disciplinary power; taking it seriously means tracking the trap through the panopticon, nineteenth-century institutions, Bordo's gendered body, and the ultrasound that opens the lecture.

First, the original setting. The diagram induces "in the inmate a state of conscious and permanent visibility that assures the automatic functioning of power" (Foucault, 1977: 315 in Calhoun reader). The trap has three components: asymmetric visibility ("in the peripheric ring, one is totally seen, without ever seeing; in the central tower, one sees everything without ever being seen", Foucault, 1977: 316 in Calhoun reader), unverifiability ("the inmate must never know whether he is being looked at... but he must be sure that he may always be so", Foucault, 1977: 315 in Calhoun reader), and internalisation (the inmate becomes her own watcher). The trap shuts when she self-regulates; the central tower can be empty.

Second, the institutional generalisation. The panoptic logic is "an indefinitely generalizable mechanism" (Foucault, 1977: 316 in Calhoun reader). The school register, progress report, photo, key-stage test (Slide 10) all share the structure. Lynch's transcript ("this will go on your permanent record") is the panoptic trap in compressed form (Lynch, 2011: 13-14). The cell can hold "a madman, a patient, a condemned man, a worker or a schoolboy" (Foucault, 1977: 314 in Calhoun reader). CCTV in shopping streets and facial recognition at airports extend the diagram into public space.

Third, the body. Bordo shows the trap is gendered and extends into everyday self-relation. Norms of slenderness and tone turn the bathroom mirror into a tower. "Bodies habituated to self-monitoring and self-normalization" (Bordo, 1992: 202-3) are the trap closed at the level of selfhood. The City-of-London gym (Slide 28), where one works out "to show you 'mean business'", is the trap in contemporary form: no foreman watches, but the subject behaves as if inspected. Bordo's diachronic move sharpens the diagnosis: the trap operated differently when plumpness signalled male success and pale skin signalled women's exemption from fieldwork (Slide 25), but the structure was the same. Fitness trackers and Instagram bodies update it again.

Fourth, the clinical scene. Kember's ultrasound is the panoptic illustration: "the scanning process eliminates the mother's body from view and the doctor has direct access to the image of the foetus" (Kember, 1998). The clinical gaze is asymmetric, unverifiable, and produces self-monitoring antenatal conduct. The trap is exactly what ideology critique misses: "it is both much more and much less than ideology" (Foucault, 1980: 102).

Fifth, the limits. The trap does not exhaust all power. Sovereign power, the Damiens execution (Slide 8), still operates wherever the state visibly seizes bodies. Biopower, Slide 24's salt and 5-a-day injunctions, acts on populations rather than individual cells. Where the field is statistical, the panoptic trap is the wrong diagram. Lynch: theory should not "answer everything" (Lynch, 2011: 15).

Sixth, the politics. The trap captures the productive character of disciplinary power: it does not just constrain, it makes subjects. The school produces the pupil, the prison the prisoner (Slide 13), the gym the well-toned body. Butler sharpens the productive thesis: power is "what we depend on for our existence" (Butler, 1997: 1-2). L10's vision theorists extend the same diagnosis into other registers: Berger's claim that "men look at women; women watch themselves being looked at" (Berger, 1972: 47) and Mulvey's "male gaze" (Mulvey, 1975: 11) name a gendered panopticism that operates without a literal tower. The weakness: if every visibility is a trap, even reciprocal visibility, we lose the distinction between accountability of power and surveillance of the powerless. A *Black Mirror* episode where everyone rates everyone else makes the point: shared visibility is not always panoptic, but sometimes is.

"Visibility is a trap" is correct as a description of the disciplinary mode, indispensable as a diagnosis of self-regulation, and incomplete as a complete theory of contemporary observation. Read alongside Bordo and Kember, the trap remains one of the most useful images in social theory.

### M9 (was Mock Q2, named-work): Critically assess Foucault's argument in *Discipline and Punish*.

*Discipline and Punish* (Foucault, 1977) makes a historical claim (Western societies shifted from sovereign to disciplinary power over the long nineteenth century) and a diagnostic claim (the prison's techniques, articulated in the panopticon, became "an indefinitely generalizable mechanism of 'panopticism'" running through schools, hospitals, factories, and the army (Foucault, 1977: 316 in Calhoun reader)).

I argue the book is convincing at the level of technique, partially vindicated at the level of subjectivity, and deliberately incomplete at the level of political economy, which Foucault brackets in favour of analytic precision.

Vindication at the level of technique. The school operationalises the three aspects of discipline with paradigmatic clarity. Registers, progress reports, photos, records of achievement, testing, and key stages (Slide 10) instantiate hierarchical observation (asymmetric invisibility), normalising judgement (deviations flagged), and the examination (the documented combination). The same cellular arrangement holds "a madman, a patient, a condemned man, a worker or a schoolboy" (Foucault, 1977: 314 in Calhoun reader). The panopticon is a diagram, not a building.

Lynch captures the same logic compactly. The transcript "begins from observation at the bottom of the pyramid, not from an edict from the top" (Lynch, 2011: 15); "this will go on your permanent record" works because "each one is observed" (Lynch, 2011: 16). Power has its principle "not so much in a person as in a certain concerted distribution of bodies, surfaces, lights, gazes" (Foucault, 1977: 316 in Calhoun reader). The "physics of power" is recognisable wherever observation, normalisation, and examination combine, from school exams to HR performance reviews to fitness-app dashboards.

Vindication of the productive thesis. Slide 13: nineteenth-century institutions produced "new kinds of people (new kinds of subjects)". The modern prisoner, schoolchild, and psychiatric patient are produced by their institutions, not caught by them. Butler extends the thesis to the subject as such: "we understand power as *forming* the subject as well as providing the very condition of its existence" (Butler, 1997: 1-2). Bordo extends it to gender: the slender, well-toned body is produced by mirror, magazine, gym, and self-talk (Bordo, 1992; Slide 28).

Strain at the level of subjectivity. *Discipline and Punish* assumes a unified subject then examined. Butler's *Psychic Life of Power* (Slide 12) pushes further: power constitutes the subject as such, so resistance cannot stand on a pre-power self. The strain is productive: it forces the reader to think about subject formation more carefully than the early framework demands.

Brackets at the level of political economy. Foucault deliberately brackets "who benefits?" to ask "how does it work?" Slide 23 hints at the cost: docile bodies "fit well into the modern capitalist economy and work well in factories and offices. They question little and behave well. And don't resist. Let alone revolt. The bourgeoisie has won!" The disciplinary apparatus serves capital, so the *how* analysis needs pairing with a Marxist *for whom*. Slide 36 frames Foucault's reply: "Power in Western capitalism was denounced by the Marxists as class domination; but the mechanics of power themselves were never analysed" (Foucault, 1980: 116). The right reading is complementarity, not rivalry. Cost-of-living and gig-economy precarity make the point: disciplinary analysis without capital is incomplete.

Three further considerations. First, the productive register: Slide 37's police-genealogy quote reminds us discipline also "assures urban supplies, hygiene, health" (Foucault, 1982: 215); it produces useful populations, opening onto biopolitics. Second, resistance: Foucault insists "where there is power, there is resistance" (Foucault, 1978: 95), and Lynch reinforces it (Lynch, 2011: 25). Third, gender: Bordo shows disciplinary norms bear more heavily on women's bodies (Slide 28), a specification *Discipline and Punish* did not develop.

A further genealogical strength is worth noting. Halewood's critique of modern thought as organised through bifurcations (Halewood, 2014: 36) clarifies what Foucault is doing methodologically: *Discipline and Punish* dismantles the very dyads (sovereign/disciplinary, normal/abnormal, observer/observed, mind/body) on which earlier accounts of power relied, and shows them as historical products of specific institutional practices rather than natural kinds. Reading L7 alongside L1 makes Foucault's anti-essentialism intelligible as a sustained refusal of fixed sociological categories.

My verdict: *Discipline and Punish* names what is happening with unique precision in the school, prison, hospital, army, clinic, and body. It is convincing at the level of technique and productive subject formation; deliberately incomplete at the level of political economy; and benefits from being read alongside Bordo and Butler. Foucault gives us the anatomy; the structural critique remains the necessary supplement.

### M10 (was Mock Q3, two-part): What does Foucault mean by power/knowledge, and why does he treat the two as inseparable?

Part one: what does Foucault mean by power/knowledge? The hyphen carries the argument. By power/knowledge Foucault means the production of human-scientific knowledge (psychiatric, pedagogical, clinical, demographic) is itself a power operation, and the exercise of power on bodies and populations cannot proceed without producing knowledge about them. Slide 3: the ultrasound "raises the question of power and its relation to knowledge." Slide 15: in the panopticon "power is linked to visibility and vision and to knowledge." Foucault: this power "imposes a law of truth on him which he must recognize... It is a form of power which makes individuals subjects" (Foucault, 1982: 212).

Part two: why are they inseparable? Three reasons.

(i) Bodies cannot be disciplined without being known. The school cannot train pupils without "registers, progress reports, school photos, records of achievement, testing, key stages" (Slide 10); each is a knowledge instrument and a disciplinary instrument simultaneously. Lynch's transcript is "the record of a student's courses and performance" and an "instrument of power" in the same artefact (Lynch, 2011: 13-14). The hospital cannot treat without the chart; the panopticon "opens up an interiority into which both the prison guard and the inmate can 'look'" (Slide 15).

(ii) Knowledge in the human sciences cannot proceed without observed, classified, normalised subjects. Slide 13: nineteenth-century institutions produced both new knowledges and "new kinds of people". Criminology required prisons; clinical medicine required clinics; pedagogy required schools. The object of human-scientific knowledge is produced by the practices that claim to describe it.

(iii) The truths produced are not false in the Marxist ideology sense. Slide 5: "It is both much more and much less than ideology" (Foucault, 1980: 102). Slide 10: power "points out what is normal and invites us to behave in a similar way, to judge ourselves in relation to this 'norm'." Truth has a history and a politics, not because fake but because produced.

Why does this matter? Because it dissolves the Enlightenment picture in which knowledge is a neutral mirror of nature and power is what obscures or applies it. Foucault is not saying all truth is power, only that the human sciences cannot be cleanly separated from the institutions that produced them. Haraway's notion of "situated knowledges" (Haraway, 1988: 581) sharpens this in a different register: knowledge is always knowledge from somewhere, and the disembodied "god-trick" of objective vision is itself a power-effect.

Examples. The Kember scan is the canonical case: a knowledge artefact (image of the foetus) and a power artefact (maternal body displaced) in the same clinical encounter. "The scanning process eliminates the mother's body from view and the doctor has direct access to the image of the foetus" (Kember, 1998). Slide 4: is it good that doctors visualise the foetus? Could this make the woman seem unimportant? Both answers "could be 'yes'".

Bordo's body norms are power/knowledge in another register. The slender, well-toned body that "means business" (Slide 28) is the product of magazines, advertising, dietary science, and self-help, all knowledge regimes producing bodies and invalidating others. Slide 22 names the effect: is "the normal" one of "the most insidious of all concepts of modernity"? Contemporary BMI categories, calorie counts, and step-targets repeat the logic.

Slide 18 supplies the gathering quote: power "categorizes the individual, marks him by his own individuality, attaches him to his identity, imposes a law of truth on him which he must recognize and which others must recognize in him. It is a form of power which makes individuals subjects" (Foucault, 1982: 212). Knowledge of the individual and power over the individual are produced together.

The inseparability is essential to the politics. If knowledge were neutral, critique could appeal to "the science"; if power were merely repressive, resistance could appeal to "the truth". Power/knowledge denies both shortcuts. Critique has to engage with how knowledge is produced and what it does, simultaneously. ChatGPT-generated content circulating as authoritative knowledge is a recent illustration: the same artefact is both a knowledge-claim and a power-effect.

Conclusion: power/knowledge is inseparable by historical analysis, not by definition. The thesis applies most cleanly to the human sciences. Regimes of truth can still be better or worse; Foucault was not a strong relativist. The Kember scan, the school's testing regime, and Bordo's body norms each show the inseparability in action, and the analysis is reactivated every time a new diagnostic category, an examination, or a body ideal is introduced.

### M11 (was Mock Q4, specific-comparison): Compare Foucault's account of disciplinary power with Marx's account of ideology.

This essay compares Marx's ideology (Slide 35) and Foucault's disciplinary power (*Discipline and Punish*, 1977). They operate at different registers and are best used together.

Marx's ideology. Slide 35: "Power is solely related to the ownership of the means of production"; "Power is in the hands of a small, wealthy minority"; "Ideology is one main tool by which power is exercised over the working-class"; "The proletariat need to 'discover' their own power." Ideology is class domination in the realm of ideas: workers share the worldview of the ruling class, exploitation is obscured, socialism's political work is to dispel that obscuring through revolutionary consciousness.

Foucault's disciplinary power. The repressive picture (power as constraint exercised by a ruling group on subordinates) misses what is distinctive about modern power. Disciplinary power operates not through cognition but through bodies: timetable, spatial partition, examination, hierarchical observation, normalising judgement (Slides 19, 21). It produces docile bodies (Slide 23). The schoolchild, soldier, patient, worker, prisoner are all docile bodies; the cell holds "a madman, a patient, a condemned man, a worker or a schoolboy" (Foucault, 1977: 314 in Calhoun reader). Disciplinary power does not need workers to believe in capitalism; it needs them to arrive on time, follow procedure, submit to examination. Power "is both much more and much less than ideology" (Foucault, 1980: 102).

Convergences. Both insist that apparent free choice is heavily structured; both reject liberal autonomy; both link subject formation to historically specific institutions. Slide 23 holds both in view: docile bodies "fit well into the modern capitalist economy... The bourgeoisie has won!"

Four differences. First, the register: ideology operates on consciousness, disciplinary power on bodies. The pupil need not believe in the key-stage test; she must sit it. Second, the location: ideology is concentrated in apparatuses controlled by the ruling class; disciplinary power is capillary and "always already there" (Foucault, 1980, cited in Lynch, 2011: 19). Foucault: "Power in Western capitalism was denounced by the Marxists as class domination; but the mechanics of power themselves were never analysed" (Foucault, 1980: 116; Slide 36). Third, the truth: ideology is false consciousness; disciplinary power produces regimes of truth, and Foucault claims no outside standpoint. Fourth, the agent: ideology presupposes a subject who could be undeceived; disciplinary power produces the subject. Butler: power "is not simply what we oppose, but also...what we depend on for our existence" (Butler, 1997: 1-2). No pre-disciplinary subject waits to be liberated.

Worked examples. The school's regime of registers, progress reports, and key stages (Slide 10): ideology asks whose interests mass schooling serves (capital's, in producing a literate and compliant workforce); discipline asks how the school's instruments examine each pupil and normalise her. The Kember ultrasound: ideology asks whether obstetric medicine is patriarchal (Slide 5: "not exactly untrue"); discipline asks how the scan reorganises visibility ("much more and much less than ideology"). Bordo on the slender body (Slides 25-32): ideology asks whose interests women's body discipline serves (capital, the slimming industry, patriarchy); discipline asks how the mirror, magazine, gym, fitness tracker, and Instagram feed produce a subject "habituated to self-monitoring and self-normalization" (Bordo, 1992: 202-3).

Foucault did not refute Marx; he changed the question. Marx asks who benefits and how consent is secured. Foucault asks how techniques work and how subjects are produced. The lecture holds both registers: Slide 23 names the capitalist benefit of docile bodies; Slides 35-36 frame Foucault as a methodological supplement to, not a dismissal of, Marxism. Gramsci's account of hegemony is the natural bridge between the two. Hegemony is rule "by consent" (Gramsci, 1971: 12), secured in the everyday institutions of civil society (school, church, press, union) rather than by the state alone, and Hall's reading (Hall, 1981: 227) treats ideological and disciplinary techniques as complementary registers of the same problem: how a modern social order reproduces itself without overt coercion. Lynch's reading reinforces the supplementarity: the analytics of power do not abolish the question of who benefits but make it possible to ask it more carefully. The right move is to keep both: ideology critique remains needed for the manosphere's misogynist worldview or for billionaire-influencer self-help; disciplinary critique remains needed for the gym, the HR review, and the ultrasound. To replace ideology with disciplinary power is to lose tools; to dismiss disciplinary power as Marxist heresy is to miss what makes modern power distinctive.

### M12 (was Mock Q5, contemporary-application): How does Foucault's notion of biopower help us think about contemporary public-health management?

Public-health management is one of the clearest contemporary expressions of biopower, which Lynch describes as acting "not directly [on] particular individuals, but rather [on] groups of people and populations as a whole" (Lynch, 2011: 14). I argue Foucault's biopower supplies the indispensable vocabulary for what happens in the everyday public-health apparatus, while also revealing the productive ambiguity at the heart of health governance.

Foucault's biopower. Where disciplinary power targets the individual body, biopower targets the population. Lynch's illustration is epidemiological: observing which groups contract lung cancer leads to identifying causes such as smoking or asbestos exposure (Lynch, 2011: 14). The rationality is to "save lives" by acting on aggregate populations. Disciplinary and biopolitical power are "two poles" of modern power over life: "a micro-level of individuals... and a macro-level of populations" (Lynch, 2011: 23).

The lecture as case-study.

First, the population-level duty of health. Slide 24 is built around "It is our duty to keep ourselves healthy" and unpacks the mechanisms. The population's salt intake is targeted; the 5-a-day campaign moralises a norm; "the government must stop obese children" targets the cohort. Pandemic contact-tracing apps and vaccination campaigns extend the same logic. None target a particular individual; all act on the population.

Second, the police-genealogy. Slide 37: "the police force was not only invented for maintaining law and order... but for assuring urban supplies, hygiene, health" (Foucault, 1982: 215). The modern police, in the broader sense, is biopolitical from inception. Today's environmental-health officers and public-health directors inherit that genealogy.

Third, the clinical apparatus. The Kember scan (returning at Slide 38) is at once a clinical encounter with one mother and part of population-level antenatal screening: "the scanning process eliminates the mother's body from view and the doctor has direct access to the image of the foetus" (Kember, 1998). Biopolitical visibility renders some bodies hyper-visible (the foetus, the population statistic) while erasing others (the maternal body). Slide 4's question generalises: who is rendered visible and who invisible by a public-health apparatus?

Fourth, the disciplinary-biopolitical body. Bordo (Slides 25-32) shows biopolitical health imperatives taken up at the embodied self. The City of London gym (Slide 28), where one works out "to show you 'mean business'", is the biopolitical injunction enacted as personal aspiration. Fitness trackers and step-counters automate the regime. Bordo's clinching formulation is disciplinary and biopolitical: "the chasm that produces bodies habituated to self-monitoring and self-normalization" (Bordo, 1992: 202-3).

Three productive ambiguities.

(i) Biopower saves lives and redistributes attention. Slide 4: "Is it a good thing that doctors can 'visualize' a foetus?... Could this lead to the woman being viewed as unimportant?" The lecturer's answer: both "could be 'yes'". The biopolitical care that produces healthier populations also disappears some bodies from view.

(ii) Biopower must be combined with disciplinary and sovereign power. The school applies disciplinary techniques to each pupil and biopolitical ones to the cohort (5-a-day reaching them through school meals). The Damiens punishment (Slide 8) is the trace of a sovereign register that persists.

(iii) Biopower is resisted. Foucault: "where there is power, there is resistance" (Foucault, 1978: 95). Lynch: "in the relations of power, there is necessarily the possibility of resistance" (Lynch, 2011: 25). Bordo's diachronic historicisation is biopolitical resistance: showing that the slender body of today is no more natural than the plump body of 1880 (Slide 25) opens the norm to contestation. Anti-vaccine politics and fat-acceptance movements demonstrate the contestation in action.

(iv) Public-health management is also a racial project. Du Bois' diagnosis of "double consciousness" (Du Bois, 1903: 8) captures how Black populations are produced as both objects of public-health concern (higher mortality, "at-risk" status) and as a constitutive outside of the imagined "general public" whom interventions claim to serve. The taxonomic origins of population thinking (Linnaeus, 1735; Blumenbach, 1775) make this visible: biopolitical categories carry their racial genealogy with them, from antenatal screening to Covid-era disparities.

Verdict: biopower is essential for thinking about contemporary public-health management, from salt-reduction targets and 5-a-day to pandemic-era vaccine drives and digital contact-tracing. It names the population-level rationality, the moralised self-government, and the productive but ambiguous visibility that the lecture's examples disclose. It needs holding in tension with disciplinary analysis of the individual body and with attention to the residual sovereign register that visibly seizes bodies. Used this way, biopower remains the most important single concept for thinking about how modern societies govern life itself.

### M13 (was Mock Q6, disjunctive): Is the panopticon a metaphor or a model? Discuss.

The disjunction (metaphor or model) is the key to reading Foucault on the panopticon. The panopticon is best understood as a *diagram*: something between metaphor and model, a schema naming the logical structure of disciplinary surveillance without claiming that any actual institution implements it perfectly, and which therefore travels productively across institutional sites.

The case for "metaphor". A metaphor figures one thing in terms of another. Bentham's prison stands metaphorically for modern surveillance: like the panopticon, contemporary disciplinary arrangements make us visible to an unverifiable watcher. As metaphor, the panopticon is rhetorically powerful but conceptually loose; it breaks down whenever an institution lacks the central tower, individual cell, or human watcher.

The case for "model". A model captures the essential mechanism and can be tested against instances. On this reading, the panopticon is Foucault's model of disciplinary power; particular institutions are evaluated for how closely they implement it. The reformative prison, model school, asylum, factory, and army would be more or less panoptic. As model, the panopticon is rigorous but risks over-extension: if every visibility-asymmetry is panoptic, the model loses discriminating power.

The case for "diagram". The Calhoun extract supplies the framing. The panopticon "automatizes and disindividualizes power. Power has its principle not so much in a person as in a certain concerted distribution of bodies, surfaces, lights, gazes" (Foucault, 1977: 316 in Calhoun reader). Discipline "may be identified neither with an institution nor with an apparatus; it is a type of power, a modality for its exercise" (Foucault, 1977: 316 in Calhoun reader). This is the language of diagram, a logical structure that crosses institutional sites. "One can speak of the formation of a disciplinary society in this movement that stretches from the enclosed disciplines... to an indefinitely generalizable mechanism of 'panopticism'" (Foucault, 1977: 316 in Calhoun reader). The diagram generalises; instances vary.

Test cases.

The cell as universal container. The panoptic cell can hold "a madman, a patient, a condemned man, a worker or a schoolboy" (Foucault, 1977: 314 in Calhoun reader). The diagram specifies the conditions (asymmetric visibility, individual confinement, central tower) under which any subject becomes observable, classifiable, and self-regulating.

The school. Slide 10's "registers, progress reports, school photos, records of achievement, testing, key stages" instantiates the diagram without an architectural tower. A distributed apparatus of records produces the panoptic effect. Lynch's transcript (Lynch, 2011: 13-14) shows the diagram operating capillary-fashion through paperwork.

The body. Bordo (Slides 25-32) shows the diagram operating without a watcher at all: the bathroom mirror becomes the tower, the woman becomes both watcher and watched, and slenderness norms supply the unverifiable standard. "Bodies habituated to self-monitoring and self-normalization" (Bordo, 1992: 202-3) are the diagram closed at the level of the embodied self. Berger's earlier formulation already captures the structure: "men look at women; women watch themselves being looked at" (Berger, 1972: 47), and Mulvey's "male gaze" (Mulvey, 1975: 11) gives the same diagram its cinematic form. Each instantiates panoptic vision without a literal tower. Selfie culture and fitness-tracker dashboards intensify the closure.

The clinical scene. Kember's ultrasound (Slide 2) is panoptic: asymmetric visibility, unverifiability of clinical evaluation, production of antenatal subjectivity. "The scanning process eliminates the mother's body from view and the doctor has direct access to the image of the foetus" (Kember, 1998).

Contemporary diagrams. Facial recognition at airports, CCTV networks, and social-media follower-counts are all panoptic in form: the watcher need not be present, the watched cannot verify when observed, and self-regulation follows. The diagram has digitised but kept its structure.

Where the diagram strains. The biopolitical injunctions of Slide 24 (salt, 5-a-day, obesity policy) target the population, not the individual in the cell. The panoptic diagram is the wrong figure here; biopower is right. Lynch warns theory should not "answer everything" (Lynch, 2011: 15).

Verdict: the panopticon is a diagram. As metaphor it under-claims; as model it over-claims. As diagram it does just what Foucault wanted: name the disciplinary logic without specifying empirical implementations, and leave room for the biopolitical and sovereign diagrams alongside it. Where asymmetric visibility, unverifiability, and internalisation are in play (school, body, clinic, social-media feed), the panopticon is the right tool; where the population is the target, biopolitics is needed alongside.

### M14 (was Mock Q7, topic-as-title): Bordo and the disciplinary body: from the slender norm to self-regulation.

My title names what Slide 28 calls "the intersections of power, the body, discipline and self-regulation... linked to what is regarded as normal." Bordo's analysis is the lecture's clearest contemporary illustration of Foucauldian disciplinary power; her diachronic move is decisive for the productive thesis; and her account exposes the gendered character of disciplinary society Foucault did not fully theorise.

The diachronic move. Slide 25: in the late nineteenth century, plump signalled male success, muscle signalled working-class status, and pale skin signalled women's exemption from fieldwork. Slide 27 tracks the inversion: thirty years ago we were "concerned with weight... encouraged to diet, 'fight the flab'. Nowadays, we have to be 'slender'. Adverts talk of being in trim, well-toned, well-defined." Body parts are framed as "in revolt": thighs, stomach, upper arms, calves. The form persists; the content changes.

This move does decisive theoretical work. It instantiates the productive thesis (Slide 13) at the level of the body: different configurations produce different bodies; the body is not the natural ground on which discipline acts but its product. It denaturalises the present: if both 1880's plump masculine body and the contemporary slender feminine body are products of historically specific norms, neither has priority as "natural".

The disciplinary mechanism. Bordo fits the lecture's three aspects of discipline precisely. Hierarchical observation: the woman is watched by the magazine, mirror, advertising image, peer group, and the City-of-London colleague who notices whether one "means business" enough for the gym (Slide 28). Today the Instagram feed and fitness-tracker dashboard add new observers. Normalising judgement: the slender, well-toned norm is the standard against which deviation registers as moral failing ("being fat is equated with being lazy. Of not caring. Of being a failure", Slide 28). Examination: the bathroom scale, calorie count, gym-mirror self-assessment, dressing-room verdict, weekly step-count.

The self-regulatory closure. Slide 17: "If power 'shouted at us' all the time we would notice it. Rather, it invites and incites us to behave in certain ways. We discipline ourselves! We self-regulate!" Bordo's clinching formulation: "Self-management in consumer culture...becomes more elusive as it becomes more pressing...lies the chasm that produces bodies habituated to self-monitoring and self-normalization" (Bordo, 1992: 202-3, Slide 29). No one needs to coerce the dieter; she coerces herself.

The gendered specification. Foucault's analysis was relatively gender-neutral; Bordo supplies the specification, and the lecture endorses it. Slide 28: "More demands are made on women than men in terms of them producing themselves as 'normal'." Slide 32: "Power operates more subtly but more closely in the regulation of women's bodies... Foucault's work on power can help us understand this situation better/more accurately." Not a departure but an application to a domain he did not develop. The contemporary Andrew Tate / manosphere phenomenon partly inverts the gendering, applying intensified body norms to young men, but it does not displace the central asymmetry Bordo identifies.

The intersection with consumer culture. Slide 32 names the tension: "We live in a consumer society, one which runs on us drinking coffee, eating cakes, take-away food etc. But we have to produce ourselves as normal individuals, in control of ourselves, and this means being in control of our bodies!" The subject is hailed as consumer (eat, drink, spend) and as self-disciplinary subject (be slender, controlled). The chasm Bordo names is precisely the gap, producing "bodies habituated to self-monitoring and self-normalization" (Bordo, 1992: 202-3).

Bordo's account also has a feminist counter built in. hooks' "oppositional gaze" (hooks, 1992: 116) names a viewing position that refuses identification with the disciplinary norms Bordo describes; the Black woman who looks back at the cinema screen or the magazine cover declines the panoptic invitation to self-monitor. Reading L7 alongside L5 shows that the disciplined body is also a site of contestation, not just normalisation.

Conclusion. Bordo's analysis is the lecture's most fully developed contemporary illustration of disciplinary power and docile bodies. The slender body, the City of London gym (Slide 28), the felt failure of missing a 5-a-day target (Slide 24), the consumer-culture paradox (Slide 32) all instantiate the panoptic diagram at the level of embodied selfhood. Butler (Slide 12) extends the analysis to the subject as such: power forms rather than constrains a pre-existing subject. The disciplinary body and the disciplined subject are produced together; the productive thesis of Slide 13 reaches its sharpest form here.

### M15 (was Mock Q8, hypothetical): How does Lynch's exposition of Foucault help us read the lecture's account of power?

Lynch's chapter "Foucault's theory of power" supplies the conceptual scaffolding the slides rely on without always making explicit. Lynch's exposition supplies four indispensable supplements: a clearer account of what Foucault is rejecting, a clearer account of the micro/macro articulation, a sharper formulation of the "intentional but non-subjective" character of power, and a precise reading of resistance.

Lynch on what Foucault rejects. Slides 34-35 set out the liberal and Marxist foils; Lynch is more fine-grained. He identifies three "mistaken, inadequate or misleading conceptions": the liberal (power as institutions and mechanisms of subservience), psychoanalytic (power as rule and law), and Marxist (power as class domination) (Lynch, 2011: 16). All three share a "juridico-discursive" representation: power as negative, prohibitive, top-down, uniform (Lynch, 2011: 16). All mistake "terminal forms" for essence. Lynch makes Slides 34-36 intelligible as a single coherent rejection.

Lynch on micro/macro. The lecture's productive thesis (Slide 13), the panoptic-society generalisation (Slide 10), and the biopolitical material (Slide 24) sit alongside one another without the structural relation being made explicit. Lynch supplies it: "we thus have a micro-level of individuals (disciplinary techniques of the body) and a macro-level of populations (biopolitics)" (Lynch, 2011: 23). The two are not rivals but two poles, the micro constituting the macro through aggregation. Lynch's pyramid analogy (Lynch, 2011: 15) is decisive: power is built "from the bottom of a pyramid" rather than imposed from the top, and the academic transcript is the worked example.

Lynch on "intentional but non-subjective". Power relations are intentional ("imbued, through and through, with calculation: there is no power that is exercised without a series of aims and objectives", Lynch, 2011: 23-24) but non-subjective ("this does not mean that it results from the choice or decision of an individual subject", Lynch, 2011: 24). The school's docile-body production (Slide 23) gestures at this without naming it: nobody decides pupils should be docile, yet the school's tactics aim at it. Lynch: "the effects of the exercise of power reach beyond any individual's (or group's) intentions or control" (Lynch, 2011: 24). This is what makes Slide 23's claim defensible without sliding into conspiracy.

Lynch on resistance. Slide 17's compressed claim risks sounding deterministic. Lynch restores resistance: "Where there is power, there is resistance, and yet... this resistance is never in a position of exteriority in relation to power" (Foucault, 1978: 95, cited in Lynch, 2011: 25). "Without resistance, without two bodies (or minds) pushing or pulling against each other, there is no power relation. And through resistance, power relations can always be altered" (Lynch, 2011: 25). This is essential for reading Bordo: the slender-body norm produces self-monitoring, but the norm is contested (by alternative aesthetics, body-acceptance discourse, historical denaturalisation), confirming disciplinary power is not totalising.

Three illustrations.

First, the Kember example. The ultrasound (Slides 2, 38) raises the question whether the doctor is "part of a patriarchal system" (Slide 5). Ideology critique is "not exactly untrue", but "it is both much more and much less than ideology" (Foucault, 1980: 102). Lynch's micro/macro framing clarifies the surplus: the scan is a micro-encounter aggregating into a macro-apparatus of antenatal screening; the productive effects cannot be reduced to any agent's intent.

Second, the school. Slide 10's list is theoretically intelligible through Lynch's reading of the transcript as a bottom-up instrument (Lynch, 2011: 13-14). "Power develops in the first instance in specific, local, individual choices, behaviours and interactions" (Lynch, 2011: 23).

Third, the body. Bordo (Slides 25-32) is most fully Foucauldian when read through Lynch's resistance clause: the historicisation of body norms (plump in 1880, slender today) is itself a resistive denaturalisation. Lynch's "power relations can always be altered" (Lynch, 2011: 25) keeps Bordo from sliding into pessimism.

A productive cross-reading is with Hall's reception of Gramsci. Hall (Hall, 1980: 36) treats hegemony and disciplinary power as complementary rather than rival accounts: hegemony names how consent is secured in civil society, discipline names how compliant subjects are produced in everyday institutions. Lynch's "micro/macro" framing makes the same move at a different scale.

Verdict: Lynch's exposition is not an alternative to Foucault but the reader's scaffold for the lecture. It clarifies what is rejected, articulates the micro/macro structure, makes the "intentional but non-subjective" claim defensible, and restores the resistance Slide 17 risks losing. The lecture and Lynch are designed to be read together; Lynch is the lecture's theoretical apparatus made explicit.

### M16 (was Mock Q9, single-author how-convincing): How convincing do you find Foucault's claim that "power is everywhere"?

Foucault: "power is everywhere; not because it embraces everything, but because it comes from everywhere" (Foucault, 1978: 93, cited in Lynch, 2011: 21). I find the claim convincing on a careful reading, unconvincing on a careless one, and politically productive only when paired with specifications preventing it from collapsing into cynicism.

The careless reading takes "power is everywhere" to mean every social relation is equally an instance of power, domination is universal, and resistance is futile. This underwrites either nihilistic acquiescence or paranoid maximalism. Neither is what Foucault meant.

The careful reading distinguishes two parts. (i) "Comes from everywhere": power is not a possession concentrated in a state, class, or institution; it is a multiplicity of force relations arising from below and aggregating into larger configurations. Lynch: "power develops in the first instance in specific, local, individual choices, behaviours and interactions" (Lynch, 2011: 23). (ii) "Not because it embraces everything": omnipresence is not totality. Lynch: "power does not 'consolidate everything' or 'embrace everything' or 'answer everything'; power alone may not be adequate to explain all, or every aspect of, social relations" (Lynch, 2011: 15). This saves the claim from totalising determinism.

Three reasons I find the careful claim convincing.

First, explanatory yield. The hypothesis forces us to look at micro-techniques that other vocabularies miss. Slide 10's "registers, progress reports, school photos, records of achievement, testing, key stages", Lynch's transcript, Slide 21's questionnaire, Bordo's bathroom mirror, the Kember ultrasound, and today's fitness trackers and algorithmic feeds are all sites an "elite-domination" framework underdescribes.

Second, the productive thesis. If power "comes from everywhere", it is productive rather than principally repressive. Slide 13: nineteenth-century institutions produced "new kinds of people". The modern prisoner, schoolchild, and psychiatric patient are products of disciplinary apparatuses. This explanation of category-proliferation is hard to obtain elsewhere.

Third, resistance internal to power. Lynch's reading restores what Slide 17's slogan can miss: "Without resistance, without two bodies (or minds) pushing or pulling against each other, there is no power relation. And through resistance, power relations can always be altered" (Lynch, 2011: 25). Omnipresence is compatible with continuous contestation.

Three reasons I find the claim unconvincing if pushed.

First, the political-economy lacuna. Slide 23: docile bodies "fit well into the modern capitalist economy" and "the bourgeoisie has won!". The disciplinary apparatus serves capital; "comes from everywhere" cannot, alone, explain why it serves the bourgeoisie. The fix is to read Foucault alongside structural analyses, not abandon him. Cost-of-living and gig-economy precarity sharpen the point.

Second, normative reticence. If power is everywhere, the critic needs criteria for distinguishing better and worse configurations. Lynch: "those who understand the claim that individuals are constituted by power relations to constitute a denial of freedom find his vision to be bleak" (Lynch, 2011: 24). His response is that Foucauldian analysis "increase[s] our self-awareness, and hence our own freedom" (Lynch, 2011: 24), but the framework remains thinner than a full normative theory.

Third, the agency problem. If power produces subjects, the subject of resistance is itself produced. Lynch resolves: "to understand subjectivity as constituted (in part) through power relations is not to deny that subjects can act intentionally" (Lynch, 2011: 24). Butler: power "is not simply what we oppose" but "what we depend on for our existence" (Butler, 1997: 1-2; Slide 12).

Worked examples. The school is a site where power "comes from everywhere" (registers, peer comparison, internalised norms): the omnipresence claim fits. Bordo's slender-body norm fits too (mirror, magazine, gym, Instagram). The Kember ultrasound, by contrast, is organised by a specific clinical apparatus; omnipresence must be paired with attention to the medical institution. Slide 24's biopolitical material (salt, 5-a-day, obesity policy) shows power coming from "the government", a specific source; omnipresence must be balanced by attention to the state. Halewood's critique of modern thought as organised through bifurcations (Halewood, 2014: 36) clarifies what the claim is really doing: "power is everywhere" dismantles the inside/outside, state/society, base/superstructure pairs through which earlier theories spatialised power, and replaces them with a topology of force relations.

Verdict: "power is everywhere" is convincing as a description of the dispersed, capillary character of modern power. It is not convincing as a complete theory superseding structural analysis. Read as a methodological injunction (look everywhere) rather than a metaphysical thesis, it is one of the most consequential claims in twentieth-century social theory, and Lynch is the indispensable scaffold for getting it right.

### M17 (was Mock Q10, two-authors): Using the work of at least two authors, evaluate Foucault's account of disciplinary power through the contributions of Bordo and Butler.

Bordo and Butler each contribute a different specification of Foucault's productive thesis. I argue: strengthened at bodily discipline (Bordo), transformed at subject formation (Butler), and qualified by the gendered specification Foucault did not develop.

Foucault's disciplinary power. Slide 10 names contemporary society a "disciplinary society" with its school instruments (registers, progress reports, key stages). Slide 13: nineteenth-century institutions produced "new kinds of people (new kinds of subjects)". Slides 19, 21: hierarchical observation, examination, normalising judgement. The product is the docile body (Slide 23). Power "categorizes the individual, marks him by his own individuality, attaches him to his identity, imposes a law of truth on him... It is a form of power which makes individuals subjects" (Foucault, 1982: 212; Slide 18).

Bordo on disciplinary norms. Slides 25-32 trace her three moves. Diachronic (Slide 25): plumpness signalled male success, muscle signalled working-class status, pale skin signalled women's exemption from fieldwork. Norms have inverted (Slide 27) but the form persists. Mechanism (Slides 27-28): contemporary culture demands "slender", "in trim", "well-toned" bodies, and "more demands are made on women than men". The City of London gym is the worked example. Closure (Slide 29): "the chasm that produces bodies habituated to self-monitoring and self-normalization" (Bordo, 1992: 202-3).

Bordo's contribution. She supplies the gendered specification Foucault needed. Slide 32: "Power operates more subtly but more closely in the regulation of women's bodies... Foucault's work on power can help us understand this situation better." Bordo applies Foucault to a domain he did not develop, making the disciplinary register the analytic for the slimming industry, magazine, mirror, gym, and now the fitness tracker and Instagram feed.

Butler on power forming the subject. Slide 12 cites Butler's *Psychic Life of Power*: "We are used to thinking of power as what presses on the subject from the outside [...] But if [...] we understand power as *forming* the subject as well as providing the very condition of its existence [...] then power is not simply what we oppose, but also, in a strong sense, what we depend on for our existence and what we harbour and preserve in the beings that we are" (Butler, 1997: 1-2).

Butler's contribution. She pushes the productive thesis to its strongest form. Foucault insists power produces subjects (Slides 13, 18); Butler insists it constitutes the very condition of subjectivity. There is no pre-power self. This radicalises (the productive thesis cuts deeper) and complicates (if power forms the subject, the subject of resistance is itself produced by power).

Lynch addresses the complication: "to understand subjectivity as constituted (in part) through power relations is not to deny that subjects can act intentionally" (Lynch, 2011: 24). Resistance is alteration of power relations from within, not return to a pre-power authenticity. Lynch: those who find in Foucault "tools with which to increase our self-awareness, and hence our own freedom, hear wellsprings of hope" (Lynch, 2011: 24).

Convergences. Both agree with Foucault on the productive thesis. Both reject voluntarist individualism and crude determinism. Both insist on the embodied subject as a site of social reproduction. Butler's earlier work in *Gender Trouble* (Butler, 1990: 25), discussed in L5, supplies the missing link: gender is a "stylised repetition of acts" rather than an inner essence, so the disciplinary norms Bordo describes do not regulate a pre-existing gender but constitute it through their citational performance. Reading L7 alongside L5 shows that disciplinary normalisation and gender performativity are two descriptions of the same productive process.

Divergences. Bordo works at disciplinary norms on the body; Butler at subject formation as such. Bordo's tools are the magazine, mirror, and gym; Butler's are citational repetition of gendered acts and psychic interiority. The lecture frames them as complementary.

Worked illustrations. The Kember scan (Slide 2) is the clearest meeting point: disciplinary (Bordo: maternal body rendered visible against a clinical norm) and subject-forming (Butler: antenatal subject constituted through the apparatus). The City gym (Slide 28) is Bordoian. Slide 32's "we have to produce ourselves as normal individuals" is Butlerian.

Verdict: Foucault's disciplinary power is strengthened by Bordo's gendered specification and transformed by Butler's account of subject formation. Both extend Foucault to domains he did not develop, and both expose the productive thesis as more radical than Slide 13's compressed version makes it appear. Reading the lecture without Bordo and Butler is reading Foucault without his most generative heirs.

### M18 (was Mock Q11, can-we): Can Foucault's framework be used to think about resistance, or does it foreclose it?

This repeats one of the oldest charges against Foucault: that his account leaves no room for resistance. I argue: yes, Foucault's framework can be used for thinking about resistance, and Lynch's reading makes the case.

The prosecution case. Three charges. (i) Power is omnipresent: "always already there, one is never outside it" (Foucault, 1980, cited in Lynch, 2011: 19). No outside means no Archimedean point to push back. (ii) Power produces the subject: "It is a form of power which makes individuals subjects" (Foucault, 1982: 212; Slide 18). If the subject of resistance is itself produced by power, resistance is just power moving against itself. (iii) Slide 17 ("We discipline ourselves! We self-regulate!") risks sounding like a verdict of inescapability.

The defence has five elements.

First, Foucault insists resistance is internal to power: "Where there is power, there is resistance, and yet... this resistance is never in a position of exteriority in relation to power" (Foucault, 1990a: 95, cited in Lynch, 2011: 25). Resistance is constitutive of power, not outside it. Without resistance, we have domination, not power.

Second, omnipresence is not totality. Lynch: "power does not 'consolidate everything' or 'embrace everything' or 'answer everything'" (Lynch, 2011: 15). The plurality of force relations is the condition for the plurality of resistances.

Third, power and resistance constitute each other. Foucault 1984: "In the relations of power, there is necessarily the possibility of resistance... if there were no possibility of resistance, of escape, of ruse... there would be no relations of power" (Lynch, 2011: 25). "If there are relations of power throughout every social field it is because there is freedom everywhere" (Lynch, 2011: 29).

Fourth, the productive thesis is itself a resource for resistance. Historicising how power produces subjects denaturalises the present and opens it to contestation. Bordo's diachronic move (Slide 25) is the clearest example: showing that the slender body of today is no more natural than the plump body of 1880 opens the norm to challenge. The same applies to the modern prisoner (Slide 14), patient, schoolchild: each is a historical product, so each is reformable. Body-positivity movements and prison-abolitionist politics show contemporary forms.

Fifth, Lynch's reading is hopeful. "Those who understand the claim that individuals are constituted by power relations to constitute a denial of freedom find his vision to be bleak. Those of us... who find in his analyses the tools with which to increase our self-awareness, and hence our own freedom, hear wellsprings of hope" (Lynch, 2011: 24). Resistance requires self-understanding, not an outside.

What Foucauldian resistance does not do. It does not promise final emancipation or a post-power society. Slide 23 ("the bourgeoisie has won!") gestures at the limit: disciplinary analysis without structural critique cannot mount a revolution. For projects of overthrowing capitalism or dismantling patriarchy, Foucault's vocabulary is inadequate alone; the fix is supplementation.

Illustrations. Bordo's historicisation of body norms is a disciplinary resistance: showing the slender norm is contingent opens it to contestation. Butler's "power is not simply what we oppose" but "what we depend on" (Butler, 1997: 1-2; Slide 12) is more radical: it denies an authentic pre-power self but opens immanent contestation. hooks' "oppositional gaze" (hooks, 1992: 116) supplies the worked feminist example: the Black woman who looks back at the screen or the disciplinary norm refuses identification from within, not from an outside. Slide 5's question ("Are doctors part of a patriarchal system?") is itself resistive: raising the question denaturalises the clinical apparatus. Slide 22's framing of "the normal" as "one of the most insidious of all concepts of modernity" is a resistive denaturalisation of the normalising judgement Slide 21 describes. Anti-vaccine politics, fat-acceptance discourse, and contestations of HR rating culture extend the register.

Verdict: Foucault's framework does not foreclose resistance, contrary to the standard prosecution case. What it forecloses is the master-narrative model (the universal subject, the final liberation). What it enables is granular analysis of how power and resistance entangle in specific institutions, bodies, and contested moments. For these tasks, Foucauldian resistance is the right scale of analysis. For structural inequality at scale, Foucault must be supplemented by Marxist and feminist structural critique. The framework opens space for political work; the work itself remains ours.

### M19 (was Mock Q12, specific-comparison): Compare Bordo's reading of disciplinary norms with Butler's account of the subject formed by power.

Bordo and Butler share a Foucauldian commitment to the productive thesis but develop it differently. Bordo's "Reading the Slender Body" (1993) works with disciplinary norms; Butler's *The Psychic Life of Power* (1997) works with the formation of the subject by power.

Bordo's disciplinary norms. Slides 25-32 trace her argument. Diachronic move (Slide 25): in the late nineteenth century, plumpness signalled male success, muscle signalled working-class status, and pale skin signalled women's exemption from fieldwork. Body norms are historical products of disciplinary configurations, not natural facts. Contemporary inversion (Slide 27): "30 years ago we were concerned with weight... encouraged to diet, 'fight the flab'. Nowadays, we have to be 'slender'. Adverts talk of being in trim, well-toned, well-defined." Body parts are framed "in revolt": thighs, stomach, upper arms, calves. Gendered specification (Slide 28): "more demands are made on women than men". Self-regulatory closure (Slide 29): "the chasm that produces bodies habituated to self-monitoring and self-normalization" (Bordo, 1992: 202-3). The body is the site at which the three aspects of discipline close as self-regulation.

Butler on power forming the subject. Slide 12: "We are used to thinking of power as what presses on the subject from the outside [...] But if [...] we understand power as *forming* the subject as well as providing the very condition of its existence [...] then power is not simply what we oppose, but also, in a strong sense, what we depend on for our existence and what we harbour and preserve in the beings that we are" (Butler, 1997: 1-2). Butler takes the productive thesis to its strongest form: power constitutes the subject as such.

Convergences. Both reject voluntarist individualism and crude determinism. Both insist on the embodied subject as a site of social reproduction, treat the productive nature of power as central, and link gendered subject-production to historical configurations.

Divergences. First, object: Bordo's is the gendered body as disciplinarily normed; Butler's is the subject as formed. Second, mechanism: Bordo's is disciplinary (observation, examination, internalised normalisation, Slides 19, 21); Butler's is more fundamental, the formation of the condition of subjectivity.
