Third, temporality: Bordo's is diachronic (Slide 25); Butler's is structural. Fourth, politics of resistance: Bordo opens resistance by denaturalising the present norm; Butler requires resistance be immanent, since there is no pre-power self.

Worked applications. The Kember scan (Slide 2) is the clearest meeting point. In Bordo's terms, the scan is a disciplinary instrument producing the antenatal body against a clinical norm (Slide 4: "could this lead to the woman being viewed as unimportant?"). In Butler's terms, it forms the maternal subject, conferring identity through the apparatus making the foetus visible. The City of London gym (Slide 28) is Bordoian: a paradigmatic scene of normalised body-work. Slide 32's "we have to produce ourselves as normal individuals" is Butlerian: subject formation through the very practices that constitute her. The Instagram filter is both: Bordoian discipline of the face and Butlerian formation of the photographed subject.

Stakes for the lecture's other examples. Slide 24's biopolitical injunctions (salt, 5-a-day, anti-obesity policy) can be read through both: Bordo names them as disciplinary normalisations of the population's bodies; Butler names them as productions of the subject as bearer-of-public-health-duty. The injunction "It is our duty to keep ourselves healthy" produces both a body-shape (Bordo) and a subject-form (Butler). The contemporary practice of running a Fitbit alongside a calorie-tracking app is a disciplinary scene of self-monitoring (Bordo) and a subject-forming scene in which the user becomes the kind of person whose worth is tracked numerically (Butler). Public-health campaigns against smoking, the moralised refusal of alcohol, and the rise of clean-eating discourse all run on both registers simultaneously. hooks' "oppositional gaze" (hooks, 1992: 116) supplies the missing third term: a resistive viewing position from which the disciplinary norms Bordo describes and the subject-formations Butler theorises can be refused without claiming an outside.

Verdict: Bordo and Butler are complementary, not competing. Bordo gives a tool for analysing disciplinary normalisation of gendered bodies; Butler gives a tool for analysing subject formation by power. The lecture endorses both. To force a choice is to lose half the feminist Foucauldian toolkit; to read them together is to get the full picture of the disciplinary subject the lecture describes.

# L8. A Question of Experience (2): Race and Social Theory

## 1. Topic Overview

This lecture moves the question of "experience" from gender (L7) to race, showing how sociology has had to confront its own complicity in racial classification while also drawing on Black theorists who treat race as a constitutive feature of modernity rather than a side issue. The argument unfolds in three parts. First, the lecturer traces scientific racism from Linnaeus (1735) and Blumenbach (1775) through nineteenth-century craniometry to twentieth-century eugenics, showing that race had no biological referent before this period. The word's etymology (French "racine," Arabic "ras") simply meant root or beginning. Only when classification was tied to power did "race" produce the pseudo-scientific differences in intelligence, character, morality and physiognomy that justified slavery and colonialism. Following Foucault, the lecture frames this as power-knowledge: science "observed" what its own categories had already produced.

Second, W.E.B. Du Bois (1868-1963) is presented as the indispensable Black sociologist of modernity. Born five years before the Emancipation Proclamation's promise was anchored in the Fifteenth Amendment, the first Black PhD from Harvard, Du Bois asks in *The Souls of Black Folk* (1903) what it means that legal emancipation produced no substantive freedom. His answer reorganises the sociology of selfhood. The veil separates Black from white worlds; double consciousness names the "peculiar sensation" of "always looking at one's self through the eyes of others"; twoness ("an American, a Negro") refuses the unitary actor presupposed by Weber, Goffman and Garfinkel. In *Dusk of Dawn* (1940) Du Bois refines this by insisting that race is not biology but social fact: the Black man is "a person who must ride 'Jim Crow' in Georgia." The revision document notes that this anticipates the "racial realism" of Critical Race Theory.

Third, the lecture turns to contemporary social theory through Toni Morrison and Paul Gilroy. Morrison's *The Origin of Others* (2017) treats race as "an effect of power" and "Othering" as a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal. Americanness, she argues, "remains color for many people." Gilroy's *The Black Atlantic* (1993) and 'Race Ends Here' (1998) refuse to bracket Africa as marginal to modernity: the slave trade is constitutive of Western modernity, racial terror is "cheerfully complicit" with occidental rationality, and we must rewrite history from the slaves' standpoint rather than merely include Black voices. The lecturer concludes: races do not exist, but the experiences constituted by the belief, practices, history and economics of race do, and they saturate institutions, media, art and ways of seeing.

The pay-off for SC301 is methodological. The lecture argues that mainstream social theory (Weber, Durkheim, Goffman, Garfinkel) built its account of the modern self on a tacit white subject, treating racialised experience as a deviation or a special case. Du Bois, Morrison and Gilroy reverse this: the Black experience of modernity is the most revealing standpoint because modernity itself was forged through slavery, racial classification and colonial domination. The colour line is, in Du Bois's Forethought, "the problem of the Twentieth Century" (Du Bois, 1903: 1) and, given the persistence of the school-to-prison pipeline, of mass incarceration and the army as what the revision document calls "a modern form of Black slavery," equally a problem of the twenty-first.

## 2. Key Concepts & Definitions

- **Scientific racism**: The nineteenth-century project of tying "race" to biology, producing pseudo-scientific differences in intelligence, character, morality and physiognomy. Originates with Linnaeus's *Systema Naturae* (1735) and Blumenbach's five-race skull typology.
- **Power-knowledge** (Foucault, applied by Gilroy): Classification "produced" the very races it claimed to "observe." Race was "a primary object of knowledge and power" (Gilroy, 1998: 252).
- **Eugenics**: Pseudo-science of "improving" racial stock; the lecture connects it to the 1933 photograph of Nazi racial measurements and to the "eugenic ravings of Francis Crick" (Gilroy, 1998: 253).
- **The colour line**: Du Bois's diagnostic of the twentieth century: "the problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color-line" (Du Bois, 1903: 1).
- **The veil**: The social barrier separating Black from white worlds; Black people are "shut out from their world by a vast veil" (Du Bois, 1903: 3).
- **Second sight**: The compensatory gift of those born "with a veil" (Du Bois, 1903: 3), a critical perspective on the dominant world they are excluded from yet forced to inhabit.
- **Double consciousness**: "This sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity" (Du Bois, 1903: 3).
- **Twoness**: "One ever feels his twoness, an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings" (Du Bois, 1903: 3).
- **The talented tenth**: Du Bois's later concept (mentioned in the revision document) for the educated Black elite whose role is to lead racial uplift.
- **Racial realism**: Du Bois's view (later taken up by CRT, as the revision document notes) that race is not biology but social fact, defined by unequal treatment, Jim Crow, segregation.
- **Othering** (Morrison): The construction of racial outsiders to stabilise the dominant group's self-image; "a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29).
- **Whiteness** (Morrison): Analysis of whiteness as a form of unmarked power; Americanness "remains color for many people" (Morrison, 2017: 17).
- **The Black Atlantic**: Gilroy's name for the transnational cultural and political space formed by slavery's middle passage; Africa, the Americas, Europe and the Caribbean as one circuit.
- **Epidermalisation** (Fanon, via Gilroy): The colonial process of making bodies meaningful by endowing them with "qualities of 'colour'" (Gilroy, 1998: 254).
- **Interest convergence** (CRT, via revision document): Racial progress occurs only when it aligns with white interests.
- **Counter-storytelling** (CRT, via revision document): Narrative methods that reveal Black epistemologies erased by dominant historiography.
- **Primal history of modernity** (Gilroy after Walter Benjamin): Modernity rewritten "from the slaves' point of view" (Gilroy, 1993: 55).
- **Tertium quid**: Du Bois's term for the "intermediate category between animal and human" into which Black people were forced (cited in Gilroy, 1993: 55).
- **Chemical gaze** (Gilroy after Foucault): The perceptual regime within which the modern idea of race "leaked out" (Gilroy, 1998: 253).

## 3. Slide-by-Slide Walkthrough

**Slides 1-3: Defining race and racism.** The lecture opens by noting that the word "race" is similar to French "racine" (root) and possibly Arabic "ras" (head, beginning). "It was only in the 19th century that it was incorporated into biology and seemed to refer to a particular biological group or type or category" (Lecture 8 slide 3). Racism is then defined as the belief that there are "real, fixed, differences in terms of character, intelligence or morals between different 'types' of humans" (slide 3).

**Slides 4-5: Provocations.** The lecturer asks: who believes there are different races? How many races are there? What criteria identify them? The everyday question "Where are you really from?" (slide 4) is flagged as the contemporary trace of racial classification.

**Slides 6-7: Linnaeus.** Linnaeus's *Systema Naturae* (1735) divided Homo Sapiens into four sub-species: Homo Europaeus, Homo Afer (Sub-Saharan Africans), Homo Asiaticus and Homo Americanus (Native Americans). Classification rested on morphology but Linnaeus also claimed differences in "temperament and psychology" (slide 6). The lecturer notes finer subdivisions ("Northern Europeans"/"Southern Europeans").

**Slide 8: Blumenbach.** Johann Friedrich Blumenbach (1752-1840) proposed five races, supposedly evidenced by skull shape: Caucasian (white), Mongolian (yellow), Malayan (brown), Negroid (black) and American (red). Again, supposed psychological differences track morphology.

**Slide 9: Power-knowledge.** "Science claimed to 'observe' racial differences. The classifications they produced appeared to give them knowledge … This power-knowledge 'produced' ways of viewing people which still have effects today" (slide 9). The lecturer ties this to Foucault (L7) and asks whether the question of "colour" runs through race talk because there "needs to be something to be 'observed' in order to classify." This is vision and power. The accompanying image juxtaposes the 1868 "Apollo Belvidere" / "Creole Negro" / "Young chimpanzee" comparison with the 1933 photograph of Nazi racial measurements.

**Slides 10-11: Du Bois on race as social fact.** "the difference in skin color was vastly overemphasized and intrinsically trivial. And yet this fact of racial distinction based on color was the greatest thing in my life and absolutely determined it" (Du Bois, 1940: 136). In a "fictional" dialogue Du Bois insists race is "a cultural, sometimes a historical fact" and concludes: "the black man is a person who must ride 'Jim Crow' in Georgia" (Du Bois, 1940: 153).

**Slide 12: Du Bois biography.** Born Massachusetts 1868, died 1963. Studied in Berlin in the 1890s; first Black PhD from Harvard; polymath; first generation of African Americans after Emancipation (1863).

**Slide 13: Post-Emancipation.** The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) declared all slaves free; the post-Civil-War amendments made it unconstitutional to deny the vote on the basis of "race" or "color" or prior slave status. Yet "writing a generation after all this, in the 1890s, Du Bois asked why nothing had really changed for African Americans" (slide 13).

**Slide 14: "Being a problem".** Du Bois's opening: "being a problem is a strange experience" (Du Bois, 1903: 2). The visiting cards anecdote: a girl refuses his card and "it dawned on me with a certain suddenness that I was different from the others … shut out from their world by a vast veil" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). Gibson's editorial gloss: "one's sense of race and racial terms comes only from experience" (Gibson, 1996: xxv).

**Slide 15: Double consciousness.** "It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The veiled "Negro" gets "no true self-consciousness but only lets him see himself through the revelation of the other world" (Du Bois, 1903: 3).

**Slide 16: Twoness vs the unitary actor.** "For Du Bois, being double is the basis of the experience of the world. This differs from the sense of unity, of being a single actor, which is presumed by Weber, Goffman, Garfinkel" (slide 16). "One ever feels his twoness, an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). "The history of the American Negro is the history of this strife … this longing to attain self-conscious manhood, to merge his double self into a better and truer self" (Du Bois, 1903: 3).

**Slide 17: The waste of double aims.** "This waste of double aims, this seeking to satisfy two unreconciled ideals, has wrought sad havoc with the courage and faith and deeds of ten thousand thousand people" (Du Bois, 1903: 4).

**Slide 18: Substantive freedom.** Despite the Emancipation Proclamation and the 15th Amendment, "The Nation has not yet found peace from its sins; the freedman has not yet found freedom in his promised land" (Du Bois, 1903: 5). "Work, culture, liberty, all these we need, not singly but together" (Du Bois, 1903: 7).

**Slide 19: Neither Africanise nor bleach.** "he wishes neither of the older selves to be lost. He would not Africanize America, for America has much to teach the world … He simply wishes to make it possible for a man to be both a Negro and an American" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The lecturer underlines the link of modernity and slavery.

**Slide 20: Modernity built race as a labour fix.** Long Du Bois quotation: "In the latter part of the seventeenth and early in the eighteenth centuries, the central and all-absorbing economic need of America was the creation of a proper labor supply to develop American wealth" (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4). "Such statutes sought to solve problems of labor and not of race or color" (Du Bois, 1898: 3). Source: Du Bois, W.E.B. 1898. 'The Study of the Negro Problems', *Annals of the American Academy*, Jan 1898: 1-23.

**Slide 21: Morrison biography.** Toni Morrison: novelist, writer, thinker. The lecturer flags the 2017 Harvard lectures published as *The Origin of Others* (Harvard University Press).

**Slide 22: Morrison's central question.** "What is race (other than genetic imagination) and why does it matter? … Race is the classification of a species, and we are the human race, period [full-stop]. Then what is this other thing, the hostility, the social racism, the Othering" (Morrison, 2017: 15). Citing Bruce Baum: "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25). "The necessity of rendering the slave a foreign species appears to be a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29).

**Slide 23: Americanness as colour.** "immigrants to the United States understood that if they wanted to become 'real' Americans they must sever or at least downplay their ties to their native country, in order to embrace their whiteness. The definition of 'Americanness' (sadly) remains color for many people" (Morrison, 2017: 17). The lecturer adds: "[Think also about Trump and what it means nowadays to be a 'Mexican-American']."

**Slide 24: Media and Othering.** "routine media presentations deploy images and language that narrow our views of what humans look like (or ought to look like) and what in fact we are like" (Morrison, 2017: 37). Suggested novels: *Beloved*, *Paradise*, *The Bluest Eye*; also Octavia Butler's *Dawn* and Angela Carter's *The Magic Toyshop*.

**Slide 25: Gilroy biography.** Paul Gilroy, currently at UCL, previously LSE, Harvard, Goldsmiths and Essex. Most famous books: *There Ain't No Black in the Union Jack*, *The Black Atlantic: Modernity and Double Consciousness*, *Between Camps* (published in the US as *Against Race*).

**Slide 26: Race as primary object of knowledge and power.** Gilroy is influenced by Foucault but does not fully agree. "'race' was a primary object of knowledge and power" (Gilroy, 1998: 252).

**Slide 27: Africa as constitutive, not peripheral.** Africa "was not on the side-lines of the West and the development of modernity." The transnational, evidenced in the slave trade, was always part of Western modernity; hence the "Black Atlantic." Ethnic/"racial" identities are outcomes of political, economic and cultural processes, not fixed essences. "We need to rethink history and modernity and not just 'include' the marginal positions that have been ignored. But to rewrite history and modernity from these positions" (slide 27).

**Slide 28: Racial terror and reason.** "racial terror is not merely compatible with occidental rationality but cheerfully complicit with it" (Gilroy, 1993: 56). Annotated "(Think of Dussel)" by the lecturer. "The time has come for the primal history of modernity to be reconstructed from the slaves' point of view" (Gilroy, 1993: 55).

**Slide 29: Standpoint, not unmediated experience.** "This unstable standpoint is to be understood in a different way from the clarion calls to … unmediated experience which sometimes appear in association with the term." "In terms of contemporary politics and social theory, the value of this project lies in its promise to uncover both an ethics of freedom to set alongside modernity's ethics of law and the new conceptions of selfhood … that are waiting to be constructed from the slaves' standpoint" (Gilroy, 1993: 56). Annotated "(Think of Du Bois)."

**Slide 30: Conclusion.** "Races do not exist. But the experiences constituted by the belief, practices, history and economics of 'race' do. This is not simply about 'racism' and individuals being racist. It is about how the modern social world is constituted on forms of racism which we might not be able to recognise immediately but are present in, for example, institutions, art galleries, music, and ways of seeing" (slide 30).

## 4. Key Theorists & Quotes

- "It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity" (Du Bois, 1903: 3).
- "One ever feels his twoness, an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body, whose dogged strength alone keeps it from being torn asunder" (Du Bois, 1903: 3).
- "He simply wishes to make it possible for a man to be both a Negro and an American" (Du Bois, 1903: 3).
- "The Nation has not yet found peace from its sins; the freedman has not yet found in freedom his promised land" (Du Bois, 1903: 5).
- "Work, culture, liberty, all these we need, not singly but together" (Du Bois, 1903: 7).
- "the holocaust of war, the terrors of the Ku-Klux Klan, the lies of carpet-baggers, the disorganization of industry … left the bewildered serf with no new watch-word beyond the old cry for freedom" (Du Bois, 1903: 5).
- "the all-pervading desire to inculcate disdain for everything black, from Toussaint to the devil" (Du Bois, 1903: 6).
- "the difference in skin color was vastly overemphasized and intrinsically trivial. And yet this fact of racial distinction based on color was the greatest thing in my life and absolutely determined it" (Du Bois, 1940: 136).
- "the black man is a person who must ride 'Jim Crow' in Georgia" (Du Bois, 1940: 153).
- "the central and all-absorbing economic need of America was the creation of a proper labor supply to develop American wealth" (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4).
- "Such statutes sought to solve problems of labor and not of race or color" (Du Bois, 1898: 3).

**Toni Morrison (1931-2019)**
- "Race is the classification of a species, and we are the human race, period [full-stop]. Then what is this other thing, the hostility, the social racism, the Othering" (Morrison, 2017: 15).
- "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25, citing Baum).
- "The necessity of rendering the slave a foreign species appears to be a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29).
- "immigrants to the United States understood that if they wanted to become 'real' Americans they must sever or at least downplay their ties to their native country, in order to embrace their whiteness. The definition of 'Americanness' (sadly) remains color for many people" (Morrison, 2017: 17).
- "routine media presentations deploy images and language that narrow our views of what humans look like" (Morrison, 2017: 37).

**Paul Gilroy (b. 1956)**
- "'race' was a primary object of knowledge and power" (Gilroy, 1998: 252).
- "the order of active differentiation that gets called 'race' may be modernity's most pernicious signature" (Gilroy, 1998: 252).
- "racial terror is not merely compatible with occidental rationality but cheerfully complicit with it" (Gilroy, 1993: 56).
- "The time has come for the primal history of modernity to be reconstructed from the slaves' points of view" (Gilroy, 1993: 55).
- "Plantation slavery was more than just a system of labour and a distinct mode of racial domination" (Gilroy, 1993: 54).
- "Scientific and biological, historical and cultural, rational and irrational, skin, bone and even blood are no longer primary referents of racial discourse" (Gilroy, 1998: 253).
- "'race' might best be approached as an after-image" (Gilroy, 1998: 253).
- "the truths of race were produced 'performatively' from the hat that biological science provided, like so many startled rabbits in front of a noisy, eager, imperial crowd" (Gilroy, 1998: 252).
- "anti-toxins capable of silencing raciology forever" (Gilroy, 1998: 255).

**Linnaeus (1735)**: divided Homo sapiens into Europaeus, Afer, Asiaticus and Americanus, claiming differences in temperament and psychology, not only morphology. Gilroy notes the orangutan-and-Negro frontispiece of his *A Genuine and Universal System of Natural History* (Gilroy, 1998: 254).

**Blumenbach (1752-1840)**: five-race typology (Caucasian, Mongolian, Malayan, Negroid, American) based on skull shape; origin of the term "Caucasian."

**Fanon (cited by Gilroy)**: epidermalisation as "a historically specific system for making bodies meaningful by endowing in them qualities of 'colour'" (Gilroy, 1998: 254).

## 5. Debates & Tensions

- **Biological vs social conceptions of race**: Scientific racism insists race is biologically real; Du Bois, Morrison and Gilroy all reject this but disagree on what to put in its place. Du Bois retains "race" as a cultural and historical fact; Gilroy presses towards "race ends here" and the abolition of raciology; Morrison occupies a middle ground, naming race as power-effect.
- **Inclusion vs rewriting**: Should we "add" Black voices to existing modernity narratives or rewrite modernity from the standpoint of the enslaved? Gilroy explicitly demands the latter, citing Walter Benjamin's "primal history."
- **Unitary vs split self**: Du Bois's double consciousness explicitly contests the unified actor of Weber, Goffman and Garfinkel. Can sociology accommodate a self that is constitutively riven?
- **Racism as individual prejudice vs structural condition**: Lecture conclusion stresses that this "is not simply about 'racism' and individuals being racist" but how the social world is constituted on unrecognised forms of racism in institutions, art, music and ways of seeing.
- **Pessimism vs progress**: The revision document notes that CRT treats racial progress as a "myth" reversed by "interest convergence." Du Bois oscillates: Emancipation has not delivered, yet *Souls* ends on the possibility that two world-races may give each to each.
- **Universalism vs particularism**: Gilroy critiques bourgeois humanism for repairing itself by adding the figures Du Bois called "tertium quid"; he wants conceptions of selfhood that are "forever disassociated from the psychological and epistemic correlates of racial subordination" (Gilroy, 1993: 56).
- **Visibility and the body**: Gilroy in 'Race Ends Here' asks whether nanoscale biology and digital imaging make race "an after-image" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). Yet Fanon's epidermalisation still organises everyday life (Gilroy, 1998: 254-255).
- **Africa as periphery vs Africa as constitutive**: Gilroy explicitly contests the view that Africa was on the side-lines of Western modernity (slide 27).

## 6. Examples & Applications

- **Jim Crow segregation**: Du Bois's empirical anchor for racial realism; the Black man is "a person who must ride 'Jim Crow' in Georgia" (Du Bois, 1940: 153). The revision document names Jim Crow as Du Bois's foremost example of race as social fact.
- **The visiting cards refusal**: Du Bois's autobiographical scene in the New England schoolhouse (Du Bois, 1903: 2-3) as the everyday mechanism by which the veil is communicated.
- **The Ku Klux Klan and carpet-baggers**: Du Bois's catalogue of the Reconstruction failure: "the holocaust of war, the terrors of the Ku-Klux Klan, the lies of carpet-baggers, the disorganization of industry" left the freedman with no substantive freedom (Du Bois, 1903: 5).
- **The Massachusetts-to-Georgia slave statutes**: Du Bois's (1898: 3-4) demonstration that racial law was a labour-supply fix; "such statutes sought to solve problems of labor and not of race or color."
- **Indented servants vs life-slaves**: Du Bois shows how legal categories diverged once "the economic superiority of the slave system" combined with religious and linguistic difference to harden a racial line (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4).
- **The 1868 "Apollo Belvidere / Creole Negro / Young Chimpanzee" plate**: Slide 9's example of scientific racism's visual rhetoric, placing the Greek ideal at the top of a hierarchy that descends through the Black body to the chimpanzee.
- **The 1933 Nazi racial measurements photograph**: Slide 9's example of scientific racism institutionalised in twentieth-century state machinery.
- **The "Where are you really from?" question** (slide 4): The everyday racialised question through which the colour line still operates.
- **Sartje Baartman and Michael Jordan / Bugs Bunny**: Gilroy's paired example of nineteenth-century display of the racialised body and contemporary "pas de deux" of "the super-human, godly Michael Jordan and Bugs Bunny" as "the reductio ad absurdum of hybridized African trixter tale-telling" (Gilroy, 1998: 252).
- **The Linnaeus frontispiece (orangutan and Negro girl)**: Gilroy reads it as showing the "suggested kinship between these sub- and anti-human species" and the entanglement of race with sex and gender (Gilroy, 1998: 254).
- **Robert Lincoln Watkins and the "micromotoscope"**: Gilroy's example of an early-twentieth-century shift from comparative anatomy to microscopy in producing racial knowledge (Gilroy, 1998: 253).
- **Francis Crick's "eugenic ravings"**: Gilroy's example of how the founding of molecular biology was implicated in the "redefinition of life in terms of information, messages and code" (Gilroy, 1998: 253).
- **NMR/MRI and PET imaging**: Gilroy notes that these technologies have "remade the relationship between the seeable and the unseen … status of bio-racial differences that vanish at these levels of resolution" (Gilroy, 1998: 253).
- **Kant's *Physische Geographie* and the split bamboo cane**: Gilroy cites Eze and Neugebauer on Kant's writing about "the qualities of Negro skin and the practical problems it presented when pain had to be inflicted with a split bamboo cane" (Gilroy, 1998: 254). Anchor case for epidermalisation avant la lettre.
- **Hegel on "the African's capacity for historical action"**: Gilroy (1998: 254-255) cites Hegel's "limitations he placed upon the African's capacity for historical action" as exemplifying "epidermal thinking in its emergent form."
- **Toussaint to the devil**: Du Bois names Toussaint Louverture in a catalogue of how white prejudice extends "from Toussaint to the devil" (Du Bois, 1903: 6); the Haitian revolutionary as the disavowed object of white contempt.
- **The Sorrow Songs**: Du Bois's Forethought announces that each chapter begins with "some echo of haunting melody from the only American music which welled up from black souls in the dark past" (Du Bois, 1903: Forethought).
- **Ethiopia the Shadowy and Egypt the Sphinx**: Du Bois names the long African past whose "powers of single black men flash here and there like falling stars" (Du Bois, 1903: 4).
- **The school-to-prison pipeline**: The revision document names this as a CRT example of how the US prison and military system functions as "a modern form of Black slavery."
- **Prisons and the army as modern slavery**: The revision document explicitly cites these as the CRT example of how "racial progress is always pushed back, and only occurs through 'interest convergence'."
- **American identity as whiteness**: Morrison's example of immigrants "embrac[ing] their whiteness" to become "real Americans" (Morrison, 2017: 17); the revision document highlights that "American identity is tied to whiteness, reinforced by media and culture / law and order / religion."
- **Trump-era "Mexican-American"** (slide 23): Lecturer's contemporary annotation on Morrison's whiteness-as-Americanness thesis.

## 7. Connections to Other Lectures

- **L1 Marx**: Slavery as constitutive of capitalism; Gilroy in *Black Atlantic* takes plantation slavery as "the foundations for a distinctive network of economic, social, and political relations" (Gilroy, 1993: 54).
- **L2 Weber**: Du Bois explicitly contrasts double consciousness with Weber's unified rational actor (slide 16); Gilroy contests Weber's occidental rationality as "cheerfully complicit" with racial terror (Gilroy, 1993: 56).
- **L3 Durkheim**: Du Bois redirects Durkheim's social-fact method; racial classification is a coercive social fact even where biology fails.
- **L4 Goffman/L5 Garfinkel**: Lecture explicitly notes Du Bois "differs from the sense of unity, of being a single actor, which is presumed by Weber, Goffman, Garfinkel" (slide 16).
- **L6 Foucault**: Power-knowledge directly applied (slide 9); Gilroy treats race as the most pernicious instance of Foucault's biopolitical classification and discusses the "chemical gaze" (Gilroy, 1998: 252).
- **L7 Gender/Feminism**: Both lectures treat experience as situated and embodied; standpoint epistemology links Black and feminist critiques. The revision document links Gilroy's "case for reconstructing modernity from the views / perspectives of enslaved people" directly to standpoint theory.
- **L9 Postcolonial/Decolonial (Said, Spivak, Dussel)**: Gilroy's "(Think of Dussel)" annotation on slide 28 makes this explicit; Black Atlantic and decolonial thought converge on rewriting modernity from the underside. The revision document notes Dussel's claim that "European modernity is based on violence."
- **L10 Globalisation**: Black Atlantic as a transnational circuit of modernity (Gilroy, 1993: 54-56).
- **Spring Term**: Morrison's argument about "routine media presentations" (Morrison, 2017: 37) connects to L8-Spring's account of media-as-hegemonic-struggle; Gilroy's chemical gaze connects to structuralist semiotics on signs of "race."

## 9. Past-Q Essay Answers

### Past Q 2025. What is meant by 'scientific racism'? How have sociologists tried to counter this concept?

In this essay I define scientific racism as the nineteenth-century project of grounding racial classification in supposedly biological fact, and show how sociologists from Du Bois through Morrison to Gilroy have countered it by treating race as a social, historical and political construction.

"Race" had no biological referent before the nineteenth century. Its etymology is benign: French "racine" (root) or Arabic "ras" (head). "It was only in the 19th century that it was incorporated into biology" (Lecture 8 slide 3). Scientific racism is the doctrine that there are "real, fixed, differences in terms of character, intelligence or morals between different 'types' of humans" (slide 3). Linnaeus's *Systema Naturae* (1735) divided Homo sapiens into Europaeus, Afer, Asiaticus and Americanus, claiming temperamental as well as morphological differences. Blumenbach (1752-1840) refined this into a five-race skull typology. The lineage runs through nineteenth-century craniometry to the 1933 photograph of Nazi racial measurements (slide 9).

Following Foucault, the lecture frames scientific racism as power-knowledge: "Science claimed to 'observe' racial differences. The classifications they produced appeared to give them knowledge. This power-knowledge 'produced' ways of viewing people which still have effects today" (slide 9). This connects to L7's biopower (Foucault, 1978): the racialised body is administered by a science whose categories its own institutions installed, and Said's L9 account of Orientalism (Said, 1978) extends the same operation into discursive racism, where the colonised East is produced as knowable object through Western scholarly classification. Gilroy concurs: "'race' was a primary object of knowledge and power" (Gilroy, 1998: 252); the "truths of race were produced 'performatively' from the hat that biological science provided" (Gilroy, 1998: 252). Scientific racism is the manufacture of racial reality by institutions tied to colonial and slaveholding power.

The first counter-move is Du Bois's. In *Dusk of Dawn* he concedes that biology cannot ground race: "the difference in skin color was vastly overemphasized and intrinsically trivial" (Du Bois, 1940: 136); but refuses the conclusion that race is therefore unreal. He relocates its reality: "Race is a cultural, sometimes a historical fact. The black man is a person who must ride 'Jim Crow' in Georgia" (Du Bois, 1940: 153). This is sociological anti-essentialism about race: its reality lies in legal and social practices, not in skulls or genes. The revision document notes this was later named "racial realism" in CRT.

Morrison's counter-move: "What is race (other than genetic imagination) and why does it matter?" (Morrison, 2017: 15). Citing Baum: "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25). Race functions through Othering: "The necessity of rendering the slave a foreign species appears to be a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29). Whiteness is the unmarked form of racial power: "the definition of 'Americanness' (sadly) remains color for many people" (Morrison, 2017: 17). The slide 23 annotation on Trump-era "Mexican-American" makes the contemporary stakes plain.

Gilroy's counter-move: in 'Race Ends Here' (1998) scientific racism rested on the "Euclidean anatomy" of racial measurement, now outflanked by molecular biology and digital imaging. "Scientific and biological, historical and cultural, rational and irrational, skin, bone and even blood are no longer primary referents of racial discourse" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). "'Race' might best be approached as an after-image" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). The "eugenic ravings of Francis Crick" (Gilroy, 1998: 253) show molecular biology was contaminated by inherited race-thinking. The science that produced scientific racism has superseded its own object.

Counter-arguing in the lab does not abolish racism in the street. "Races do not exist. But the experiences constituted by the belief, practices, history and economics of 'race' do" (slide 30). Generic policing concerns, Black Lives Matter mobilisations after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor, racialised wealth gaps and Brexit-era hostile-environment debates show racial categorisation continuing to organise institutional life. The revision document's CRT examples (school-to-prison pipeline; carceral-military continuation of slavery) extend the diagnosis.

Scientific racism is the modern project of dressing racial hierarchy in biological clothing; sociologists have countered it by relocating race's reality to social structure (Du Bois), to the affective work of othering (Morrison) and to the changing technologies of vision (Gilroy). The counter is unfinished because the legacy of scientific racism is sedimented in institutions and habits of perception that survive the discrediting of its biological premises.

### Past Q 2024. How did European modernity benefit from unequal race relations? Discuss with reference to two theorists.

In this essay I argue that European modernity was constituted by unequal race relations, not merely accompanied by them, through Du Bois and Gilroy. The wealth, philosophy and self-image of European modernity were materially and conceptually subsidised by the racial subordination of African peoples.

Du Bois's economic and legal foundation. In 'The Study of the Negro Problems' (1898), "the central and all-absorbing economic need of America was the creation of a proper labor supply to develop American wealth" (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4). The supply problem was solved by importing Africans and creating a racial category through statute: "Such statutes sought to solve problems of labor and not of race or color" (Du Bois, 1898: 3). "Dozens of enactments, from Massachusetts to Georgia, were made 'for the proper regulation of slaves and servants'" (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4), and the racial line hardened when "the economic superiority of the slave system" combined with linguistic, religious and morphological difference. Race emerged as a legal-economic device because slavery was more profitable than indenture; it congealed afterwards into the natural fact scientific racism would later "discover." Modernity benefited twice: from unpaid labour and from the ideological asset of being the racially enlightened standard. As Du Bois says in *Dusk of Dawn*: "the difference in skin color was vastly overemphasized and intrinsically trivial. And yet this fact of racial distinction based on color was the greatest thing in my life and absolutely determined it" (Du Bois, 1940: 136).

Gilroy radicalises this. In *The Black Atlantic* he abandons the comforting story that slavery was a regrettable side-business. "Plantation slavery was more than just a system of labour and a distinct mode of racial domination" (Gilroy, 1993: 54); it provided "the foundations for a distinctive network of economic, social, and political relations" (Gilroy, 1993: 55). The Atlantic triangle of European masters, Caribbean plantations and African slaves was the laboratory of modern bureaucratic management, industrial finance and consumption. Gilroy's polemic cuts to the benefit question: "racial terror is not merely compatible with occidental rationality but cheerfully complicit with it" (Gilroy, 1993: 56). Modernity did not benefit despite slavery; rationality and slavery rose together.

The cultural and epistemic dividend follows. European science gained authority by classifying non-European peoples as inferior. As Gilroy puts it, "'race' was a primary object of knowledge and power" (Gilroy, 1998: 252). Knowledge production was an arm of empire. Linnaeus's orangutan-and-Negro frontispiece, in which "the suggested kinship between these sub- and anti-human species" anchors the European self-image (Gilroy, 1998: 254), is one example. Slide 9's 1868 plate placing "Apollo Belvidere" above the "Creole Negro" and the "Young Chimpanzee" is another. Even bourgeois humanism, Gilroy notes, relied on excluding those Du Bois called a "tertium quid", an "intermediate category between animal and human" (cited in Gilroy, 1993: 55).

A counter-argument holds that modernity was progressive and slavery a pre-modern residue. I reject this. The legal innovations that produced racial slavery were modern inventions, as Du Bois (1898: 3-4) documents in the statutes that hardened the slave/servant boundary. Emancipation was incomplete: "The Nation has not yet found peace from its sins; the freedman has not yet found in freedom his promised land" (Du Bois, 1903: 5). The revision document specifies the continuity: the prison and the army as "a modern form of Black slavery," and CRT's interest convergence thesis. Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor makes the continuity contemporary.

If modernity benefited from slavery, then a sociology that simply adds Black voices to a fundamentally white narrative is inadequate. We must, with Gilroy, attempt "the primal history of modernity reconstructed from the slaves' points of view" (Gilroy, 1993: 55). The slaves' standpoint reveals what the masters' standpoint conceals. "We need to rethink history and modernity and not just 'include' the marginal positions that have been ignored" (slide 27). The L2 framing of colonial modernity sharpens this: Howard French (2021) argues African labour and African gold financed the European centuries we call "modern," while Dussel (1993) holds that "European modernity is based on violence" against its colonial underside. Gilroy's Black Atlantic is the African contribution to modernity that L2 names.

European modernity benefited from unequal race relations in three reinforcing ways: economically through unpaid labour (Du Bois, 1898), culturally through "scientific" racial classification (Linnaeus, Blumenbach, slide 9), and politically through the self-image of a free Europe defined against unfree others.

### Past Q 2023. What is meant by "scientific racism"? How have sociologists tried to counter this concept?

In this essay I define scientific racism as the nineteenth-century project of grounding racial classification in supposedly biological fact, and show how sociologists from Du Bois through Morrison to Gilroy have countered it by treating race as social construction.

"Race" had no biological referent before the nineteenth century. Etymology: French "racine" (root) or Arabic "ras" (head). "It was only in the 19th century that it was incorporated into biology" (Lecture 8 slide 3). Scientific racism is the doctrine that there are "real, fixed, differences in terms of character, intelligence or morals between different 'types' of humans" (slide 3). The lineage is Linnaeus's *Systema Naturae* (1735), with "temperament and psychology" (slide 6); Blumenbach's (1752-1840) five-race skull typology (slide 8); the 1868 "Apollo Belvidere / Creole Negro / Young Chimpanzee" plate (slide 9); the 1933 photograph of Nazi racial measurements (slide 9).

Following Foucault: "Science claimed to 'observe' racial differences. This power-knowledge 'produced' ways of viewing people which still have effects today" (slide 9). Gilroy concurs: "'race' was a primary object of knowledge and power" (Gilroy, 1998: 252); "truths of race were produced 'performatively' from the hat that biological science provided" (Gilroy, 1998: 252). Scientific racism is the manufacture of racial reality by classificatory institutions tied to colonial and slaveholding power.

The first counter-move is Du Bois's. In *Dusk of Dawn* he concedes that biology cannot ground race: "the difference in skin color was vastly overemphasized and intrinsically trivial" (Du Bois, 1940: 136); but refuses the conclusion that race is therefore unreal. He relocates its reality: "Race is a cultural, sometimes a historical fact. The black man is a person who must ride 'Jim Crow' in Georgia" (Du Bois, 1940: 153). This is the first sociological anti-essentialism about race: its reality lies in legal and social practices, not in skulls or genes. The revision document notes this is the source of CRT's "racial realism": race is real as social fact, fictive as biology.

The second counter-move is Morrison's. In *The Origin of Others* she presses: "What is race (other than genetic imagination) and why does it matter?" (Morrison, 2017: 15). Citing Baum: "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25). Race functions through Othering: "The necessity of rendering the slave a foreign species appears to be a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29). The dominant group needs racial others to stabilise its own normality. The L9 postcolonial extension is Said (1978), who shows that the same operation works at the level of discourse: scholarship, novels and journalism produce "the Orient" as a body of knowledge that confirms European normality, the discursive sibling of scientific racism's biological classification. Whiteness is not the absence of race but the unmarked form of racial power.

The third counter-move is Gilroy's. In 'Race Ends Here' (1998) he argues that scientific racism rested on the "Euclidean anatomy" of comparative racial measurement, which has been outflanked by molecular biology and digital imaging. "Scientific and biological, historical and cultural, rational and irrational, skin, bone and even blood are no longer primary referents of racial discourse" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). At molecular resolution, "'race' might best be approached as an after-image" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). The "eugenic ravings of Francis Crick" (Gilroy, 1998: 253) show that molecular biology was itself contaminated by inherited race-thinking; the broader trajectory has nonetheless undermined the perceptual regime that produced race. The science that produced scientific racism has superseded its own object.

Counter-arguing scientific racism in the lab does not abolish racism in the street. Du Bois, Morrison and Gilroy all stress that racism persists as institutional and cultural fact even after biology repudiates it. "Races do not exist. But the experiences constituted by the belief, practices, history and economics of 'race' do" (slide 30). Black Lives Matter mobilisations after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor show the persistence. The revision document specifies CRT's institutional sites: the school-to-prison pipeline; prisons and the army as "modern form of Black slavery"; "racial progress is always pushed back, and only occurs through 'interest convergence'."

I conclude that scientific racism is the modern project of dressing racial hierarchy in biological clothing, and that sociologists have countered it by relocating race's reality to social structure (Du Bois), to the affective work of othering (Morrison) and to the changing technologies of vision (Gilroy). The counter is unfinished because the legacy of scientific racism is sedimented in institutions and habits of perception that survive the discrediting of its biological premises.

### Past Q 2022. Drawing from at least two of W.E.B Du Bois, Toni Morrison and Paul Gilroy, discuss the implications of "race" for contemporary society.

In this essay I draw on Du Bois, Morrison and Gilroy to argue that race, though biologically empty, has profound implications for contemporary society in three registers: the constitution of the self, the production of national belonging, and the structure of global modernity.

The first implication is for selfhood. In *The Souls of Black Folk* (1903) Du Bois introduces double consciousness as the experiential consequence of living within the colour line: "It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The self is constitutively split: "One ever feels his twoness, an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The unitary actor presupposed by Weber, Goffman and Garfinkel is unavailable to racialised subjects (slide 16). L6 standpoint epistemology develops this directly: Hill Collins (1990) names Du Bois as an explicit ancestor of Black feminist standpoint, and Mohanty (1984) shows how Western feminism's construction of the "Third World Woman" reproduces Morrison's Othering at a global scale.

The second implication is for national belonging. In *The Origin of Others* Morrison observes that "immigrants to the United States understood that if they wanted to become 'real' Americans they must sever or at least downplay their ties to their native country, in order to embrace their whiteness. The definition of 'Americanness' (sadly) remains color for many people" (Morrison, 2017: 17). National identity is not just a passport but a racialised performance. The lecturer adds: "[Think also about Trump and what it means nowadays to be a 'Mexican-American']" (slide 23). The revision document echoes: "American identity is tied to whiteness, reinforced by media and culture / law and order / religion." Morrison's othering thesis names the mechanism: "The necessity of rendering the slave a foreign species appears to be a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29). Brexit-era hostile-environment debates and Trump-era policy framings show the same dynamic in contemporary form.

The third implication is structural. In *The Black Atlantic* and 'Race Ends Here', Gilroy refuses to treat slavery and colonialism as side-issues. "The order of active differentiation that gets called 'race' may be modernity's most pernicious signature" (Gilroy, 1998: 252). "Plantation slavery was more than just a system of labour and a distinct mode of racial domination" (Gilroy, 1993: 54); it built modernity through the Atlantic slave system. The modern social world is built on these racialised foundations, and Morrison's "routine media presentations" (Morrison, 2017: 37) continue to "narrow our views of what humans look like." Gilroy's normative claim follows: we must reconstruct modernity from the slaves' point of view (Gilroy, 1993: 55), not merely add Black voices.

Examples across all three thinkers give contemporary content. The revision document's CRT catalogue (school-to-prison pipeline; prisons and the army as "modern form of Black slavery"; interest convergence; counter-storytelling) operationalises all three implications. Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor makes the structural diagnosis newsworthy; cultural references like *Get Out* and *Selma* stage the racialised perception for critique.

The objection that race is a declining force in a globalising multicultural world fails on each thinker's evidence. Du Bois warned that equality in law is not enough: "Work, culture, liberty, all these we need, not singly but together" (Du Bois, 1903: 7). Morrison's evidence: "routine media presentations deploy images and language that narrow our views of what humans look like" (Morrison, 2017: 37). Gilroy's evidence: the chemical gaze (Gilroy, 1998: 252) and Fanon's epidermalisation (Gilroy, 1998: 254-255) still shape how bodies are read. Generic affirmative-action debates and cost-of-living racialised wealth gaps show that formal anti-discrimination has not dissolved the structure.

Race has three deep implications for contemporary society. Through Du Bois, it shapes the structure of racialised selfhood, producing the doubled, second-sighted experience that mainstream sociology must learn from. Through Morrison, it shapes national belonging by making whiteness the unmarked currency of full citizenship. Through Gilroy, it shapes global modernity by reproducing the asymmetries laid down by the Atlantic slave system. Race is biologically empty and sociologically full.

### Past Q 2021. Du Bois asked: "How does it feel to be a problem?" Outline and assess his response to this question.

In this essay I outline Du Bois's response and assess it on three criteria: descriptive accuracy, conceptual originality, political adequacy.

Du Bois opens *Souls* with the question and defers it: "To the real question, How does it feel to be a problem? I answer seldom a word" (Du Bois, 1903: 2). The question is a polite circumlocution for the white interlocutor's racialised gaze. The response unfolds in three moves: an autobiographical scene, a conceptual formulation of double consciousness, and a programmatic call for substantive equality.

The autobiographical scene is the visiting cards incident. As a New England schoolboy, Du Bois recalls a newcomer who "refused my card, refused it peremptorily, with a glance. Then it dawned upon me with a certain suddenness that I was different from the others; or like, mayhap, in heart and life and longing, but shut out from their world by a vast veil" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). Being a problem feels like the unwilled recognition that one is on the wrong side of an invisible barrier. The veil names this barrier; second sight names the compensatory gift: "the Negro is a sort of seventh son, born with a veil, and gifted with second-sight in this American world" (Du Bois, 1903: 3).

The conceptual formulation is double consciousness: "this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). This doubling is structural, not a deficit to be repaired by assimilation. "One ever feels his twoness, an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body, whose dogged strength alone keeps it from being torn asunder" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The aim is not to abandon either pole: "He simply wishes to make it possible for a man to be both a Negro and an American" (Du Bois, 1903: 3).

The programmatic move is the demand for substantive rather than formal equality. Despite the Emancipation Proclamation and the Fifteenth Amendment, "The Nation has not yet found peace from its sins; the freedman has not yet found in freedom his promised land" (Du Bois, 1903: 5). Du Bois catalogues the failures: "the holocaust of war, the terrors of the Ku-Klux Klan, the lies of carpet-baggers, the disorganization of industry" (Du Bois, 1903: 5). He ends: "Work, culture, liberty, all these we need, not singly but together" (Du Bois, 1903: 7). Being a problem feels like being formally free but substantively unfree.

On descriptive accuracy, Du Bois's response is remarkable. The visiting cards scene captures the everyday mechanism by which racial difference is communicated, not by lynching or Jim Crow law but by a glance and a refused card. "Where are you really from?" (slide 4) is the visiting-card refusal at the front door of citizenship. Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor gives institutional content.

On conceptual originality, double consciousness is one of the most important contributions of American social theory. It differs from "the sense of unity, of being a single actor, which is presumed by Weber, Goffman, Garfinkel" (slide 16). Gilroy reads it as anticipating "the new conceptions of selfhood and individuation that are waiting to be constructed from the slaves' standpoint" (Gilroy, 1993: 56). L10 extends Du Bois's "second-sight" into visual culture: hooks (1992) names the "oppositional gaze" of the Black spectator who looks back, refusing to be the passive object of the white world's "tape." Second sight becomes a politics of looking.

On political adequacy, the response is more ambivalent. The demand for merger of African and American selves can sound assimilationist; Du Bois insists he "would not Africanize America" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). Gilroy worries the demand to merge may understate the rupture slavery represents; his "primal history of modernity reconstructed from the slaves' points of view" (Gilroy, 1993: 55) implies some doublings should not be merged. CRT's myth-of-racial-progress thesis gives Du Bois's optimism a sober check.

Limitations. Du Bois's frame is gendered ("self-conscious manhood"), obscuring gendered racial experience. His American focus underplays the transnational frame Gilroy's Black Atlantic recovers. The analytical core survives these critiques.

Du Bois's response is descriptively acute, conceptually transformative, and politically incomplete but generative. Being a problem feels like always seeing yourself through someone else's eyes; the response is to fight for a world in which that doubling becomes optional rather than imposed.


## 10. Mock-Q Essay Answers

### Mock 1. Scientific racism as power-knowledge tied to vision.

In this essay I argue that the lecture treats scientific racism not as the discovery of biological fact but as a form of power-knowledge tied to vision. The slides set this out in two compressed steps. Slide 3 notes that "race" derives from the French "racine" (root) and the Arabic "ras" (head, beginning) and observes that "it was only in the 19th century that it was incorporated into biology and seemed to refer to a particular biological group or type or category" (slide 3). Slide 9 follows with the diagnostic claim: "Science claimed to 'observe' racial differences. The classifications they produced appeared to give them knowledge … This power-knowledge 'produced' ways of viewing people which still have effects today" (slide 9). The lecturer then asks "is this one reason why the question of 'colour' runs throughout discussions of 'race', as there needs to be something to be 'observed' in order to classify?" and concludes that race "is tied to questions of vision and power" (slide 9).

I read this as three linked claims. First, the term "race" had no biological referent before the nineteenth century. The etymology is benign and the modern doctrine that there are "real, fixed, differences in terms of character, intelligence or morals between different 'types' of humans" (slide 3) is a recent invention, not a long-running observation. Second, the apparent biological referent was manufactured by classificatory institutions. Linnaeus's *Systema Naturae* (1735) divided Homo Sapiens into Homo Europaeus, Homo Afer, Homo Asiaticus and Homo Americanus, claiming differences in "temperament and psychology" (slide 6). Blumenbach (1775) refined the scheme into five races, supposedly evidenced by skull shape (slide 8). Third, the resulting categorisations did not describe a pre-existing reality; they produced one. Slide 9's juxtaposition of the 1868 "Apollo Belvidere / Creole Negro / Young Chimpanzee" plate with the 1933 photograph of Nazi racial measurements is the visual proof that the same classificatory logic ran from comparative anatomy to twentieth-century state machinery.

Gilroy concurs. "'Race' was a primary object of knowledge and power" (Gilroy, 1998: 252) and the "truths of race were produced 'performatively' from the hat that biological science provided, like so many startled rabbits in front of a noisy, eager, imperial crowd" (Gilroy, 1998: 252). His phrasing makes the slide's diagnosis transferable: race was not seen first and named second; it was named, measured and inscribed first, and then it appeared to be seen. The L7 link is direct. Foucault's power-knowledge (Foucault, 1977) names the operation by which institutions produce the objects they claim merely to observe; race is its racial case. L7's biopower (Foucault, 1978) names the population-level technique by which modern states administer life through racial classification, so the perceptual operation slide 9 describes is also a governmental one.

The vision component is what slide 9 sharpens. The lecturer's question about "colour" notes that classification needs an observable feature; the body's surface is recruited as the visible mark. Gilroy's reading of Fanon's epidermalisation as "a historically specific system for making bodies meaningful by endowing in them qualities of 'colour'" (Gilroy, 1998: 254) names the perceptual training the visual rhetoric of slide 9's plate performed. This is also why Du Bois, despite refusing biology, insists that "the difference in skin color was vastly overemphasized and intrinsically trivial. And yet this fact of racial distinction based on color was the greatest thing in my life and absolutely determined it" (Du Bois, 1940: 136). Colour was made meaningful by the institutions that decided to look at it; once made meaningful, it became binding.

Three implications follow. First, refuting the biology does not abolish the perception. Slide 30's conclusion is exact: "Races do not exist. But the experiences constituted by the belief, practices, history and economics of 'race' do." Second, contemporary "ways of seeing" inherit the training. Morrison's "routine media presentations deploy images and language that narrow our views of what humans look like" (Morrison, 2017: 37) is power-knowledge in its everyday register, and Black Lives Matter mobilisations make the visual stakes legible. Third, the contemporary "Where are you really from?" question (slide 4) is the everyday performance of the classificatory operation slide 9 describes: it presumes a visible mark that requires explanation.

Scientific racism is the modern manufacture of racial categorisation by classificatory institutions whose authority rested on a claim to neutral observation. The lecture's diagnostic is that this is power-knowledge in the visual register; the perceptual habits it trained outlive the doctrine that produced them.

### Mock 2. "Where are you really from?" and being a problem.

In this essay I argue that the lecture treats the contemporary question "Where are you really from?" (slide 4) as the everyday trace of the colour line, performing in miniature the operation Du Bois described as "being a problem". The two slide moments belong together: slide 4 lists the question alongside the lecturer's prompts on how races are identified, and slide 14 opens Du Bois's account of *The Souls of Black Folk* with "being a problem is a strange experience" (Du Bois, 1903: 2) followed by the visiting card scene where "it dawned on me with a certain suddenness that I was different from the others … shut out from their world by a vast veil" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The slides invite the comparison.

The question performs three operations. First, it presumes a visible mark that must be explained. Slide 9's diagnosis applies: the questioner has been trained to expect "something to be 'observed' in order to classify" (slide 9). The body becomes the trigger for a request to account for one's presence. Second, it doubles the answerer's location. The questioner accepts "England" or "London" only as the first answer, and pursues a "real" origin elsewhere; the addressee's national belonging is treated as derivative, with whiteness as the implicit norm. This is Morrison's mechanism: "The definition of 'Americanness' (sadly) remains color for many people" (Morrison, 2017: 17), generalised to "Britishness" by the slide's open-ended framing. Third, it positions the addressee as a problem in the precise Du Boisian sense: a presence that the questioner cannot incorporate without further information.

Du Bois's response is the framework the lecture asks us to apply. "The real question, How does it feel to be a problem? I answer seldom a word" (Du Bois, 1903: 2). The visiting cards refusal is the prototype of "Where are you really from?" because both are conducted through ordinary social mechanisms (a glance, a card, a casual question) rather than overt segregation. The veil ("shut out from their world by a vast veil," Du Bois, 1903: 3) names the social barrier the question communicates. Second sight ("the Negro is a sort of seventh son, born with a veil, and gifted with second-sight in this American world," Du Bois, 1903: 3) names the addressee's resulting critical capacity: the person asked the question can see the question for what it is, while the questioner often cannot. Double consciousness ("this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity," Du Bois, 1903: 3) names the consequence: the addressee is forced into the doubled perspective the question imposes.

Three contemporary implications follow. First, the question is a sorting operation. The L9 postcolonial extension sharpens this: Said's *Orientalism* (Said, 1978) shows how Western scholarship constructs "the Orient" as a knowable elsewhere, and "Where are you really from?" is the everyday version performed on bodies present in Western metropoles. Second, the question is structurally racialised even where the questioner intends no racism. Morrison's "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25) names why: power needs to mark difference to confirm its own normality. Third, the question is contemporary. Brexit-era hostile-environment debates and Trump-era policy framings around "Mexican-Americans" (slide 23) show the same logic at policy scale.

Objections. One reading insists the question is innocent. Du Bois's reply applies: he was the first Black Harvard PhD and still places the visiting card moment as decisive. Race operates through habits the questioner does not need to choose. A second objection claims contemporary mobility makes the question reasonable. The Du Boisian reply: the question is selective. It is asked of those whose presence is read as requiring explanation; its absence for racially unmarked bodies tells us what work it does.

The everyday question "Where are you really from?" performs the operation Du Bois named "being a problem" and communicates the colour line through ordinary social interaction. The lecture's invitation to read slide 4 alongside slide 14 makes the diagnostic continuity audible: a doctrine that began with Linnaeus and Blumenbach now circulates as a polite enquiry, and the addressee is forced into the doubled perspective the question imposes.

### Mock 3. What Du Bois adds beyond the unitary actor of Weber, Goffman and Garfinkel.

In this essay I argue that Du Bois adds an account of the self that mainstream classical sociology cannot produce, because the racialised subject is constitutively doubled rather than unitary. Slide 17 makes the claim explicit: "Being double is the basis of the experience of the world. This differs from the sense of unity, of being a single actor, which is presumed by Weber, Goffman, Garfinkel" (slide 17). The instruction is clear, and the Spring revision slide adds: "don't just say he is like Mead or Goffman or Cooley. We want to know what Du Bois adds to the argument" (Spring revision slide on Race and Experience).

The unitary actor is the tacit subject of classical and interpretivist sociology. Weber's rational actor is a single seat of meaning and motive. Goffman's dramaturgical actor manages impressions across front and back regions but presupposes a stable performer. Garfinkel's ethnomethodological member competently produces accountable action. All three presuppose a self that, however reflexive, is one. Du Bois reports a different experience. "It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The self is split because the social world is split.

Three components specify what Du Bois adds. First, doubling is involuntary. "One ever feels his twoness, an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body, whose dogged strength alone keeps it from being torn asunder" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The classical actor chooses roles; the Du Boisian subject is imposed-upon. Second, doubling is structural, not psychological. The veil ("shut out from their world by a vast veil," Du Bois, 1903: 3) names a social barrier; the racialised actor's split self is its experiential consequence. Third, doubling generates a critical capacity: second sight. "The Negro is a sort of seventh son, born with a veil, and gifted with second-sight in this American world" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The subject who must see themselves through the dominant world's "tape" also sees the tape.

Each component challenges classical sociology. Weber's verstehen presumes a coherent actor whose motives are recoverable from a single point of view; Du Bois insists racialised motives are doubled and the recovery operation will misread one half if it presumes unity. Goffman's impression management presumes a stable backstage; Du Bois shows the racialised actor's backstage is also occupied by the dominant world's gaze, so the back/front partition does not hold. Garfinkel's accountable member is competent within shared norms; the colour line is a norm to which the Du Boisian subject's compliance is unwilling and partial. The classical actor would be a unitary self with situated impressions; the Du Boisian subject lives the impressions as constitutive of selfhood.

The L7 cross-link sharpens this. Foucault's account of how power produces subjects (Foucault, 1977) supplies the missing apparatus: the institutions of slavery, Jim Crow, segregation and labour-market sorting are the machinery that produced the doubled subject Du Bois describes. Where Foucault studies the disciplinary production of docile bodies, Du Bois shows the racialised production of doubled souls.

Two objections matter. First, Mead, Cooley and Goffman do allow for taking the role of the other; is Du Bois's contribution just a vivid variant? No, because role-taking in classical interactionism is reciprocal and broadly symmetrical, while Du Bois's doubling is asymmetric and coerced. Mead's generalised other is a self-organising input; Du Bois's "tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity" is an instrument of subordination. Second, twoness might be transitional. The revision document's CRT note rebuts this: "racial progress is always pushed back, and only occurs through 'interest convergence'." The conditions of doubling persist.

Du Bois's pay-off is methodological. The sociology of selfhood cannot universalise from the white actor and add racialised cases as deviations. The lecturer's instruction (slide 17) makes this explicit: classical sociology presupposes a unity the racialised subject cannot inhabit. Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor gives the diagnosis ongoing content. What Du Bois adds is a foundational claim that the unitary actor was always the unmarked white actor, and that a sociology of the self under the colour line must theorise constitutive doubling rather than treating it as deviation.

### Mock 4. "Both a Negro and an American": why Du Bois's demand is harder than it sounds.

In this essay I argue that Du Bois's demand for the doubled subject to be "both a Negro and an American" (Du Bois, 1903: 3) is harder than it sounds because the modernity that grants the legal form of equality is the same modernity that built the substantive subordination it is supposed to dissolve. Slide 20 sets the demand: "He simply wishes to make it possible for a man to be both a Negro and an American" and adds "this is not as easy as it might sound. And this is partly because of the link of modernity and slavery (which we have talked about before)" (slide 20). Slide 19's title sharpens this: "Equality in law is not enough" (slide 19).

Du Bois's demand has three coordinates. First, refusal of separation. "He would not Africanize America, for America has much to teach the world" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The Black demand is not exit from American modernity. Second, refusal of assimilation. He would not "bleach his Negro soul in a flood of white Americanism, for he knows that Negro blood has a message for the world" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The demand is not erasure of Black particularity. Third, substantive equality. "The Nation has not yet found peace from its sins; the freedman has not yet found freedom in his promised land" (Du Bois, 1903: 5); "Work, culture, liberty, all these we need, not singly but together" (Du Bois, 1903: 7).

Why is the demand harder than it sounds? Three reasons, all anchored to slide 20's "link of modernity and slavery". First, the legal form of equality was already granted and proved insufficient. Slide 13: "In 1863, during the American Civil War, Abraham Lincoln declared in the 'Emancipation Proclamation' that all slaves were free, forever. … Writing a generation after all this, in the 1890s, Du Bois asked why nothing had really changed for African Americans" (slide 13). Formal abolition did not produce substantive freedom; the Both demand sits in the gap.

Second, the modernity that built the legal form also built the substantive subordination. Slide 21 reproduces Du Bois's (1898) account: "the central and all-absorbing economic need of America was the creation of a proper labor supply to develop American wealth. … Such statutes sought to solve problems of labor and not of race or color" (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4). The racial line was a labour-supply solution congealed into legal category; the institutions of modern America were built around it. Granting the vote did not reconstruct them. The L2 framing extends this: Howard French (2021) shows African labour and African gold financed European modernity; Dussel (1993) holds that "European modernity is based on violence". The Both demand is therefore a demand for reconstruction of a modernity whose architecture was racial.

Third, the catalogue of obstacles is structural. Du Bois lists "the holocaust of war, the terrors of the Ku-Klux Klan, the lies of carpet-baggers, the disorganization of industry" (Du Bois, 1903: 5) as the post-Reconstruction reversal. The revision document's CRT note generalises: "racial progress is always pushed back, and only occurs through 'interest convergence'"; "the School to Prison pipeline, Prisons and the Army are a modern form of Black slavery". Each reproduces substantive subordination under the form of legal equality.

Gilroy reads the difficulty more sharply. "Racial terror is not merely compatible with occidental rationality but cheerfully complicit with it" (Gilroy, 1993: 56). The Both demand is hard because the rationality of American modernity was forged in racial terror; reconfiguring it requires "the primal history of modernity to be reconstructed from the slaves' point of view" (Gilroy, 1993: 55), not merely a legal supplement. Morrison adds the affective ground: othering as "a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29) explains why dominant groups resist substantive Both-ness even where they concede formal equality.

The Both demand is therefore structural, affective and rational at once. Brexit-era hostile-environment debates and Trump-era policy framings illustrate how substantive Both-ness keeps being deferred even where legal anti-discrimination is granted; cost-of-living and racialised wealth gaps illustrate why "equality in law is not enough" (slide 19). Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor names the contemporary mobilisation.

Du Bois's demand is harder than it sounds because the modernity that grants the form is the modernity that built the substance, and dismantling the second requires more than amending the first. The slide 20 prompt is exact: legal Both-ness without structural Both-ness is the Du Boisian disappointment of the 1890s, repeated.

### Mock 5. Rewriting, not including: Gilroy on race, modernity and racial terror.

In this essay I argue that Gilroy's demand to "rewrite history and modernity from these positions" (slide 29) follows from his claim that "racial terror is not merely compatible with occidental rationality but cheerfully complicit with it" (Gilroy, 1993: 56). If terror and rationality rose together, adding marginal voices to a fundamentally white modernity narrative is not enough; the narrative needs reconstructing.

Slide 29 sets out four claims Gilroy holds together. First: "Africa was not on the side-lines of the West and the development of modernity." Second: "The transnational (as evidenced in the slave trade) was always a real part of Western modernity. Hence the 'Black Atlantic.'" Third: "Ethnic/'racial' identities are not fixed but are outcomes of wider political, economic, and cultural processes." Fourth: "We need to rethink history and modernity and not just 'include' the marginal positions that have been ignored. But to rewrite history and modernity from these positions" (slide 29). The four claims are stages of one argument. Africa is constitutive, the Atlantic is the circuit, racial identity is its product, and the historiographical conclusion is reconstruction.

Slide 30 supplies the polemical engine. "Racial terror is not merely compatible with occidental rationality but cheerfully complicit with it" annotated "(Think of Dussel)" (slide 30). The annotation is decisive. Dussel (1993) holds that "European modernity is based on violence" against its colonial underside; Gilroy specifies the racial register of that violence. The complicity is "cheerful" because the racially terrorising operations of slavery, colonial extraction and Atlantic shipping were not exceptions to occidental rationality; they were among its highest expressions, bureaucratised, financed and morally rationalised by the same institutions that produced Kant, Hegel and modern political economy.

Three implications follow. First, periodisation. If terror and rationality are co-original, modernity cannot be dated from rational achievements without dating it from racial atrocities. The L2 framing extends this: Howard French (2021) shows African labour and African gold subsidising European modernity; Dussel (1993) treats violence as constitutive. Gilroy's "racial terror" is the form that violence takes in modernity's racial register.

Second, methodology. "The time has come for the primal history of modernity to be reconstructed from the slaves' point of view" (Gilroy, 1993: 55), the slide-30 demand. The standpoint of the enslaved is not one position among many but the position that reveals what the masters' standpoint conceals. Adding Black voices to an existing modernity narrative does not change the diagnosis; reconstructing the narrative from the slaves' standpoint does. This is why slide 29's "not just 'include' … but to rewrite" is operative: inclusion preserves the master narrative; rewriting dismantles it.

Third, normative content. Gilroy's reconstruction implies an "ethics of freedom to set alongside modernity's ethics of law and the new conceptions of selfhood … waiting to be constructed from the slaves' standpoint" (Gilroy, 1993: 56). Modernity's ethics of law gave Du Bois the Fifteenth Amendment without giving him freedom. An ethics of freedom would specify what Du Bois's "Work, culture, liberty, all these we need, not singly but together" (Du Bois, 1903: 7) requires institutionally. Gilroy's project is the conceptual extension of Du Bois's demand at Atlantic scale.

Du Bois supplies the legal-economic anchor Gilroy generalises. The slave statutes "from Massachusetts to Georgia" (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4) show colonial law inventing race to organise labour.
