Gilroy reads the same evidence at higher pitch: "Plantation slavery was more than just a system of labour and a distinct mode of racial domination"; it provided "the foundations for a distinctive network of economic, social, and political relations" (Gilroy, 1993: 54). Morrison adds the affective dimension. "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25); othering as "a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29) names the identarian machinery rationality requires to keep the terror cheerful.

Objections. One claim is that "cheerful complicity" is rhetorically excessive. Reply: the phrase is precise. Cheerful means without the dissonance one would expect; that is the analytical claim. A second objection holds that contemporary modernity has shed its complicity. Du Bois's racial realism rebuts: "the black man is a person who must ride 'Jim Crow' in Georgia" (Du Bois, 1940: 153); the institutions persist. Black Lives Matter as a movement makes the persistence newsworthy.

Gilroy's "rewrite, not include" follows necessarily from "racial terror is … cheerfully complicit with [occidental rationality]". If race built modernity, modernity cannot be made just by adding race; it must be reconstructed. The slide-29 demand is the historiographical form of the slide-30 polemic.

### Mock 6. Gilroy's unstable standpoint and the new conceptions of selfhood.

In this essay I argue that Gilroy's "unstable standpoint" is a deliberate refusal of the metaphysics of unmediated experience and a positive proposal for new conceptions of selfhood constructed from the slaves' standpoint. Slide 31 reproduces the key passages: "This unstable standpoint is to be understood in a different way from the clarion calls to … unmediated experience which sometimes appear in association with the term" and "in terms of contemporary politics and social theory, the value of this project lies in its promise to uncover both an ethics of freedom to set alongside modernity's ethics of law and the new conceptions of selfhood … that are waiting to be constructed from the slaves' standpoint" annotated "(Think of Du Bois)" (slide 31).

Three claims follow.

First, "unstable" is normative, not deficient. A stable standpoint pretends to be the unmediated voice of an essentialised experience. Gilroy refuses this. The slaves' standpoint is unstable because it is constructed historically, transmitted through cultural production, and exposed to internal heterogeneity. Stability would be a return to the essentialism the Black Atlantic project critiques. Instability is the methodological condition of a standpoint that wants to be analytically rigorous rather than identity-rhetorical.

Second, "in a different way from … unmediated experience" repudiates one strand of standpoint discourse. Some uses of "standpoint" invoke the lived experience of an oppressed group as automatically revealing the truth of its oppression. Gilroy says this confuses position with privilege of perspective. A standpoint is not the unmediated voice of the position; it is the analytic angle the position makes available, conditional on developing critical perspective. The Spring revision slide on Race and Experience makes the same demand on Du Bois: "don't just say he is like Mead or Goffman or Cooley. We want to know what Du Bois adds to the argument", and Du Bois's twoness is the original instability Gilroy generalises. Black Atlantic standpoint is "unstable" because heterogeneous and constructed; this is its strength, not its weakness.

Third, the project is positively constructive: "new conceptions of selfhood … waiting to be constructed from the slaves' standpoint" (Gilroy, 1993: 56). Mainstream classical sociology presupposed a unitary actor, the white actor whose situational embeddedness was unmarked. The slaves' standpoint makes a non-unitary selfhood thinkable. Du Bois's twoness is the prototype: "One ever feels his twoness, an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The annotation "Think of Du Bois" makes the genealogy explicit. The Gilroyan conception of selfhood is the Du Boisian doubling generalised diasporically.

The L6 link is direct. Standpoint epistemology in L6 (Hartsock, Harding, Hill Collins) holds that the subordinated position is epistemically privileged because political struggle has won the critical perspective from which the dominant position's blind spots become visible. The Spring revision slide on Race and Experience says Du Bois's experience-of-race claim is the racial version of this argument. Hill Collins (1990) explicitly names Du Bois as ancestor of Black feminist standpoint. Gilroy's "unstable standpoint" is the disciplined version of this lineage: subordinated position plus critical development, with the explicit refusal of essentialism.

What does the project deliver? Gilroy lists two outputs: an "ethics of freedom" and "new conceptions of selfhood". The first is normative: modernity's ethics of law gave Du Bois the Fifteenth Amendment without giving him substantive freedom, so an ethics of freedom must specify what emancipation requires beyond formal rights. The second is analytic: a self-concept that does not presuppose the unitary actor of Weber, Goffman and Garfinkel (slide 17). The doubled, second-sighted Du Boisian self is one version; the Black Atlantic subject is another.

Two objections. First, instability looks like a hedge. Reply: stability is the hedge; it pretends to certainty the historical record cannot provide. Second, the Black Atlantic standpoint can sound too encompassing. Reply: Gilroy treats it as one orientation, not the only valid one. The L7 biopower link sharpens this: Foucault's account of population-level administration (Foucault, 1978) names the techniques the slaves' standpoint reveals as racially specific.

Contemporary purchase. CRT's counter-storytelling operationalises the unstable standpoint as legal method; Black Lives Matter stages it as political mobilisation; *Selma* dramatises the new self-conceptions. The slide's "waiting to be constructed" is exact.

Gilroy's unstable standpoint is a disciplined, non-essentialist standpoint epistemology of the Black Atlantic, anchored in Du Bois and oriented to constructing the new conceptions of selfhood modernity's unitary actor cannot accommodate.

### Mock 7. Morrison on othering, whiteness as Americanness, and national belonging.

In this essay I argue that Morrison's account of othering describes how race functions as power-effect through the affective work of confirming the dominant group as normal, with whiteness as the unmarked currency of national belonging. Slide 24 sets out the central claim: "Race is the classification of a species, and we are the human race, period [full-stop]. Then what is this other thing, the hostility, the social racism, the Othering" (Morrison, 2017: 15). She cites Baum: "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25). And the operative thesis: "The necessity of rendering the slave a foreign species appears to be a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29). Slide 25 specifies the contemporary form: "immigrants to the United States understood that if they wanted to become 'real' Americans they must sever or at least downplay their ties to their native country, in order to embrace their whiteness. The definition of 'Americanness' (sadly) remains color for many people" (Morrison, 2017: 17). The lecturer annotates: "[Think also about Trump and what it means nowadays to be a 'Mexican-American']" (slide 25).

Three components.

First, race is an effect of power. The clause does two things at once. Negatively, it denies that race is a property of the racialised, since racialised properties are produced by the operation of power on the body. Positively, it names race as a transitive operation: race happens to people because power needs it to happen. The revision document echoes: "Race as an effect of power, for the dominant group to stabilise its own identity – whiteness." Othering is the productive mechanism.

Second, othering is desperate. The word matters. Morrison's "desperate attempt" (Morrison, 2017: 29) names the affective economy: dominant identity is not securely held; it requires the manufactured difference to feel normal. The lecturer's slide 23 annotation on Trump-era "Mexican-American" reads as a contemporary illustration: the rhetorical work the policy framings performed was to confirm white-American normality by producing Latino bodies as the threatening other. Brexit-era hostile-environment debates do the same work for British whiteness. The desperation is the analytical claim: power needs othering because dominant identity is fragile without it.

Third, whiteness is the unmarked form of racial power. "The definition of 'Americanness' (sadly) remains color for many people" (Morrison, 2017: 17). The parenthetical "sadly" is Morrison's diagnostic shrug at the empirical fact. Immigrants who "embrace their whiteness" enter Americanness through a racial gate. The revision document specifies the mechanism: "American identity is tied to whiteness, reinforced by media and culture / law and order / religion." Whiteness is not the absence of race but the unmarked racial currency of full national belonging.

Morrison also supplies the everyday machinery. "Routine media presentations deploy images and language that narrow our views of what humans look like" (Morrison, 2017: 37). Media is the routine site of othering. The L9 postcolonial extension via Said (1978) shows how the same operation works at the level of scholarship, producing "the Orient" as a knowable body of knowledge that confirms European normality.

How does this operate in contemporary national-belonging debates? Three illustrations. First, "Where are you really from?" (slide 4) performs Morrison's othering at conversational scale: whiteness as Americanness reads non-white bodies as not-yet-fully-here. Second, Trump-era framings of "Mexican-American" (the lecturer's annotation) and Brexit-era hostile-environment debates show the policy version. Third, Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor stages the counter-mobilisation; *Get Out* dramatises the affective machinery.

Objections. One holds that Morrison universalises a US-specific dynamic. Reply: the colour-as-Americanness thesis is US-specific in form but its mechanism generalises. Brexit demonstrates the British version. A second objection: othering theory under-determines structural conditions. Reply: Du Bois (1898) shows the legal-economic infrastructure; Gilroy (1993) shows the Atlantic scale; Morrison shows the affective machinery.

The L7 biopower cross-link sharpens this: Foucault's claim that power administers life through population-level categorisation (Foucault, 1978) names the apparatus through which Morrison's affective othering becomes institutionally durable.

Morrison's account of othering specifies the affective machinery by which whiteness reproduces itself as the unmarked currency of national belonging. The slide-24 framework (race as power-effect, othering as desperate normalising work) and the slide-25 specification (Americanness as colour, with the Trump annotation) operate together. Contemporary national-belonging debates are not exceptions; they are the routine sites at which the machinery operates.

### Mock 8. "One ever feels his twoness, an American, a Negro." Discuss this passage from Du Bois.

In this essay I discuss Du Bois's twoness passage, "One ever feels his twoness, an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body, whose dogged strength alone keeps it from being torn asunder" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). It should be read as a sociological diagnosis of what the colour line does to selfhood under formal equality, neither identity-confusion complaint nor assimilation programme.

The passage closes 'Of Our Spiritual Strivings', which has already laid down the question "How does it feel to be a problem?" (Du Bois, 1903: 2), the refused visiting card and the veil ("shut out from their world by a vast veil," Du Bois, 1903: 3), the gift of second sight ("born with a veil, and gifted with second-sight in this American world," Du Bois, 1903: 3), and double consciousness ("this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others," Du Bois, 1903: 3). The twoness sentence is the experiential apex of this chain.

I read four claims in the passage. First, the doubling is involuntary ("One ever feels"); it is an imposed perceptual condition, not chosen identity politics. Second, the two poles are non-negotiable: not "a Negro or an American" but "an American, a Negro." Each is constitutive. Third, the conflict is structural, not psychological: "two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals." Fourth, the body is the site of strain: "in one dark body, whose dogged strength alone keeps it from being torn asunder." Du Bois locates racial experience in the dark body that bears it, not in the soul abstracted from physiology.

The passage closes off two alternatives Du Bois rejects. The first is racial separation, "Africanise America": "He would not Africanize America, for America has too much to teach the world and Africa" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The second is racial assimilation: "He would not bleach his Negro soul in a flood of white Americanism, for he knows that Negro blood has a message for the world" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The twoness passage is the only available alternative: hold the two strivings together, not by reconciling them but by refusing to surrender either.

This is Du Bois's central contribution to a social theory of the self. Mainstream classical sociology assumed a unitary subject. Du Bois insists that the racialised subject in a white-majority polity cannot be unitary because the polity itself is double: nominally inclusive, structurally exclusive. This contrasts with "the sense of unity, of being a single actor, which is presumed by Weber, Goffman, Garfinkel" (slide 16). Twoness is the experiential consequence of the colour line as a social fact.

The passage has contemporary purchase. "Where are you really from?" (slide 4) performs the same operation Du Bois names: it invites a doubling by treating the racialised subject as not-quite-here. The revision document's note that "American identity is tied to whiteness" extends the diagnosis to twenty-first-century citizenship debates. Morrison's "the definition of 'Americanness' (sadly) remains color for many people" (Morrison, 2017: 17) generalises Du Bois's American/Negro doubling: any non-white claim on Americanness produces twoness. Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor makes the diagnosis newly audible.

Objections. The first is that twoness over-essentialises a binary that fragments into many. The right reply, supplied by Crenshaw's intersectionality, is that the Black woman experiences more than two strivings but the structural logic still applies. The second is that twoness pathologises racialised subjectivity. Du Bois's coupling of double consciousness with second sight is the answer: the doubled subject sees what the unitary subject cannot. CRT's counter-storytelling formalises this perceptual advantage.

Gilroy extends the passage diasporically. In *The Black Atlantic* he argues that the slaves' standpoint demands "the new conceptions of selfhood and individuation that are waiting to be constructed from the slaves' standpoint" (Gilroy, 1993: 56). The twoness passage is one such conception in embryo. L6 standpoint theory makes the same move at higher generality: Hill Collins (1990) explicitly names Du Bois as ancestor of Black feminist standpoint, treating twoness as the foundational racial standpoint from which the unitary white subject's self-image can be seen as such.

The twoness passage is Du Bois's most concentrated diagnosis of the racialised self under formal equality. It names an imposed doubling, refuses the false choices of assimilation and separation, and grounds Black critical perception in the body that endures the strain. It anticipates the standpoint epistemology Gilroy will globalise and CRT will translate into counter-storytelling.

### Mock 9. Critically assess Gilroy's argument in *The Black Atlantic* with reference to the role of slavery in modernity.

In this essay I critically assess Gilroy's *The Black Atlantic* (1993) on slavery's constitutive role in modernity. Gilroy's thesis is analytically powerful and substantially correct, but its full force depends on combining it with Du Bois's legal-economic account (Du Bois, 1898) and Morrison's account of racial othering.

Gilroy's thesis. "Plantation slavery was more than just a system of labour and a distinct mode of racial domination"; it provided "the foundations for a distinctive network of economic, social, and political relations" (Gilroy, 1993: 54). The polemical line: "racial terror is not merely compatible with occidental rationality but cheerfully complicit with it" (Gilroy, 1993: 56). The normative pay-off: "the primal history of modernity [must] be reconstructed from the slaves' points of view" (Gilroy, 1993: 55). Africa was not on the side-lines but constitutive.

The argument has three components. First, economic: the Atlantic slave trade was the laboratory of modern capitalism. Second, cultural: the "creative, communicative use of the memory of slavery" (Gilroy, 1993: 55) shapes contemporary diasporic culture. Third, epistemic: the slaves' standpoint is privileged because the masters' standpoint conceals what the slaves' reveals.

Du Bois's earlier work supplies the legal-economic grounding. In 'The Study of the Negro Problems' (1898), "the central and all-absorbing economic need of America was the creation of a proper labor supply to develop American wealth" (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4); the solution was African slavery, and "such statutes sought to solve problems of labor and not of race or color" (Du Bois, 1898: 3). The slave/servant boundary hardened because "the economic superiority of the slave system, and the fact that the slaves were neither of the same race, language nor religion as the servants and their masters" combined to produce "a difference in legal and social standing" (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4). Race was made by the colonial state to organise the labour supply. The L2 framing extends this: Howard French (2021) shows that African labour and African gold were the financial sinews of European modernity, the African world-making that Gilroy's Black Atlantic theorises.

Morrison adds the affective component. Modernity's complicity with racial terror requires an affective economy: "The necessity of rendering the slave a foreign species appears to be a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29). Gilroy's structural claim and Morrison's affective claim are complementary: the structure could not have been built without the affective work of othering, and the affective work would not have endured without the structural foundations.

I address three critiques. The first asks whether Gilroy's claim is too sweeping. Does treating slavery as "modernity's most pernicious signature" (Gilroy, 1998: 252) obscure the heterogeneity of modern experiences? Gilroy's reply, in his treatment of the standpoint as "unstable" (Gilroy, 1993: 56), is that the slaves' standpoint is an analytical orientation, not an unmediated experience: it reveals features the masters' position conceals, without claiming to be the only valid one.

The second critique asks whether Gilroy underplays resistance and creativity. His frame includes "creative, communicative" cultural work, the "vernacular variety of unhappy consciousness" of *The Black Atlantic* (Gilroy, 1993: 56). The Sorrow Songs that close Du Bois's *Souls* are one Black Atlantic instance; the Forethought announces that each chapter begins with "some echo of haunting melody from the only American music which welled up from black souls in the dark past."

The third asks: what does Gilroy's frame demand? The revision document's CRT examples (school-to-prison pipeline; prisons and the army as "a modern form of Black slavery"; the myth of racial progress reversed by interest convergence; counter-storytelling) give concrete normative content. Each is a contemporary site at which the Black Atlantic's structural legacy is reproduced. Black Lives Matter as a movement, mobilising after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor, is the latest visible instance of counter-storytelling against that legacy.

The three thinkers together show that slavery was not modernity's regrettable side-business but its foundation and enduring grammar. Gilroy gives us the structural picture; Du Bois (1898) the legal-economic mechanism; Morrison the affective machinery. The revision document's framing applies: "Modernity / world is shaped by African people through resistance, slavery and cultural exchange. Challenge to ethnic / nationalistic models of history. Africa is central to modernity."

Gilroy's argument in *The Black Atlantic* is analytically powerful and substantially correct. Slavery built modernity economically, legally, culturally and epistemically. Critique refines but does not undo the thesis. The corollary is that any sociology that treats slavery as an exotic past underestimates the modern present.

### Mock 10. What does Du Bois mean by the "veil", and why does he treat it as constitutive of African American experience?

In this essay I reconstruct what Du Bois means by the veil and show why he treats it as constitutive of African American experience.

The veil enters *Souls* in the visiting card scene. As a New England schoolboy, Du Bois recalls that "it dawned upon me with a certain suddenness that I was different from the others; or like, mayhap, in heart and life and longing, but shut out from their world by a vast veil" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The veil is a metaphor for social exclusion that operates without overt segregation: no wall, no law required, just the refused card, the averted glance. It is invisible from the white side and palpable from the Black.

Three properties follow. First, the veil is perceptual: it organises how the two sides see each other. Black people see themselves "through the revelation of the other world" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). Second, it bestows second sight: "the Negro is a sort of seventh son, born with a veil, and gifted with second-sight in this American world" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). Third, it generates double consciousness: "this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity" (Du Bois, 1903: 3).

Why is the veil constitutive? Three reasons.

First, historical-structural. The veil is the lingering presence of slavery and post-Emancipation failure. "The Nation has not yet found peace from its sins; the freedman has not yet found in freedom his promised land" (Du Bois, 1903: 5). Du Bois catalogues the failures: "the holocaust of war, the terrors of the Ku-Klux Klan, the lies of carpet-baggers, the disorganization of industry" (Du Bois, 1903: 5). In *Dusk of Dawn*: "The black man is a person who must ride 'Jim Crow' in Georgia" (Du Bois, 1940: 153). The veil is what makes Jim Crow durable.

Second, sociological-relational. The racialised self is constituted in relation to the white world's perception. There is no Black selfhood "behind" the veil independent of it; the experience of being on the wrong side produces the doubled selfhood. "How does it feel to be a problem?" (Du Bois, 1903: 2) is constitutive, not occasional. The Du Boisian self "differs from the sense of unity, of being a single actor" presumed by Weber, Goffman and Garfinkel (slide 16).

Third, phenomenological. The veil organises every encounter, every glance. Du Bois's doubled literary method communicates the texture of veiled experience. The Forethought announces that each chapter begins with "some echo of haunting melody from the only American music which welled up from black souls in the dark past"; veiled experience speaks through Black musical tradition.

Three alternatives fail. The individualist ("any Black person can transcend the veil by talent") is rebutted by Du Bois personally: the first Black Harvard PhD still describes the visiting cards moment as definitive. The assimilationist is rejected: "He would not bleach his Negro soul in a flood of white Americanism" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The separatist is rejected too: "He would not Africanize America, for America has too much to teach the world and Africa" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The veil is constitutive because it cannot be exited by individual, assimilationist or separatist means.

Contemporary purchase. "Where are you really from?" (slide 4) is the contemporary refused card. The revision document's CRT note that "racial progress is always pushed back" generalises the veil's persistence. Morrison's "routine media presentations deploy images and language that narrow our views of what humans look like" (Morrison, 2017: 37) shows the veil in contemporary media; L10 develops the perceptual side directly through hooks (1992) on the "oppositional gaze," the Black spectator's refusal to be passively seen through the veil and active recovery of second sight as critical practice.

Gilroy worries the veil might encase Black experience in fixity. In 'Race Ends Here' he is wary of "the absolute sovereignty of unmediated experience" (Gilroy, 1993: 56) and seeks "anti-toxins capable of silencing raciology forever" (Gilroy, 1998: 255). Du Bois has a Gilroyan resource: second sight is a critical capacity political action can deploy, not a permanent metaphysical condition.

The veil names the invisible-from-one-side social barrier that produces double consciousness, second sight and doubled selfhood under formal equality. Du Bois treats it as constitutive because it is historical-structural, sociological-relational and phenomenological. The veil is what the colour line feels like from the wrong side.

### Mock 11. Compare Du Bois's double consciousness with Fanon's epidermalisation as discussed by Gilroy.

In this essay I compare Du Bois's double consciousness (1903) with Fanon's epidermalisation as Gilroy discusses it (Gilroy, 1998: 254-255). They share a structural diagnosis (the racialised subject sees themselves through the dominant world's eyes) but differ in colonial frame, bodily emphasis and political consequence.

Du Bois's double consciousness, in *Souls* (1903), names "this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The triad: veil ("shut out from their world by a vast veil," Du Bois, 1903: 3), second sight ("born with a veil, and gifted with second-sight," Du Bois, 1903: 3), twoness ("an American, a Negro; two souls, two unreconciled strivings," Du Bois, 1903: 3). The frame is post-Emancipation US.

Gilroy describes Fanon's "epidermalization" as the colonial process of making the Black body meaningful by depositing "qualities of 'colour'" on its surface: "the dismal order of power and differentiation, defined by its intention to make the mute body disclose the truth of its racial identities, can be apprehended through the critical notion of 'epidermalization'" (Gilroy, 1998: 254). It is "a historically specific system for making bodies meaningful by endowing in them qualities of 'colour'" (Gilroy, 1998: 254). The white-child scene from the revision document gives the everyday phenomenology: the child's seeing produces the Black body as racial.

The structural diagnosis is shared. The racialised subject is not free to inhabit a unitary self because the dominant world's perception constitutes the subject as racial. Du Bois's "tape of a world" is the precursor of Fanon's colonial gaze; the veil is the precursor of the epidermal screen; second sight is the precursor of Fanon's phenomenology of being looked at.

Three differences.

First, frame. Du Bois writes from post-slavery US; Fanon from the late colonial Francophone world. Twoness is national-internal: both poles are claims on the same polity. Fanon names "an era where colonial power had made epidermalizing into a dominant principle of political power" (Gilroy, 1998: 255).

Second, bodily emphasis. Du Bois names "two warring ideals in one dark body" (Du Bois, 1903: 3); the body is the site of strain but not the explicit object. Fanon foregrounds the body: "Epidermalized power violated the human body in its symmetrical, intersubjective, social humanity" (Gilroy, 1998: 255). "The human sensorium has had to be educated" (Gilroy, 1998: 251) to read race off the body.

Third, political consequence. Du Bois ends *Souls* hoping to merge the two souls into "a better and truer self" (Du Bois, 1903: 3) and demanding "Work, culture, liberty" (Du Bois, 1903: 7). Gilroy's Fanon is more pessimistic and more focused on overturning the colonial-epidermal regime. Gilroy hopes attending to contemporary analogs might yield "the anti-toxins capable of silencing raciology forever" (Gilroy, 1998: 255).

Gilroy synthesises: Du Bois's twoness and Fanon's epidermalisation name two stages of one experiential analytic. He uses Du Bois's standpoint epistemology and Fanon's epidermal vocabulary to argue for the slaves' standpoint as the privileged position from which to rewrite modernity (Gilroy, 1993: 55-56). L7 supplies the wider apparatus: Foucault's biopower (Foucault, 1978) names the modern administration of life through population-level racial classification, which is the technique that lets epidermalisation function institutionally and lets double consciousness become a sociological generality rather than only a personal sensation.

The analytic still operates. The 1868 "Apollo Belvidere / Creole Negro / Young Chimpanzee" plate (slide 9) is epidermal logic in visual form. The 1933 Nazi racial measurements (slide 9) instrumentalise the same logic. Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor shows the body still being read epidermally; *Get Out* dramatises the regime culturally.

The objection that the two concepts have been over-applied is met by historical specificity. Used carefully they remain distinct: double consciousness is the perceived doubling of the self; epidermalisation is the imposed making-meaningful of the body's surface.

Politically, both ground anti-racism in the perceptual privilege of the subordinated. CRT's counter-storytelling and racial realism operationalise Du Boisian double consciousness; Gilroy's rejection of bourgeois humanism (1993: 55) extends Fanonian epidermal critique into a critique of modern philosophical anthropology.

Du Bois's double consciousness and Fanon's epidermalisation, as Gilroy reads it, are siblings of one Black Atlantic analytic. They share the structural diagnosis, differ in national versus colonial frame, psychological versus bodily emphasis, and reformist versus revolutionary horizon. Together they constitute the experiential foundation on which contemporary critical race theory rests.


### Mock 12. Using the revision document's CRT material, explain how Du Bois's "racial realism" is extended by Critical Race Theory.

In this essay I explain how Critical Race Theory extends Du Bois's foundational move. CRT preserves Du Bois's anti-essentialism while generalising his diagnosis of post-Emancipation failure into a structural account of contemporary racial law.

The lecture sources CRT's "racial realism" to *Dusk of Dawn*: race is challenged biologically while "foregrounding reality of racial experience as a social fact, not an essence but experienced in terms of unequal treatment" (revision document §8). Du Bois's foundational claim: "the difference in skin color was vastly overemphasized and intrinsically trivial. And yet this fact of racial distinction based on color was the greatest thing in my life and absolutely determined it" (Du Bois, 1940: 136). The "and yet" is the move CRT inherits. The Black man is "a person who must ride 'Jim Crow' in Georgia" (Du Bois, 1940: 153); race is real because the practice is real.

CRT generalises this into the proposition that the US is still a white-supremacist society: "Critical Race Theory claims that US is still a white supremacist society and that there is a myth of racial progress" (§8). This is the structural form of Du Bois's "The Nation has not yet found peace from its sins; the freedman has not yet found in freedom his promised land" (Du Bois, 1903: 5). Where Du Bois names the post-Emancipation failure, CRT names the post-Civil-Rights failure: formal legal equality granted, substantive racial subordination persists.

Four CRT extensions of Du Bois's realism follow.

First, rejection of the myth of racial progress. The revision document: "racial progress is always pushed back, and only occurs through 'interest convergence' (when it is in white interests)" (§8). This recapitulates Du Bois's observation that the Emancipation Proclamation and Fifteenth Amendment were not enough. Each apparent racial advance is liable to be reversed when the white majority's interest in it wanes.

Second, interest convergence. This generalises Du Bois's catalogue of how Reconstruction was undone, "the holocaust of war, the terrors of the Ku-Klux Klan, the lies of carpet-baggers, the disorganization of industry" (Du Bois, 1903: 5), into a general law of racial politics. Generic affirmative-action debates illustrate the dynamic: legal and institutional gains contract when dominant-group interest fades.

Third, institutional specification. The revision document names: "The School to Prison pipeline, Prisons and the Army are a modern form of Black slavery." Each is a concrete site at which racial subordination is reproduced. The pipeline names how school discipline feeds Black students into the criminal justice system; prisons and the army are carceral and military continuations of the labour-extraction logic Du Bois (1898) traced in seventeenth-century slave statutes. Black Lives Matter mobilisations after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor have made these sites publicly visible; generic policing concerns operate at the same level.

Fourth, counter-storytelling as method. The revision document: "Counter-storytelling can be used as a methodology to reveal Black epistemologies" (§8). This is the methodological cousin of Du Bois's second sight: "born with a veil, and gifted with second-sight in this American world" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). The subordinated subject has epistemic privilege about the structure that subordinates her. CRT formalises Du Boisian second sight into a research method.

Morrison and Gilroy connect to CRT. Morrison's "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25) supplies the affective component; Gilroy's demand to "re-write" history from Black perspectives (§8) parallels counter-storytelling. L6 supplies the epistemic lineage: Hill Collins (1990) names Du Bois as ancestor of Black feminist standpoint, so CRT's counter-storytelling is the legal-methodological inheritor of the same epistemic claim, namely that the subordinated position has analytical purchase the dominant position lacks.

CRT's extension is faithful to Du Bois. Du Bois already held that race is social fact, that legal emancipation was insufficient, and that the subordinated have a privileged epistemic position. CRT adds institutional specificity, a general principle of progress-and-reversal, and a research method.

The objection that CRT's pessimism overshoots Du Bois's hope misfires. Du Bois ends *Souls* with the possibility that "two world-races may give each to each" (Du Bois, 1903: 7). CRT's myth-of-racial-progress claim specifies what Du Bois implied: legal change without structural change is reversible. *Selma* dramatises the gap between formal legal victory and substantive racial reality.

CRT extends Du Bois's racial realism in four directions: rejecting the myth of racial progress, formalising interest convergence, specifying institutional sites of racial reproduction, and developing counter-storytelling as method. Gilroy's *Black Atlantic* extends the lineage to the diasporic scale; Morrison's *Origin of Others* supplies the affective motor; CRT supplies the institutional and methodological extension.

### Mock 13. Is whiteness a racial identity or a structural position? Discuss.

In this essay I argue whiteness is best understood as a structural position that, in racialised societies, also becomes available as a racial identity. The two registers are connected, with the structural position generating the identity. I make the case through Morrison, Du Bois and Gilroy.

To call whiteness a racial identity is to treat it as self-ascription, felt belonging, culture. To call it structural is to treat it as the unmarked position in a racial hierarchy conferring material and symbolic advantages without subjective identification. The two are not mutually exclusive but generate different politics.

I think whiteness is primarily structural. Three reasons.

First, historically, whiteness has been produced by the operations of racial classification, not by a pre-existing community claiming the name. Morrison observes that "immigrants to the United States understood that if they wanted to become 'real' Americans they must sever or at least downplay their ties to their native country, in order to embrace their whiteness. The definition of 'Americanness' (sadly) remains color for many people" (Morrison, 2017: 17). Whiteness was achieved through political and cultural processes, not inherited.

Second, sociologically, whiteness operates as unmarked-ness: the default racial position against which other positions are read as racially specific. Du Bois named the dynamic when he described the racialised self as seeing itself "through the revelation of the other world" (Du Bois, 1903: 3), the "other world" being the white world whose racial position is invisible to itself. Morrison's othering, "a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29), depends on whiteness functioning as the normal. L9 postcolonial extends this: Said (1978) shows the same operation in Orientalist scholarship, where "the West" is the unmarked vantage from which "the Orient" is described, the discursive counterpart to whiteness as structural anchor. Gilroy's analysis of "the order of active differentiation that gets called 'race'" (Gilroy, 1998: 252) names the structural anchor itself.

Third, materially, whiteness organises institutional practice. Du Bois's 1898 essay shows that the modern racial categorisation was a labour-supply solution: "such statutes sought to solve problems of labor and not of race or color" (Du Bois, 1898: 3); but once enacted, the racial categories acquired their own institutional life. The revision document's contemporary examples (the school-to-prison pipeline, prisons and the army as "modern form of Black slavery") reproduce the structural advantage of whiteness even where no individual official claims it as identity. Cost-of-living racialised wealth gaps operate at the same level.

The identity register matters too. Morrison's immigrants "embrace their whiteness" (Morrison, 2017: 17); the embrace is identity-claiming. The slide 23 annotation on Trump-era rhetoric about "Mexican-Americans" and Brexit-era hostile-environment debates show contemporary politics mobilising white identity. The defence of whiteness as identity is the affective ground of its defence as structure.

The structural position is primary and produces the identity. When unchallenged, whiteness operates as unmarked default; when challenged, it becomes self-conscious and the identity register thickens.

Three test cases. First, "Where are you really from?" (slide 4): whiteness as structure operating; the questioner does not need to claim white identity to perform the racial sorting. Second, the 1868 "Apollo Belvidere / Creole Negro / Young Chimpanzee" plate (slide 9): whiteness as identity (the Greek ideal) protecting whiteness as structure. Third, immigrant Americanisation: identity-acquisition is at the same time structural-position acquisition. Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor highlights the inverse: structural disparities prompting both anti-racist counter-storytelling and reactive white identity-claiming.

Can whiteness as identity be politically productive? Some anti-racist scholarship treats white self-reflection as necessary; Gilroy in 'Race Ends Here' and *Against Race* worries that doubling down on racial identity may entrench what anti-racism should dismantle. White self-reflection is useful only insofar as it acts on the structural position.

Du Bois's normative horizon ends *Souls* with the demand that "He simply wishes to make it possible for a man to be both a Negro and an American" (Du Bois, 1903: 3). Gilroy hopes for "anti-toxins capable of silencing raciology forever" (Gilroy, 1998: 255). The end-state is one where neither whiteness nor any other racial category is the structural position.

Whiteness is both racial identity and structural position, with the structural primary. Disparities operate at the structural level; the identity register thickens when the structural position is challenged. Anti-racist politics that targets only identity without redistributing structural position will fail. Politics that redistributes structural position will dissolve the identity register because whiteness as identity is parasitic on whiteness as structure.

### Mock 14. Discuss Du Bois's claim that race emerged as a labour-supply solution.

In this essay I discuss Du Bois's claim in 'The Study of the Negro Problems' (1898) that race emerged in the seventeenth-century American colonies as a labour-supply solution. The claim is foundational, anticipates Gilroy's structural argument, and anchors Morrison's "race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25).

Slide 20 reproduces the passage: "In the latter part of the seventeenth and early in the eighteenth centuries, the central and all-absorbing economic need of America was the creation of a proper labor supply to develop American wealth. This question had been answered in the West Indies by enslaving Indians and Negroes. In the colonies of the mainland it was answered by the importation of Negroes and indented servants" (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4). The racial slave system was the answer to a labour-supply question, not the implementation of pre-existing racial doctrine.

The second move is legal. "Dozens of enactments, from Massachusetts to Georgia, were made 'for the proper regulation of slaves and servants'" (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4). The statutes regulated labour, not races. Du Bois's gloss is decisive: "Such statutes sought to solve problems of labor and not of race or color" (Du Bois, 1898: 3). The racial line was a by-product of labour regulation.

The third move is the hardening. "Two circumstances, however, soon began to differentiate in the problem of labor: the economic superiority of the slave system, and the fact that the slaves were neither of the same race, language nor religion as the servants and their masters" (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4). Economic superiority of slavery combined with linguistic, religious and morphological difference produced the racial categorisation scientific racism would later "discover."

The fourth move is formalisation. "Colonial statutes soon ceased to embrace the regulations applying to slaves and servants in one chapter, and laws were passed for servants on the one hand and for Negro slaves on the other" (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4). The legal architecture diverged; the racial category was inscribed in colonial law.

The passage is foundational anti-essentialism. Race is not the natural cause of slavery; slavery is the cause of race. The statutes did not implement a racial doctrine; they produced it.

This connects to scientific racism. Linnaeus (1735), Blumenbach's typology, the 1868 "Apollo Belvidere / Creole Negro / Young Chimpanzee" plate and the 1933 Nazi racial measurements (slide 9) are all downstream of the legal-economic apparatus. Scientific racism operated on bodies the colonial statutes had already sorted. Foucault's power-knowledge framing fits: the science observed what the slave economy had already organised.

Gilroy. *The Black Atlantic* argues that "Plantation slavery was more than just a system of labour" (Gilroy, 1993: 54); it provided "the foundations for a distinctive network of economic, social, and political relations" (Gilroy, 1993: 55). Du Bois's 1898 essay gives Gilroy's structural claim its legal-economic mechanism. The L2 decolonial framing sharpens the point: Dussel (1993) holds that "European modernity is based on violence," and Du Bois's slave statutes are precisely the colonial-legal violence on which modern wealth was built. Gilroy's polemic that "racial terror is not merely compatible with occidental rationality but cheerfully complicit with it" (Gilroy, 1993: 56) reads the same evidence at higher pitch.

Morrison. Her "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25) and the dominant group's "desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29) describe the affective machinery the legal-economic machinery requires. The planter benefited materially from the statutes; he then needed racial categorisation to feel normal in the world they built.

Contemporary purchase. The revision document's CRT examples (school-to-prison pipeline; prisons and the army as "modern form of Black slavery") extend the argument forward: the colonial-statute logic of categorising bodies for labour is reproduced in categorising bodies for incarceration. Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor exposes the contemporary face.

Objections. First, the account is too materialist. Reply: Du Bois's later work (*Dusk of Dawn*, *Souls*) supplies the cultural and phenomenological correlates. Second, the account is US-specific. Reply, via Gilroy: the Black Atlantic generalises the diagnosis.

Du Bois's 1898 claim is foundational, accurate and generative. Race emerged as a labour-supply solution; the racial doctrine was downstream of the slave statutes; scientific racism then dressed the categorisation in biological clothing. Gilroy generalises to the Black Atlantic; Morrison adds the affective dimension; CRT extends to contemporary institutions. The 1898 essay is the empirical and legal anchor that grounds the lecture's argument that race is socially produced, not biologically discovered.

### Mock 15. Does the science Gilroy describes in 'Race Ends Here' vindicate or refute scientific racism?

Drawing on Gilroy's 'Race Ends Here' (1998), modern science refutes scientific racism as doctrine while creating conditions under which racial categorisation persists as an after-image. The case rests on Gilroy and on Du Bois's and Morrison's accounts of why doctrinal refutation is necessary but not sufficient.

Gilroy describes a "shift from natural history to biology" and further to molecular biology and digital imaging: "Optical microscopes transformed what could be seen but the new technologies of seeing on ever smaller and smaller scales moved the threshold of visibility" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). MRI and similar imaging have "remade the relationship between the seeable and the unseen" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). The "Euclidean anatomy" of nineteenth-century scientific racism has been outflanked.

"Scientific and biological, historical and cultural, rational and irrational, skin, bone and even blood are no longer primary referents of racial discourse" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). Bio-racial differences vanish "at these levels of resolution" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). The lecture: "Races do not exist" (slide 30).

This refutes scientific racism as doctrine. The technical apparatus on which the doctrine rested (skull-shape comparison after Blumenbach, racial typology after Linnaeus, craniometric measurement) has been superseded. Gilroy's metaphor: "perhaps 'race' might best be approached as an after-image, a lingering symptom of looking too intently or too casually into the damaging glare emanating from colonial conflicts at home and abroad" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). An after-image is real to the perceiver but has no current external referent. Scientific racism's biological referent is gone; its perceptual residue remains.

Three limits to doctrinal refutation.

First, the molecular science that refutes nineteenth-century scientific racism is not innocent. "The eugenic ravings of Francis Crick, the Nobel prize winning co-discoverer of DNA" (Gilroy, 1998: 253) show that "the fateful change of scale involved in the founding of molecular biology" inherited race-thinking.

Second, perceptual habit outlasts doctrine. Fanon's epidermalisation names "the dismal order of power and differentiation, defined by its intention to make the mute body disclose the truth of its racial identities" (Gilroy, 1998: 254). The body is still read racially; the 1868 "Apollo Belvidere / Creole Negro / Young Chimpanzee" plate (slide 9) trained a way of seeing whose habits persist.

Third, "Euclidean anatomy" has not been overturned but recontextualised. The "anatomical scale" retains "that special baggage of perspectival inclinations, perceptual habits and scalar assumptions" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). Race-thinking is displaced into new vocabularies.

Du Bois. Genomic refutation vindicates Du Bois's anti-essentialism: "the difference in skin color was vastly overemphasized and intrinsically trivial" (Du Bois, 1940: 136). But the "and yet" remains: "this fact of racial distinction based on color was the greatest thing in my life and absolutely determined it" (Du Bois, 1940: 136). Du Bois's realism, "the black man is a person who must ride 'Jim Crow' in Georgia" (Du Bois, 1940: 153), means race persists as social practice.

Morrison. "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25) explains why doctrinal refutation is not enough. Power continues to produce racial categorisation, and "rendering the slave a foreign species appears to be a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29) describes the affective economy power exploits. Where doctrine is refuted but power persists, race persists.

Gilroy's normative claim: to find raciology's "contemporary analogs not where he looked, on the surface of the body, but deep within it. Their pursuit may yet yield the anti-toxins capable of silencing raciology forever" (Gilroy, 1998: 255). The molecular era can produce conditions under which raciology fades, but only if the perceptual and institutional habits are also dismantled. L7's biopower (Foucault, 1978) names what those institutional habits do: race is administered as a population-level technology of life, so Gilroy's "chemical gaze" is biopower migrating from skull to genome rather than disappearing.

Two objections. First, group genetic differences supposedly vindicate the concept of race. Gilroy's reply (1998: 254): the molecular scale dissolves the categorical boundaries scientific racism required. Second, after-images fade but race does not. Du Bois and Morrison reply: race does not fade because institutions and power continue to reproduce it.

The slide-30 conclusion captures the two-part answer: "Races do not exist. But the experiences constituted by the belief, practices, history and economics of 'race' do." The science refutes the doctrine; the experiences and institutions persist. The vindication is partial: scientific racism is refuted in the lab but not abolished in the institution. The intellectual war is won; the practical war is not. Gilroy's "anti-toxins" remain a normative aspiration whose conditions of possibility he is still mapping.

### Mock 16. How convincing do you find Morrison's claim that whiteness creates the Other?

In this essay I find Morrison's claim that whiteness creates the Other convincing and defend it on three grounds: it captures the historical record, explains the affective dynamics of racism, and provides a productive analytical frame for institutional analysis. I qualify the claim only by noting that it works best paired with Du Bois's structural account and Gilroy's Black Atlantic frame.

In *The Origin of Others* Morrison presses: "What is race (other than genetic imagination)?" (Morrison, 2017: 15). Race is the residue of power exerted to confirm the dominant group's normality: "The necessity of rendering the slave a foreign species appears to be a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29). Citing Baum: "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25). Othering is racism's productive mechanism: whiteness manufactures the Others that make it possible as a stabilised dominant position. The revision document: "race / whiteness creates the concept of the 'Other'" (§8).

This inverts the familiar account. A naive view treats race as a property of the racialised. Morrison reverses: whiteness is the operation, Black is the residue.

I evaluate on three grounds.

First, the historical record. Du Bois had already shown seventeenth-century slave statutes were responses to a labour-supply problem: "Such statutes sought to solve problems of labor and not of race or color" (Du Bois, 1898: 3). The legal infrastructure was a creation of white legal authority. Whiteness, precisely, made Blackness.

Second, the affective dynamics of contemporary racism. Morrison's account explains the disproportion between the threat racialised others pose and the intensity of the reaction. The "desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29) describes the register. The revision document: "American identity is tied to whiteness, reinforced by media and culture / law and order / religion" (§8). Brexit-era hostile-environment debates and Trump-era policy framings show the dynamic in real time.

Third, the productive analytical frame for institutional analysis. The revision document's CRT examples (school-to-prison pipeline; prisons and the army as "modern form of Black slavery"; interest convergence) read as Morrison-applied: each pattern is whiteness producing the other to confirm itself. Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor makes the production visible.

Rivals. First, racism as individual prejudice. Morrison explains why racism persists where individual prejudice is unusual; production is in institutions, not just hearts.

Second, racism as economic exploitation incidentally racial. Du Bois shows slave statutes as responses to labour supply, but the account underplays the affective and identarian dimensions. Why has racism persisted across capitalist restructuring? Morrison's effect-of-power framing handles this: power produces race because power needs race to confirm itself.

Third, racism as biological misperception science can correct. Morrison explains why this fails: race is not a perceptual error but a power operation. Gilroy: racial differentiation is "modernity's most pernicious signature" (Gilroy, 1998: 252), not a removable confusion.

I qualify Morrison's account. Whiteness creates the Other by exploiting a historical accumulation Du Bois has already named: the colour line, the veil, the post-Reconstruction failure. Without Du Bois's structural picture, Morrison's account can sound voluntaristic. With it, Morrison specifies the affective machinery that keeps an inherited structural settlement reproducing.

Gilroy. *The Black Atlantic* shows that modernity required "the figures of black folks who had previously been confined to the intermediate category between animal and human that Du Bois identifies as a 'tertium quid'" (Gilroy, 1993: 55). Morrison's othering was Atlantic in scale. L9 postcolonial extends the same operation transnationally: Mohanty (1984) shows how Western feminism constructs the "Third World Woman" as a homogeneous Other to stabilise its own emancipated self-image, the textbook example of Morrisonian othering working through scholarship.

Examples. The slide 23 annotation on Trump-era rhetoric about "Mexican-Americans" is Morrison applied in real time. Her media-othering thesis (slide 24): "routine media presentations deploy images and language that narrow our views of what humans look like" (Morrison, 2017: 37). Cultural references like *Get Out* and *Black Mirror* stage and critique the narrowing.

Morrison's claim is convincing because it fits the historical record, explains contemporary affective dynamics, and grounds productive institutional analysis. It works best paired with Du Bois's structural picture and Gilroy's Black Atlantic scale, but it identifies the affective core other accounts miss. Whiteness is a project of self-confirmation that requires manufactured difference. The project succeeds because the manufactured difference is mistaken for the explanation rather than the symptom.


### Mock 17. Answer with reference to Gilroy's 'Race Ends Here': what does it mean to say that race has become an "after-image"?

In this essay I explain what Gilroy means by saying race has become "an after-image" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). The metaphor combines a thesis about technological-perceptual change with a normative project of overcoming raciology; I assess its purchase against the lecture's wider analysis.

Gilroy writes that "'race' might best be approached as an after-image, a lingering symptom of looking too intently or too casually into the damaging glare emanating from colonial conflicts at home and abroad" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). The image is optical: an after-image is the visual trace left on the retina after the source of light is removed. It is real to the perceiver but has no current external referent. Race is the after-image of scientific racism: a perceptual reality whose biological cause is gone.

Three claims.

First, technological-perceptual change. The "Euclidean anatomy" of nineteenth-century scientific racism, measuring skulls and classifying physiognomies, produced race as an observable scientific object. Linnaeus (1735) and Blumenbach's five-race typology belong to this regime. But contemporary techniques (molecular biology, MRI, digital imaging) have outflanked it: "Scientific and biological, historical and cultural, rational and irrational, skin, bone and even blood are no longer primary referents of racial discourse" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). The technical apparatus that supported scientific racism has been replaced by one that does not see race.

Second, the persistence of perception. Racial perception continues despite the dissolution of the biological referent: "raciological ways of organizing and classifying the world have retained that special baggage of perspectival inclinations, perceptual habits and scalar assumptions" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). Race exists out of step with the scientific moment that produced it; it survives its own refutation.

Third, the normative claim. Gilroy hopes for "anti-toxins capable of silencing raciology forever" (Gilroy, 1998: 255). 'Race Ends Here' is programmatic.

The metaphor does important work. First, it captures something true about scientific racism's afterlife: Du Bois's insight that "the difference in skin color was vastly overemphasized and intrinsically trivial" (Du Bois, 1940: 136) was powerless on its own to dissolve race because race operates as perception. Second, it locates the political problem in perceptual training. Third, it suggests race may yet end, since after-images fade.

But the metaphor has limits.

First, it underplays institutional reproduction. After-images fade because no new light reinforces them; race does not fade because institutions reproduce it. The revision document: "racial progress is always pushed back" through interest convergence (§8). The school-to-prison pipeline and the carceral-military continuation of slavery are sources of fresh "light"; Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor makes the recharging visible.

Second, the metaphor risks suggesting scientific argument can dissolve race. Decades of argument have not. Du Bois's racial realism explains the persistence more directly.

Third, it underplays the agential dimension Morrison emphasises. Race is actively produced by power: "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25); "rendering the slave a foreign species appears to be a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29). The metaphor risks freezing race in the past while it is still being made.

Gilroy has a reply. The metaphor displaces biological scientific racism specifically; it does not deny race's institutional life. He acknowledges racial differentiation "may be modernity's most pernicious signature" (Gilroy, 1998: 252) and persists where biology no longer underwrites it.

Other Gilroy concepts extend the analysis. Fanon's "epidermalization" names the colonial process by which bodies are made meaningful through "qualities of 'colour'" (Gilroy, 1998: 254) and continues even where the biological theory has been retired. The "chemical gaze" of contemporary biomedical technologies (Gilroy, 1998: 252) produces new perceptual regimes that can reinscribe race. L10 supplies the counter-pressure: hooks (1992) on the "oppositional gaze" shows that the Black spectator can look back at the after-image, refusing the passive position scientific racism's visual training prescribed.

Du Bois tests the metaphor. *Dusk of Dawn*: "the black man is a person who must ride 'Jim Crow' in Georgia" (Du Bois, 1940: 153). The after-image needs addition: institutions continue to use it as current reality. The metaphor gives the perceptual diagnosis; Du Bois the institutional.

Gilroy's after-image captures something important (race persists as perceptual reality after biological supports have collapsed) but is incomplete on its own. Race is reproduced as well as remembered; institutions, media and political mobilisations actively manufacture racial categorisation. 'Race Ends Here' is best read as a normative call rather than a descriptive claim; the fade requires the political and institutional work the metaphor hopes to provoke.

### Mock 18. Using at least two authors, explain why "race ends here" is harder than it sounds.

In this essay I use Du Bois, Morrison and Gilroy himself to explain why Gilroy's slogan that race ends here (1998) is harder than it sounds. The slogan is right biologically and admirable normatively, but the social, institutional and affective infrastructure of race is far harder to dismantle than the doctrine that has been refuted.

Gilroy hopes for "anti-toxins capable of silencing raciology forever" (Gilroy, 1998: 255) and treats race as "an after-image" (Gilroy, 1998: 253). Scientifically, molecular biology and digital imaging have outflanked the "Euclidean anatomy" of scientific racism. Politically, cultural and technological shifts may enable the end of raciology.

But Gilroy names the difficulty. Racial differentiation "may be modernity's most pernicious signature" (Gilroy, 1998: 252); it is deeply embedded. Raciological habits "retained that special baggage of perspectival inclinations, perceptual habits and scalar assumptions" (Gilroy, 1998: 253).

Du Bois specifies the social difficulty. *Dusk of Dawn* anticipates Gilroy by separating biology from social reality: "the difference in skin color was vastly overemphasized and intrinsically trivial. And yet this fact of racial distinction based on color was the greatest thing in my life and absolutely determined it" (Du Bois, 1940: 136). The "and yet" is the problem. Even where biology fails to ground race, the practice remains binding: "the black man is a person who must ride 'Jim Crow' in Georgia" (Du Bois, 1940: 153). Ending race requires ending the practices that constitute it.

Morrison specifies the affective difficulty. "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25) names the mechanism. "Rendering the slave a foreign species appears to be a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29) names the affective payoff. Until the affective economy of othering is dismantled, race will keep being recreated. The L9 postcolonial extension is Said (1978), whose account of Orientalism shows discursive racism (the East as essentialised body of knowledge) outliving its biological cousin: scientific racism ends, discursive racism continues.

Five reasons follow.

First, institutional inertia. Du Bois's colonial labour statutes (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4) show the depth of embedding. The revision document's CRT examples (school-to-prison pipeline; prisons and the army as "modern form of Black slavery") name the carceral, educational and military institutions that continue to operate with racial categorisation. Ending these requires reformatting data infrastructures, retraining personnel, changing statutory frameworks.

Second, perceptual habit. Fanon's epidermalisation, bodies endowed with "qualities of 'colour'" (Gilroy, 1998: 254), names the deep perceptual training. The 1868 "Apollo Belvidere / Creole Negro / Young Chimpanzee" plate (slide 9) is one visual technology that did the original training; its descendants continue to operate.

Third, the political utility of race. Morrison's account explains why political actors keep recreating the category. The slide 23 annotation on Trump-era rhetoric about "Mexican-Americans" and Brexit-era hostile-environment debates show contemporary instances. Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor shows race re-emerging as the medium of counter-mobilisation.

Fourth, the symmetric problem of anti-racist mobilisation. Anti-racism uses racial categories to measure disparities and organise solidarity. CRT operationalises this through counter-storytelling; Gilroy in *Against Race* (2000) acknowledges the tension and wants a transitional anti-racism that uses racial categories to dismantle racialisation. Generic affirmative-action debates illustrate the dilemma.

Fifth, the historical depth of the Black Atlantic. Gilroy treats slavery as constitutive: "Plantation slavery provided the foundations for a distinctive network of economic, social, and political relations" (Gilroy, 1993: 54). The wealth and institutions of European modernity were forged through the Black Atlantic. Ending race requires rewriting modernity itself. Gilroy's normative demand: "the primal history of modernity [must be] reconstructed from the slaves' points of view" (Gilroy, 1993: 55).

The Gilroyan reply. 'Race Ends Here' is a normative target. I accept this, but the programme has to overcome institutional inertia, perceptual habit, political utility, the symmetric problem of anti-racist measurement and the historical depth of the Black Atlantic.

Du Bois shows race is real because racism is real; biological refutation is necessary but not sufficient. Morrison shows race is an effect of power; refuting the doctrine does not deprive power of the affective work race performs. Gilroy's slogan is correct in principle but requires institutional and affective work the slogan cannot do.

Race ends here is harder than it sounds because race is reproduced by institutions, perceptual habits, political utility, anti-racist measurement and the historical depth of modernity. Gilroy is right about the direction; Du Bois and Morrison show why the journey is longer.

### Mock 19. Can sociology abolish race without losing the analytical category?

In this essay I argue that sociology cannot abolish race in the present without losing analytical and political traction, but that it can and should work towards a future in which the category becomes unnecessary. The argument rests on the distinction between abolishing race as biological doctrine (already done in principle) and abolishing race as analytical category (premature, but worth aspiring to). I make the case through Du Bois, Morrison, Gilroy and CRT.

The question can mean several things: should sociology stop using the category? Can its use be reformed without dropping it? What is the timeline of category-loss? I take all three readings seriously.

The strongest abolitionist case is Gilroy's. In 'Race Ends Here' (1998) and *Against Race* (2000) he hopes for "anti-toxins capable of silencing raciology forever" (Gilroy, 1998: 255) and worries that sociological use of racial categories can reinscribe what it tries to dismantle. The categorising practices of sociology are continuous with the classificatory practices that originally produced race. Each measurement reinforces the category's salience. L9 supplies a sharper version of the dilemma: Fanon (1967) sees that the "white gaze" produces the Black subject as racial, so any anti-racism that simply names the racial subject risks repeating the gaze it opposes. The abolitionist programme would have sociology stop using race at all.

The case is ethically attractive but practically premature. Three reasons.

First, race remains real as social fact. Du Bois's mature position in *Dusk of Dawn* is that race is biologically trivial but socially decisive: "the black man is a person who must ride 'Jim Crow' in Georgia" (Du Bois, 1940: 153). The revision document's CRT examples (school-to-prison pipeline; prisons and the army as a "modern form of Black slavery") name contemporary institutional sites where racial categorisation operates. Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor, racialised cost-of-living and wealth gaps, generic policing concerns all require racial measurement to be named. Stopping measurement would make these disparities harder to see and address.

Second, race operates as power-effect that continues to be reproduced. Morrison's "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25) names the mechanism. Sociology has to track the production to analyse it. An abolitionist sociology would describe institutional racism without naming the categorising operation institutional racism performs.

Third, anti-racist politics requires racial measurement. CRT's diagnostic work depends on the racial category: interest convergence requires data showing differential treatment; counter-storytelling requires identifying the subjugated standpoint. Removing the category does not remove the inequality but does remove the political tools for naming it.

Four reform moves.

First, treat the category as historical and constructed. "Races do not exist" biologically (slide 30); Du Bois's "Race is a cultural, sometimes a historical fact" (Du Bois, 1940: 153) is the right framing.

Second, distinguish use from reification. Sociology can use racial categories without claiming they track natural kinds; the same logic applies to class and gender.

Third, design categorisation to be self-undermining. The category exists because the disparity exists; dismantle the disparity, and the category becomes unnecessary. Gilroy's "anti-toxins" (Gilroy, 1998: 255) is the right horizon.

Fourth, integrate Morrison and Du Bois. Track the affective work (Morrison) alongside the structural reproduction (Du Bois, CRT).

Three objections. First, Gilroy: any use of race entrenches it. Reply: not measuring race makes it invisible, not absent. Reflexive use, not abolition.

Second, colour-blindness: race-conscious sociology contributes to the divisions it studies. CRT's reply: colour-blindness in a racially structured society protects the structure. Generic affirmative-action debates show the trade-off.

Third, methodological: race in survey data conflates self-identification, ascription and ancestry. The right response is refinement, not abolition.

Du Bois's "Equality in law is not enough" applies. Formal abolition of racial categorisation in law does not abolish the social fact. Cultural references like *Get Out* and *Selma*, and Brexit-era and Trump-era policy framings, show the gap between formal de-categorisation and substantive structure.

Sociology should work towards a future where race is no longer needed analytically, because the infrastructure has been dismantled. The work is generational. In the meantime, use the category reflexively, with the aim of dissolving the conditions that require it.

Sociology cannot abolish race in the present without losing the traction needed to measure and contest disparities, but it can work towards a future where the category becomes unnecessary. The intermediate path is reflexive use: race as historical and constructed, held analytically rather than reified. Du Bois, Morrison and Gilroy support this. The end of race is a horizon, not a starting move.

### Mock 20. Discuss the role of the Sorrow Songs and Black cultural production in Du Bois's *Souls*.

In this essay I discuss the role of the Sorrow Songs and Black cultural production in Du Bois's *Souls of Black Folk* (1903). I argue they function as the affirmative counterpoint to the diagnostic of the veil and double consciousness. Where double consciousness names the doubling imposed by the colour line, the Sorrow Songs name the cultural production by which the doubled subject creates something irreducible to the dominant world.

The Forethought announces the architectural role of the Sorrow Songs: "Before each chapter, as now printed, stands a bar of the Sorrow Songs, some echo of haunting melody from the only American music which welled up from black souls in the dark past" (Du Bois, 1903: Forethought). Each chapter opens with two epigraphs: a fragment of European poetry and a bar of musical notation from a Black spiritual. Du Bois's editorial decision is programmatic: the European canon and the Black spiritual share the page.

The Sorrow Songs return at chapter ends: "there is no true American music but the wild sweet melodies of the Negro slave; the American fairy tales and folk-lore are Indian and African" (Du Bois, 1903: 7). The Sorrow Songs are evidence that the Black presence in America is constitutive, not residual.

Three functions follow.

First, evidential. The Sorrow Songs are Du Bois's evidence that Black life under the veil produces something distinctive. America's defining music is Black; America's self-image as white obscures this. The cultural production rebuts the white world's "amused contempt and pity" (Du Bois, 1903: 3).

Second, methodological. *Souls* is doubled. Du Bois writes as sociologist (the 1898 labour-statute analysis) and as man of letters (chapter epigraphs, lyrical passages, closing chapter on the Sorrow Songs). The doubling of method matches the doubling of consciousness. Black cultural production is the medium through which Du Bois's analysis becomes possible.

Third, normative. The Sorrow Songs anchor Du Bois's hope. *Souls* ends with the demand that "two world-races may give each to each those characteristics both so sadly lack" (Du Bois, 1903: 7). They are "the soul-beauty of a race which his larger audience despised" (Du Bois, 1903: 4); they make the merger into "a better and truer self" (Du Bois, 1903: 3) worth pursuing.

The lecture presents Du Bois as the indispensable Black sociologist of modernity; the Sorrow Songs show he is also a Black artist of modernity. The "creative, communicative use of the memory of slavery" Gilroy (1993: 55) names as central to the Black Atlantic is exemplified here: a musical practice born under slavery becomes the cultural matter of post-Emancipation Black life.

Gilroy. *The Black Atlantic* treats Black music as the bar of the Sorrow Songs writ large, extended to a transnational Black cultural circuit. Du Bois's textual practice prefigures Gilroy's theorisation: Black culture is constitutive of, not derivative from, modernity. The polemic that "racial terror is not merely compatible with occidental rationality but cheerfully complicit with it" (Gilroy, 1993: 56) sharpens Du Bois's musical evidence: the music welled up from souls held under that terror.

Morrison. Her observation that "routine media presentations deploy images and language that narrow our views of what humans look like" (Morrison, 2017: 37) provides the contemporary contrast. Du Bois's epigraphs widen the view; Morrison's complaint is that contemporary media narrow. L10 develops the widening into a politics of looking: hooks (1992) on the "oppositional gaze" treats Black visual and cultural production as active counter-seeing, the heir of Du Bois's Sorrow Songs in a media-saturated present. Cultural references like *Get Out* and *Selma* operate in this tradition.

The objection that the Sorrow Songs risk romanticising Black suffering misfires. Du Bois keeps suffering and cultural production tightly coupled. The songs "welled up from black souls in the dark past" (Du Bois, 1903: Forethought); they are not separable from the conditions that produced them.

A second objection, that Black gifts to America assimilate the political demand, Du Bois resists. The demand is substantive equality: "Work, culture, liberty, all these we need, not singly but together" (Du Bois, 1903: 7). The cultural offering is part of the case for equality, not a substitute.

The Sorrow Songs serve three roles: evidential, methodological, and normative. Du Bois's text prefigures the Black Atlantic; Morrison's worry about media narrowing finds in Du Bois's editorial widening one of its remedies. The Sorrow Songs are the affirmative half of *Souls*: not denial of the veil, but proof that the veiled subject creates.

### Mock 21. What does Gilroy mean by saying race is modernity's "most pernicious signature"?

In this essay I explain what Gilroy means by race as "modernity's most pernicious signature" (Gilroy, 1998: 252). The phrase carries three claims: racial categorisation is constitutive of modernity, integrally damaging, and articulated in a grammar linking science, nationality and political power.

Gilroy writes: "Though it preceded the distinctive quality of sociality we distinguish as modern, the order of active differentiation that gets called 'race' may be modernity's most pernicious signature. It articulated reason and unreason. It knitted together science and superstition. Raciology required that enlightenment and myth be intertwined. 'Race' and nationality supplied the logic and mechanism of their interconnections" (Gilroy, 1998: 252).

Three components.

First, the "signature" metaphor. A signature is both authorship and authenticity. Modernity authored race; race authenticates modernity. Race is not a by-product but a defining mark.

Second, "most pernicious." Modernity has many signatures: capitalism, industrial production, bureaucratic administration. Among these, race is the most damaging. Scientific racism authorised slavery, colonial extraction and genocidal violence; the lecture's lineage from Linnaeus (1735) through Blumenbach to the 1933 photograph traces the perniciousness.

Third, articulation. Race "articulates reason and unreason." Modernity presents itself as reason over myth; race shows modern reason produced scientific racism and modern enlightenment produced racial myths.

The geopolitical dimension. "'race' and nationality supplied the logic and mechanism of their interconnections" (Gilroy, 1998: 252). The European nation-state defined itself racially (against the colonised, against the slaves); the racial science of Blumenbach and his successors supplied the categorisation; colonial bureaucracy enforced it. Modernity's national-rational form has race built into its joints.
