Du Bois supplies legal-economic evidence. The slave statutes "from Massachusetts to Georgia" (Du Bois, 1898: 3-4) were the original signing. The racial line was inscribed in colonial law to organise labour; modernity then read it as natural. *Dusk of Dawn* exposes the trick: "the difference in skin color was vastly overemphasized and intrinsically trivial" (Du Bois, 1940: 136); the signature was signed by power, not nature.

Morrison supplies the affective dimension. "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25). The signature is not just legal-administrative but identarian. The affective work of othering ("a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal," Morrison, 2017: 29) maintains the signature even when the legal ink has faded.

Three implications.

First, periodisation. If race is modernity's signature, then modernity cannot be dated from rational achievements alone without dating it from racial atrocities. Slide 28: "Africa was not on the side-lines of the West and the development of modernity."

Second, critique. "Racial terror is not merely compatible with occidental rationality but cheerfully complicit with it" (Gilroy, 1993: 56) follows. Rationality and racial terror rose together. The L2 decolonial pairing is direct: Dussel (1993) treats "European modernity" as "based on violence" against its colonial underside, while Howard French (2021) shows African labour and African gold subsidising the so-called rational European centuries. Gilroy's "signature" is the racial form of the violence Dussel names and the labour-extraction French quantifies.

Third, normative. Ending race requires changing modernity itself. Gilroy's demand to "rewrite history and modernity from these positions" (slide 27) follows. Adding Black voices does not change the signature; the signature has to be erased.

Two objections. First, the framing is too totalising. Reply: race "may be" the most pernicious signature, not the only one. But any aspect that does not contend with the racial signature is not yet fully theorised.

Second, the metaphor essentialises modernity. Reply: Gilroy treats modernity as a project with characteristic signatures, not an essence. The signature is a historical product, not an essential property.

Contemporary purchase. The revision document's CRT framing of "racial progress is always pushed back" (§8) gives the signature claim contemporary content: where formal racial inclusion is granted, the signature reappears in the next cycle. Slide 9's 1868 plate and 1933 photograph are visual versions; Morrison's "routine media presentations" (Morrison, 2017: 37) is its quieter form. Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor, Brexit-era hostile-environment debates, and Trump-era policy framings show the signature re-signed today.

Gilroy's claim carries constitution (race is integral to modernity), perniciousness (race is the most damaging defining mark), and articulation (race is the seam where reason and unreason meet). The implications are periodisation, critique and normative direction. Du Bois supplies legal-economic evidence; Morrison supplies affective machinery; CRT supplies institutional specification. Race is modernity's most pernicious signature because modernity could not have been what it became without it.

### Mock 22. Compare Morrison and Gilroy on race as an effect of power.

In this essay I compare Morrison's race as power-effect (2017) with Gilroy's race as power-knowledge (1998, citing Foucault). The two are complementary: Morrison gives the affective machinery, Gilroy the perceptual and technoscientific. Together they specify what Du Bois's racial realism left in outline.

Morrison: "Race, in short, is an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25, citing Baum). Race is not natural but a product of power; power works through Othering: "The necessity of rendering the slave a foreign species appears to be a desperate attempt to confirm one's own self as normal" (Morrison, 2017: 29). The affective payoff is the dominant group's normality. Morrison identifies the why.

Gilroy: "'race' was a primary object of knowledge and power" (Gilroy, 1998: 252). The "Euclidean anatomy" of scientific racism produced race as scientific object (Gilroy, 1998: 253); "truths of race were produced 'performatively' from the hat that biological science provided" (Gilroy, 1998: 252); "the human sensorium has had to be educated" (Gilroy, 1998: 251). Gilroy identifies the how. The L7 frame underwrites this: Foucault's biopower (Foucault, 1978) is the technique by which modern states administer racial categorisation at population scale, and Gilroy's power-knowledge claim is biopower in its racial register.

Four convergences.

First, the constructed character of race. Morrison: "What is race (other than genetic imagination)?" (Morrison, 2017: 15). Gilroy: "The specious ontologies of 'race' are anything but spontaneous and natural" (Gilroy, 1998: 252). Race is made, not found.

Second, the centrality of power. Morrison: "an effect of power" (Morrison, 2017: 25). Gilroy: "a primary object of knowledge and power" (Gilroy, 1998: 252).

Third, the productive role of these operations. Power produces race, does not merely act on it. Morrison: othering produces the other to confirm the dominant self. Gilroy: scientific classification performatively produces racial categories.

Fourth, historical specificity. Morrison traces race to colonial and slave-trade history; Gilroy specifies the techniques (Linnaeus 1735, Blumenbach, craniometry, 1933 racial measurements). Both historicise race within modernity.

Three divergences.

First, the analytical entry-point. Morrison enters through identity and affect (what does whiteness need?); Gilroy enters through technique and perception (what apparatuses produced racial visibility?).

Second, the contemporary direction. Morrison emphasises the persistence of othering in routine media (Morrison, 2017: 37) and national identity (Morrison, 2017: 17). Gilroy emphasises technological-perceptual change ("'race' might best be approached as an after-image," Gilroy, 1998: 253) and the normative horizon ("anti-toxins capable of silencing raciology forever," Gilroy, 1998: 255). Morrison is more pessimistic about the continuity of othering; Gilroy more optimistic about dissolution of the perceptual regime.

Third, political consequence. Morrison implies anti-racism must dismantle the affective economy of othering; Gilroy implies it must dismantle the perceptual-technoscientific regime. The two can be combined but emphasise different sites.

The accounts are complementary. Morrison gives the affective machinery; Gilroy gives the perceptual. Together they specify what Du Bois's racial realism left in outline.

Du Bois's racial realism has four engines. Du Bois (1898) shows the legal-economic engine: race produced by colonial labour statutes. *Dusk of Dawn* (1940) shows the social-fact engine: race real because Jim Crow is real. Morrison adds the affective engine: race persists because othering serves the dominant group. Gilroy adds the perceptual engine: race persists because the sensorium has been trained to see it.

CRT operationalises all four. The revision document presents CRT as inheriting Du Bois's realism (§8): race as social fact, the US still white-supremacist, racial progress reversed by interest convergence, counter-storytelling as method. CRT's institutional examples (school-to-prison pipeline; carceral-military continuation of slavery) are sites at which Morrison's othering and Gilroy's perceptual regime do their work. Black Lives Matter after George Floyd and Breonna Taylor, and ongoing media representation debates, show the joint operation; *Get Out* and *Black Mirror* dramatise the regime.

Two objections. First, Morrison and Gilroy say the same thing in different vocabularies. Reply: Morrison's affective vocabulary names the maintenance work; Gilroy's perceptual names the technoscientific apparatus.

Second, combining the two over-determines race. Reply: the over-determination is the empirical situation. Race is solid because produced by multiple machineries at once. Dissolving it requires acting on all of them.

Morrison and Gilroy converge on race as effect of power but diverge on entry-point. The accounts are complementary. With Du Bois's racial realism, they specify race as produced by legal, economic, affective and perceptual machineries operating together. Slide 30: "Races do not exist. But the experiences constituted by the belief, practices, history and economics of 'race' do." Belief, practices, history and economics: Morrison's affect, Gilroy's perception, Du Bois's law, Du Bois's economy. Race is the effect of all four.

# L09, Post-Colonial Theory

## 1. Core Argument

Post-colonial theory insists that colonialism is not a regrettable side-event in the rise of European modernity but its constitutive condition. My core argument runs through four moves. First, colonialism has three intertwined faces, settlement (the displacement of indigenous populations by the colonising power), economic exploitation (the appropriation of land, labour and resources tied tightly to the rise of capitalism) and unequal power relations (Lecture 9 slides). Howard French, in *Born in Blackness*, contends that we must not "ignore the role of Africa in the development of modernity" and that the point is not to "add Africa in" but to "invert the current view" (French, 2021, [VERIFY p.?]); the Portuguese trade of Indian cotton for African gold to mint European coinage in the 1500s makes the global texture of modernity inescapable. Second, the West is constituted discursively against the Rest. Stuart Hall's discourse of the West and the Rest works through binary oppositions, "rational/irrational, cultured/savage, mind/body, progress/tradition, science/magic" (slide 9; Hall, 1992), and these binaries are not descriptions but hierarchies which the discourse "simplifies" (Hall, 1992: 280) into a single dichotomy. Third, Said's account of Orientalism shows that "the Orient is not only adjacent to Europe; it is also the place of Europe's greatest and richest and oldest colonies… and one of its deepest and most recurring images of the Other" (Said, 1978: 87) and that "the relationship between Occident and Orient is a relationship of power, of domination, of varying degrees of a complex hegemony" (Said, 1978: 89). Following Foucault, Said treats Orientalism as a discourse that "manage[s], and even produce[s], the Orient politically, sociologically, militarily, ideologically, scientifically, and imaginatively" (Said, 1978: 88-9). Fourth, the colonised are denied subjectivity. Fanon's analysis of colonial subjectivity in *Black Skin, White Masks* registers the white child's hail, "Look, a Negro!" (Fanon, 1967: 323), that fixes him as object: "I am being dissected under white eyes, the only real eyes. I am fixed" (Fanon, 1967: 325). Mohanty's critique of "Third World Woman" extends this, the figure is "an effect of discourse" (Mohanty, 1984: 261), not an empirical group, and Spivak's question of subaltern speech asks whether the oppressed can articulate themselves outside the categories of the coloniser. Enrique Dussel's intervention deepens these arguments: modernity is "a European phenomenon, but one constituted in a dialectical relation with a non-European alterity that is its ultimate content" (Dussel, 1993: 65). Post-colonial theory, then, is a critique of modernity's myth of self-origination, of its binaries, of its epistemic violence, and of its denial of voice to those it makes peripheral.

## 2. Thinkers and Concepts

- **Edward Said (1935-2003)**, Born in Jerusalem under the British Mandate, raised in Egypt, taught in New York. *Orientalism* (1978). Key concepts: Orientalism, the Orient as Europe's contrasting Other, false binary divisions, discourse/power following Foucault, "flexible positional superiority" (Said, 1978: 26), the imperial archive.
- **Stuart Hall (1932-2014)**, Jamaican-British cultural theorist. *Formations of Modernity* (1992). Key concepts: the West and the Rest, the West as historical not geographical construct, discourse as "system of representation" (Hall, 1992: 277), binary oppositions, internal others (Jews, Eastern Europeans, women).
- **Frantz Fanon (1925-1961)**, Born in Martinique, French Antilles; psychiatrist, fought in French resistance and later in Algerian liberation. *Black Skin, White Masks* (1952), *The Wretched of the Earth* (1961). Key concepts: object/subject dialectic, the colonial gaze, the denial of subjectivity, the colonial wound, decolonisation as struggle for voice.
- **Chandra Mohanty (1955–)**, Born in Mumbai; teaches at Syracuse. *Under Western Eyes* (1988). Key concepts: the third-world woman, discursive colonisation, women as "the other of the other," refusal of universal sisterhood.
- **Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (1942–)**, Indian-American literary theorist. *Can the Subaltern Speak?* (1988). Key concepts: the subaltern, epistemic violence, strategic essentialism, the impossibility of pure recovered voice.
- **Howard French**, *Born in Blackness* (2021). Argues Africa is central to making modern world; inversion of perspective.
- **Enrique Dussel (1934-2023)**, Argentine-Mexican liberation philosopher. *Eurocentrism and Modernity* (1993). Key concepts: the myth of modernity, the colonial wound, the colonial difference, trans-modernity, the fallacy of developmentalism, 1492 as birth of modernity.
- **W. E. B. Du Bois** and **Michel Foucault** are flagged on slide 25 as comparative reference points for Fanon's account of being subject and object; both come from earlier lectures and are imported here only as cross-references.

## 3. Presentation Notes (slide-by-slide)

- **Slide 1, Title**: Post-Colonial Theory. Frames the lecture as a critical inquiry into how colonialism organises modernity and its discursive after-life.
- **Slide 2, Re-cap of the Cantino Planisphere**: The 1502 Portuguese map "focuses not on land masses and cities but on coasts and oceans and links between countries", a visual cue that early modernity was made of oceanic circuits, slavery and West African resources, even though standard interpretations downplay this.
- **Slide 3, Re-cap on French**: Howard French's *Born in Blackness* (2021) is summarised: "we must not ignore the role of Africa in the development of modernity" and "the point is not simply to 'add' Africa in but to invert the current view" (French, 2021 [VERIFY p.?]).
- **Slide 4, Inverted cartography example**: "The Portuguese use cotton from India to buy gold in Africa to use as coinage in Europe (in the 1500s!)", the global texture of capital accumulation precedes industrial modernity. "But our maps are all made in a certain way…" introduces the politics of representation.
- **Slide 5, Some countries which used to be colonies of Britain**: A timeline of British colonial endings, the US states (until 1776), Canada (1867), Australia (1900), Ireland (1922), India/Pakistan (1947), Ghana (1957), Jamaica (1962), Hong Kong (1997), plus Palestine and Iraq as administered territories. "All the people who lived in these countries were British subjects" under London authority.
- **Slide 6, France colonized…**: Vietnam/Cambodia, much of North Africa (Algeria, Morocco), West and Central Africa (Ivory Coast, Cameroon, Gabon), West Indies (Martinique), Middle East (Syria, Lebanon). Establishes that the French empire was structurally comparable.
- **Slide 7, Colonialism, three elements**: (i) settlement of land, people from one country claim ownership and displace the indigenous population; (ii) the economic relationship, a direct link between capitalism and colonialism that benefits the colonizer; (iii) unequal power relations, colonialism dominates the indigenous population. This is the working definition for the lecture.
- **Slide 8, The British Empire (around 1924)**: Map slide showing imperial maximum; visual reinforcement that "empire" was a globe-spanning structure, not a marginal episode.
- **Slide 9, Stuart Hall on the West and the Rest**: The West and modernity are created in terms of what they are not. The binary table: rational/irrational, cultured/savage, mind/body, progress/tradition, science/magic. This is the conceptual heart of the lecture.
- **Slide 10, Said on Orientalism**: Biographical, Edward Said (1935-2003), born in Jerusalem under the British Mandate, brought up in Egypt, taught in New York. Key claim: "The relationship between Occident and Orient is a relationship of power, of domination" (Said, 1978: 89).
- **Slide 11, Imagination and fantasy and Writing the Orient**: "The Orient is not only adjacent to Europe; it is also the place of Europe's greatest and richest and oldest colonies, the source of its civilization and languages… and one of its deepest and most recurring images of the Other" (Said, 1978: 87).
- **Slide 12, The Orient as construction**: "The Orient is a construction, it is not just an invention, it is not just made up, but it is a legacy and a result of ways of thinking, acting, studying, trading, and dominating which still have effects today." Contemporary examples listed: Iraq, EU boundaries, immigration, Islam, "Arabia".
- **Slide 13, Video link**: External resource on Orientalism (YouTube clip).
- **Slide 14, Constructing (false) binary divisions**: "Orientalism is a style of thought based upon an ontological and epistemological distinction made between 'the Orient' and 'the Occident'" (Said, 1978: 88). "European culture gained in strength and identity by setting itself off against the Orient as a sort of surrogate and even underground self" (Said, 1978: 89).
- **Slide 15, "Come join us"**: Animation/transition slide.
- **Slide 16, Stereotypes of the Orient**: Orient as timeless; Orient as mysterious; "The Orient was almost a European invention, and has been since antiquity a place of romance, exotic beings, haunting memories and landscapes, remarkable experiences" (Said, 1978: 87); Orient as feminine (passive, luxurious); Orient as immoral, decadent.
- **Slide 17, "To Read Later"**: Reading prompt slide.
- **Slide 18, Orientalism as discourse legitimating empire**: "All the above legitimate French and British colonialism." Foucauldian framing: "without examining Orientalism as a discourse one cannot possibly understand the enormously systematic discipline by which European culture was able to manage, even produce, the Orient politically, sociologically, militarily, ideologically, scientifically, and imaginatively during the post-Enlightenment period" (Said, 1978: 88-9).
- **Slide 19, Chandra Mohanty**: Born in Mumbai (1955-). 'Under Western Eyes: Feminist Scholarship and Colonial Discourses' (*Feminist Review* 30, Autumn 1988; the cited essay was first published in Boundary 2 in 1984). "The notion of 'Third world woman' is an effect of discourse. It does not represent a real empirical group but is produced in Western (and some western feminist) approaches to understanding the world."
- **Slide 20, Women as the other of the other**: "This average third world woman leads an essentially truncated life based on her feminine gender… and being 'third world' (read: ignorant, poor, uneducated, tradition-bound, domestic, family-oriented, victimized etc.)" (Mohanty, 1984: 261).
- **Slide 21, Western women's self-representation**: "This, I suggest, is in contrast to the (implicit) self-representation of Western women as educated, modern, as having control over their own bodies and sexualities, and the freedom to make their own decisions" (Mohanty, 1984: 261).
- **Slide 22, The assumption Mohanty challenges**: "The assumption of women as an already constituted, coherent group with identical interests and desires, regardless of class, ethnic or racial location or contradictions, implies a notion of gender… which can be applied universally and cross-culturally" (Mohanty, 1984: 261).
- **Slide 23, Specificity as method**: Theorise differences within oppressed groups; do not assume all 'victims' experience colonialism alike, especially on male violence. "Male violence must be theorized and interpreted within specific societies, both in order to understand it better, as well as in order to effectively organize to change it" (Mohanty, 1984: 262).
- **Slide 24, Fanon, on the experience of colonialism**: Frantz Fanon (b. 1925, French Antilles), educated in Martinique and Paris, doctor and psychiatrist, influenced by Sartrean existentialism. Two main works: *Black Skin, White Masks* (1952) and *The Wretched of the Earth* (1961).
- **Slide 25, Four crucial points**: Being an object; being a subject (cf. Du Bois, Foucault); white (men) as the subjects of history; the denial of subjectivity to people who have been colonized. Note on dated language reflecting the period of writing.
- **Slide 26, The experience of colonialism as racism**: The railway-carriage scene: "'Look, a Negro!'… 'Mama, see the Negro! I'm frightened!'… I made up my mind to laugh myself to tears, but laughter had become impossible" (Fanon, 1967: 323).
- **Slide 27, Being an object, psychological consequences**: "I am being dissected under white eyes, the only real eyes. I am fixed" (Fanon, 1967: 325). "My body was given back to me sprawled out, distorted, recolored…" (Fanon, 1967: 324).
- **Slide 28, "To Read Later", Forms of subjectivity**: "The white world, the only honourable one, barred me from all participation. A man was expected to behave like a man. I was expected to behave like a black man" (Fanon, 1967: 324). "Since the other hesitated to recognise me, there remained only one solution: to make myself known" (Fanon, 1967: 324).
- **Slide 29 (continuation of Fanon discussion)**: The making-known is not the removal of an external block but the active creation of a new self; this prefigures *The Wretched of the Earth* and revolutionary anti-colonial subjectivity.
- **Slide 30, Conclusion**: Colonialism was a huge economic, cultural, historical, military and political event developing from the 1600s; Europe was deeply involved in Asia, Africa, North and South America; there were differences within and between colonised groups; the lecture asks how to think the legacy of colonialism without reducing post-colonial subjects to the 'Other' of the West.
- **Slide 31, Who can speak for whom?**: Spivak signalled here as the next step; the question of subaltern speech, epistemic violence, and the limits of recovery.
- **Slide 32, The Mercator Projection**: Visual technology of imperial perspective; Greenland looks comparable to Africa though Africa is roughly fourteen times larger.
- **Slide 33, Other ways of seeing the world, Gall-Peters projection**: Equal-area projection that restores tropical-zone proportions; visual companion to the postcolonial critique.

## 5. Common Pitfalls

- Treating "post-colonial" as merely "after colonialism" temporally; it is rather a theoretical stance on the continuing presence of colonial structures, including in formally independent states.
- Reducing Said to "the West invented the East". Said is careful that "the Orient is not an inert fact of nature" but also that "it would be wrong to conclude that the Orient was essentially an idea, or a creation with no corresponding reality" (Said, 1978: 25-6). The Orient exists; Orientalism is the discourse about it.
- Treating Hall's binaries as descriptive of two real groups; they are productive fictions that organise power.
- Treating the subaltern as just "the poor". The lecture flags Spivak at the end (slide 30) as raising the question of who can speak for whom; the subaltern is the structurally voiceless, not simply the materially poor.
- Forgetting that Hall warns against treating "the West" as homogeneous; "the West has always contained many internal differences" (Hall, 1992: 279), and the West also has its "internal others" such as Jews, Eastern Europeans regarded as "barbaric", and Western women represented as inferior to Western men (Hall, 1992: 280).
- Forgetting the symmetry: "the Rest" is just as internally differentiated as "the West", from the Middle East and Far East to Africa, Latin America, indigenous North America and Australasia (Hall, 1992: 280).
- Forgetting Dussel's point that modernity has *two* faces: an emancipatory concept and a sacrificial myth, and the critique must hold both (Dussel, 1993: 75).
- Treating French's argument as "adding Africa". French's point is "not simply to 'add' Africa in but to invert the current view" (slide 4).

## 6. Lecture Map

Lecture 9 opens by returning to the Cantino Planisphere and to Howard French's argument that Africa is central to modernity (slides 2-4). The slide on three elements of colonialism, settlement, economic relationship, unequal power (slide 7), sets the basic vocabulary. The historical sweep is sketched through British and French colonial maps (slides 5-6, 8). The conceptual heart is Hall's table of binaries, rational/irrational, cultured/savage, mind/body, progress/tradition, science/magic (slide 9). Said is then introduced biographically (slide 10) and the Orient is presented as "imagination and fantasy" (slide 11), construction (slide 12), false binary (slide 14), stereotype-machine (slide 16), and Foucauldian discourse (slide 18). Mohanty appears with the "Third World Woman" critique (slides 19-23), Fanon with the experience of being seen and fixed (slides 24-29), and the lecture closes with Spivak's question of who can speak for whom and an invitation to think with alternative cartographies, Gall-Peters and the World Upside Down (slides 30-33). The accompanying readings are: Said via Ashcroft's reader, where the key passages on Orientalism as discourse, power and "flexible positional superiority" appear (Ashcroft pp. 24-27); Hall's *Formations of Modernity* pp. 276-280, which lays out the four functions of the concept "the West" and the simplifying logic of the discourse; and Dussel's Frankfurt lectures, which historicise modernity from 1492 and articulate the myth of modernity in seven points.
