The grammar metaphor is not casual: it borrows Saussure's claim that meaning arises from "difference within a system" (Saussure, 1916) and Barthes's account of myth as the level at which signs "transform history into nature" (Barthes, 1972: 140). Flow is the televisual register in which that mythic transformation is performed across an evening. Hall's argument is a direct application of Williams's flow concept to racial ideology on television.

Three further consequences matter. First, flow makes media political-economic. *Communications* (Williams, 1962) and *Television* (Williams, 1974) both insist that the financing of broadcasting, the £20,000,000 on the Arts Council against £365,000,000 on advertising (Williams, 1958: 22), is the determining structural fact about how flow is built. The advert is not an interruption of the flow; in commercial television, it is what the flow is for.

Second, flow refuses the transmission model. The viewer is not a passive recipient of discrete messages; she is the inhabitant of a sequence whose cumulative effect on her common meanings is the proper object of analysis. This is the same move Williams makes against the "masses" thesis: the audience is not a mass to be administered with ideology, it is a "crowded people in the course of an extraordinarily rapid and confusing expansion of their lives" (Williams, 1958: 24).

Third, flow lets the analyst read media as embedded in everyday life. Media are neither autonomous machines administering ideology nor neutral conduits of information; they are cultural forms whose flow is a programming decision with social and economic conditions. BBC popular culture today, *EastEnders*, *Doctor Who*, *Strictly Come Dancing*, the *Great British Bake Off*, is precisely such a flow, its meaning emerging cumulatively across the evening rather than from any single episode.

The limit is that Williams in 1974 was analysing scarce-channel broadcasting in which one flow was imposed on all viewers within a national schedule. Streaming platforms, *Black Mirror* and *Adolescence* on Netflix, autoplay sequences and algorithmically curated TikTok feeds, individualise the flow. Each viewer now inhabits a personalised sequence rather than a shared evening. The Williams question still bites, "what is the flow doing to the cumulative production of meaning?", but the unit has to be reconstructed: not the evening but the algorithmically programmed personal feed, whose political economy (advertising, data extraction, platform capture) is exactly what Williams said the analyst must read.

Look at the sequence, not the unit; look at who programmed the sequence and on what economic basis; refuse both technological determinism and the discrete-programme picture. That is the cultural form of media analysis BCS gave us, and it is still the right starting point in the streaming era.

### Essay M14. Using Hall's encoding/decoding model to read *Love Thy Neighbour*.

Stuart Hall's encoding/decoding model (Hall, 1980) remains the indispensable analytic instrument for British cultural sociology of media. The ITV sitcom *Love Thy Neighbour*, which Hall himself analyses in "The Whites of Their Eyes: Racist Ideologies and the Media" (Hall, 1981a), is the textbook case both because Hall picks it and because its operations are transferable to other television texts.

Hall's model rejects the linear-transmission picture. Media messages are not parcels of meaning that producers pack and audiences unpack intact. Producers *encode* messages using "frameworks of knowledge," "relations of production," and "technical infrastructure" (lecture slide 13); the message circulates as "programme as 'meaningful' discourse"; and audiences *decode* using their own frameworks. Encoding and decoding are not symmetrical: there is no guarantee that the meaning encoded is the meaning decoded. The semiotic backbone is Saussurean: signs make meaning through "difference within a system" rather than reference to things in the world (Saussure, 1916), and television's denotative surface carries connotative and mythic levels of the kind Barthes anatomised in *Mythologies* (Barthes, 1972). Hall identifies three positions: dominant-hegemonic (the viewer takes the preferred meaning straight); negotiated (the viewer broadly accepts but inflects); and oppositional (the viewer reads within an alternative framework) (Hall, 1980). The model is underwritten by Gramsci's hegemony (Gramsci, 1971): dominant readings are not neutral but ideological, secured by common sense, contestable.

*Love Thy Neighbour* is built around a white working-class couple, Eddie and Joan Booth, in Twickenham, and a Black couple, Bill and Barbie Reynolds, next door (Hall, 1981a). Hall argues that the show encodes a "grammar of race": negative racial stereotypes, slave figure, native, clown / entertainer, circulating as traces "even if not so apparent," and race itself framed as "a problem" (lecture slide 14). Frameworks of knowledge: post-imperial Britain's commonsense racial categories. Relations of production: ITV as commercial popular broadcasting. Technical infrastructure: studio-sitcom form with live laughter track.

A dominant-hegemonic reading accepts the preferred meaning as "a comedy about two ordinary couples whose racial banter is good-natured English fun." The viewer reads Eddie Booth's slurs as harmless jokes, hears the laughter track as confirmation, and treats the grammar of race as comic rather than ideological. The slave figure, native, clown / entertainer are encoded as traces through which racial stereotypes can be reproduced under cover of comic licence.

A negotiated reading accepts the show is "just a comedy" while inflecting it. A working-class viewer in Twickenham, recognising her own street, might find the Booths sympathetic and the Reynoldses funny while laughing at Eddie's stupidity rather than at the slur, or take the show as a chance to think about her own neighbours.

An oppositional reading detotalises the preferred meaning. *Love Thy Neighbour* is itself an exhibit in the racial ideology Hall is naming: the comic frame is precisely what does the ideological work, because "comedy protects / defends viewer from acknowledging racism" (Hall, 1981a). The encoding produces the grammar of race even where viewers report not noticing it. Hall calls this "contradictions and ambivalence": readings that might contradict the encoding yet still do its ideological work.

Hall's argument extends to *Policing the Crisis* (Hall et al., 1978), where press-and-state encoding of "mugging" produced a racialised criminal-on-the-streets common sense that secured authoritarian state response to the 1970s organic crisis. The same machinery, encoding, dominant / negotiated / oppositional decoding, hegemony, does the work.

The model transfers cleanly to contemporary television. *Adolescence* (Netflix) encodes a framework about online radicalisation and young men; dominant readings take its moral framing as obvious truth, negotiated readings inflect by class and place, oppositional readings (from inside the manosphere, or from media-literate Andrew Tate critics) read the encoding itself. *Black Mirror* episodes invite dominant readings of technological pessimism, negotiated readings that affirm individual platforms, oppositional readings of capitalist political economy. BBC programmes such as *Doctor Who* and *EastEnders* encode British national popular meanings that streaming-era audiences variously accept, negotiate or oppose.

The pay-off is that all three readings are real audience responses, occurring simultaneously, and the sociologist's job is not to declare one correct but to map the field. The preferred encoding is *not* guaranteed to land. A teenage Black British viewer of *Love Thy Neighbour* in 1972 was not obliged to receive the encoded grammar of race; her oppositional decoding was exactly the empirical fact the model was built to handle. Encoding/decoding remains the right tool, and *Love Thy Neighbour* is the model case-study because encoding, decoding, contradiction and ambivalence are visible in a single half-hour cultural form.

### Essay M15. Hall's grammar of race and racial ideology on television.

Stuart Hall's "The Whites of Their Eyes: Racist Ideologies and the Media" (Hall, 1981a) provides the foundational BCS framework for analysing race in popular television. Its strength lies in three moves: identification of a "grammar of race" in the encoded image, demonstration that ideological work proceeds through *traces* rather than overt slurs, and the insight that comedy structurally licenses the racist content of the comic text.

Hall identified a "grammar of race" in 1970s British television (lecture slide 14). Negative racial stereotypes were encoded through three figures: the slave figure, the native, and the clown / entertainer. These were often present as "traces" even when not overt; race was framed as "a problem"; and decoding produced "contradictions and ambivalence", with a comic frame that "protects / defends viewer from acknowledging racism" (Hall, 1981a). The hegemonic work could proceed precisely because comic framing licensed a "we don't really mean it" decoding. The grammar of race did not require crude vilification; it required structural positioning of Black characters in the slave / native / entertainer slots.

The textbook case is *Love Thy Neighbour*: the ITV sitcom built around Eddie and Joan Booth in Twickenham and their Black neighbours Bill and Barbie Reynolds (Hall, 1981a). Hall's reading is structural rather than content-focused. The grammar of race is not located in any single slur but in the way the Booth-Reynolds pairing positions the Reynoldses as comic objects whose blackness is the *occasion* for the joke. The encoding produces traces of the entertainer position even where individual scenes look "balanced." The decoding splits: a dominant reading takes the show as harmless; a negotiated reading laughs at Eddie's stupidity; an oppositional reading, especially from Black British viewers, names the comic frame as the ideological mechanism.

A second case is *Policing the Crisis* (Hall et al., 1978), where the grammar of race operates not in comedy but in the press construction of "mugging" as a racialised street-crime moral panic. The study shows how a relatively limited phenomenon became a major political issue in 1970s Britain, with media, policing and state power interacting to produce ideological responses to wider social and economic crises. The slide-16 image grid, petrol shortage forecourt, National Front rally, Winter-of-Discontent refuse, "Britain on Half Time" headline, the policing of a Black man, NUR pickets, Powell's "stop this flow of coloured immigrants" cutting, an anti-police-violence protest, assembles the visual conditions in which the grammar of race operates across the organic crisis. Race is framed as a problem, encoded with traces of older imperial stereotypes, and read in contradiction and ambivalence by audiences who may not fully recognise what they receive.

Contemporary applications are immediate. The grammar of race still encodes Black British figures in 1970s-inherited slots, but contemporary television also encodes new versions: the Andrew Tate / manosphere figure as a racialised-and-gendered moral panic, *Adolescence* (Netflix) and *Black Mirror* episodes encoding race and class together in cumulative flow, the post-Brexit press encoding of immigration and asylum that recycles the "problem" framing Hall identified. The slave / native / entertainer grammar is residual; new grammars are emergent; the analytical engine is the same.

The conceptual sharpness of Hall's framework links three pieces. First, encoding/decoding (Hall, 1980) supplies the model of media meaning. Second, Gramsci's hegemony (Gramsci, 1971) supplies the political theory: dominant groups secure consent by making meanings feel like common sense, the half-articulated "*senso comune*" through which subordinate groups live their conditions. Hall's encoding/decoding essay and "Whites of Their Eyes" (Hall, 1980; 1981a) are the explicit turn to Gramsci that takes BCS beyond Williams and Hoggart. Third, the grammar of race (Hall, 1981a) supplies the specific cultural mechanism. Together they let the sociologist analyse race in popular television without reducing it to overt content or evaporating it into discourse.

The limit, acknowledged inside BCS, is that Hall is writing about a particular British televisual moment. The framework asks to be extended, and the slide-17 sociological legacy, Mirza's *Young, Female and Black* (1992) and the rest, is where the extension was done. But the analytical engine is Hall's, and it still works: the grammar of race is encoded, decoded in contradictions and ambivalence, and comedy still protects viewers from acknowledging racism. Hall is not yet historical; he is the toolkit.

### Essay M16. Thompson on history from below and the sociology of culture.

E. P. Thompson's *The Making of the English Working Class* (Thompson, 1963) supplies British Cultural Studies with its most important historiographical commitment, history from below. The move matters for the contemporary sociology of culture because it refuses to let either economic structures or elite ideologies do the explanatory work that lived experience and cultural agency must do.

Thompson's preface contains the most quoted sentence in British social history: he wanted to rescue the poor stockinger, the Luddite cropper, the hand-loom weaver, the utopian artisan, even the deluded follower of Joanna Southcott, from "the enormous condescension of posterity." The English working class did not appear as the deposit of an economic structure; it *made itself*, in chapels, friendly societies, Corresponding Societies, food riots, radical pamphlets, hymns and trade-union banners. Class is "a relationship, not a thing", something people do, in struggle, with one another and against others.

Three concepts matter for L14. First, the lived experience of class: class is felt before it is structured. Thompson's artisans experience exploitation as a moral as well as economic outrage and respond in idioms, religious, customary, traditional, that do not look "modern" but are the work of cultural self-making. Second, history from below: the historian writes from the standpoint of those who did not leave parliamentary speeches but appear in criminal records, parish reports, magistrates' notes and seditious pamphlets. Third, the moral economy: Thompson's 1971 essay showed eighteenth-century food riots were not blind hunger eruptions but principled enforcement of customary fair-price norms against new market behaviour. The crowd had a theory; the historian has to take it seriously.

The pay-off is fourfold. First, against structuralist Marxism, Thompson supplied an account of class in which agency and culture were not afterthoughts to be "explained" by the relations of production but the medium in which class came into being. The famous Thompson-Althusser exchange in *The Poverty of Theory* (1978) ran on exactly this point. Thompson's wager rhymes with Gramsci's: the working class's "good sense" is "embedded in its practical activity" (Gramsci, 1971), and the historian's job is to find it there rather than in the official ideology. Hall would later articulate Thompson and Gramsci as twin sources of BCS's anti-determinist commitment (Hall, 1980).

Second, against Frankfurt School pessimism, Thompson's working class was not a "mass" administered by ideology but a self-organising cultural formation. Williams's "no masses" thesis and Thompson's "the class made itself" are the same move from different disciplinary angles.

Third, Thompson supplied a method of reading sources from below. The minute book of a Friendly Society, the chapel hymn-book, the penny pamphlet, the union banner are legitimate documents of cultural analysis. The slide-17 inheritors, Willis (1977), Mirza (1992), Skeggs (1997), McKenzie (2015), all draw on this licence.

Fourth, the moral economy concept travels into the rest of the lecture. Williams's working-class institutions, trade-union branch, Co-op, friendly society, the Labour movement, the "kept men" his father remarked on (Williams, 1958: 11, 15), are moral-economy formations: customary norms about how working people should be treated, defended in idioms that exceed pure economic calculation. Hoggart's first half is a portrait of 1930s working-class culture organised around precisely such customary norms (Hoggart, 1957).

Cases inside the lecture materials show the framework operating. The slide-16 image grid, NUR pickets, Winter-of-Discontent refuse, anti-police-violence protests, makes the moral-economy claim: customary norms of fair pay and decent policing being defended through collective action. *Policing the Crisis* (Hall et al., 1978) reads the criminalisation of the "mugger" as the breaking of an older moral-economic settlement between communities and the state.

Contemporary applications travel cleanly. The cost-of-living crisis, food banks, and Brexit can all be read in Thompson's idiom: as moments when older moral-economic settlements (fair wages, mutual obligation, public provision) break and provoke responses in customary as well as new idioms. Lisa McKenzie's *Getting By* (2015) is explicitly Thompson on austerity-Britain estates.

The limits are real. Thompson wrote about white English men in the early industrial revolution; gender and race are largely absent. The slide-17 corrections, Mirza on young, female and Black experience; Skeggs on class and gender; McKenzie on estates under austerity, make clear what Thompson's "below" excluded. But these are corrections from within his method, not refutations of it. History from below remains the right commitment. It tells us that the proper unit of analysis is not the apparatus, the ideology, or the structure, but the lived activity by which working people make themselves into something they were not before.

### Essay M17. "Culture is a site of struggle." Discuss with reference to two BCS thinkers.

The BCS slogan "culture is a site of struggle" is best understood by reading Williams and Hall together: Williams supplies the *ontology* (culture is the whole way of life in which struggles over meaning happen), Hall supplies the *mechanics* (encoding, decoding, hegemony, common sense, moral panic). The phrase is not a vague claim that "culture is political"; it is a specific claim about how power operates in late capitalism.

Williams refuses the two positions that would deny culture is a site of struggle. The first is the elite literary view, culture as a finished inheritance to be transmitted to those capable of receiving it. Williams's Cambridge teashop is full of "cultivated people" who "showed you they had it" (Williams, 1958: 12). The teashop is the institutionalised endpoint of the Arnoldian programme, "the pursuit of our total perfection by means of getting to know … the best which has been thought and said" (Arnold, 1869), and of F. R. Leavis's claim that "in any period it is upon a very small minority that the discerning appreciation of art and literature depends" (Leavis, 1930). If culture is already settled in the teashop, it is not struggle but curatorship. Williams refuses: "if that is culture, we don't want it; we have seen other people living" (Williams, 1958: 12). The second is reflectionist Marxism, which treats culture as the secondary expression of an economic base. Williams accepts that "a culture is a whole way of life, and the arts are part of a social organisation which economic change clearly radically affects" (Williams, 1958: 14) but refuses the "directive element." Culture is *both* shaped by production *and* a domain in which production relations are contested, naturalised, refused, lived.

The struggle is fought through common meanings. "A culture is common meanings, the product of a whole people" (Williams, 1958: 15). Common meanings are "made and remade." The struggle is over which meanings become common and on whose terms. Williams's own argument with the highbrow argot, with Leavis's dying-culture diagnosis and with the Marxist directive on prescribed forms is itself a series of struggles over what "culture" will be allowed to mean. Residual / dominant / emergent name a dynamic field, not a static base/superstructure schema but a culture in motion.

Hall gives Williams's ontology Gramscian mechanics. Hegemony (Gramsci, 1971), the process by which dominant groups secure consent rather than relying on force, names the form of the struggle. The dominant order wins by making its meanings feel natural, "common sense." The encoding/decoding model (Hall, 1980) gives the struggle a precise location: in the encoding moment, dominant frameworks of knowledge install a preferred reading; in the decoding moment, audiences may take it whole, negotiate it, or oppose it. The struggle happens in living rooms, in the press, in classrooms, in the encoded text and the decoding moment.

*Policing the Crisis* (Hall et al., 1978) is the textbook case. Hall and colleagues show how street robbery became, through media labelling and policing intensification, the "mugging" moral panic of the mid-1970s. The struggle is over what counts as the public problem: racial criminality (dominant) or youth unemployment, deindustrialisation, and a state in crisis (oppositional). The hegemonic outcome was the former; the cost was the closing-down of alternative political readings of the organic crisis. Culture is the site at which the crisis is *resolved* into one ideological story rather than another.

*Love Thy Neighbour* at sitcom scale shows the model: the encoded preferred reading installs the grammar of race in the comic frame; negotiated and oppositional decodings contest the meaning in the living room (Hall, 1981a). The hegemonic reading wins because comic licence makes racial encoding feel like common sense. Contemporary materials extend it: Brexit as a struggle over "Britain"; *Adolescence* (Netflix) and *Black Mirror* in the streaming era; the manosphere as a site of emergent struggle.

The cost of treating culture as a site of struggle is that the sociology of culture becomes harder. Reflection theory was easier, find the base, derive the superstructure. Williams-Hall analysis requires close reading of texts, attention to encoding regimes and decoding practices, ethnography of audiences, and historical placement in residual / dominant / emergent fields. It also runs a political risk: cultural intervention (a TV drama, a song, a meme) is taken seriously as politics, which can flatter the producer into thinking he is the revolution. Williams and Hall both warned against this. The risk is the price of taking culture, and ordinary people, seriously.

### Essay M18. "There is a distinct working-class way of life." The politics of British Cultural Studies.

Williams's sentence "There is a distinct working-class way of life, which I for one value" (Williams, 1958: 15) is the most precise single statement of the politics of British Cultural Studies. It does three things: it asserts a class culture exists; it values that culture without sentimentalising it; and it makes the analyst declare himself politically. All three moves are constitutive of BCS.

The first move refuses two erasures. The elite literary erasure says working people have no culture worth the name; they consume what their betters make for them. It is the position of Arnold's "raw and half developed" working class (Arnold, 1869), of F. R. Leavis's "very small minority" who alone exercise "discerning appreciation" (Leavis, 1930), and of Q. D. Leavis's *Fiction and the Reading Public* (Leavis, 1932), which read mass-market fiction as evidence of working-class cultural deficit. The determinist Marxist erasure says working-class culture is just bourgeois culture imposed on the workers; there is no autonomous form. Williams insists the working-class way of life exists in its own right, "with its emphases of neighbourhood, mutual obligation, and common betterment, as expressed in the great working-class political and industrial institutions" (Williams, 1958: 15). The claim points to actual social formations, trade unions, friendly societies, the Co-op, the Labour movement, the Nonconformist chapel network, working-men's adult-education institutions, which were not bourgeois inventions and which had distinct internal cultures.

The second move, valuing without sentimentalising, is harder. Hoggart slides into elegy: the 1930s as self-made culture killed by 1950s candy-floss. Thompson slides at moments into heroic identification. Williams declines both. He values the working-class way of life "not only because I was bred in it, for I now, in certain respects, live differently. I think this way of life … is in fact the best basis for any future English society" (Williams, 1958: 15). The valuation is forward-looking, not nostalgic. He is clear-eyed about what was hard: "dirty water, an earth bucket, a fourmile walk each way to work, headaches, broken women, hunger and monotony of diet" (Williams, 1958: 17). The working-class way of life is not romanticised.

The third move, the analyst declares himself, is the constitutive BCS gesture. "I for one value" makes the writer accountable. He is taking a side. The political position is socialist-democratic, committed to the proposition that "the ordinary people should govern" (Williams, 1958: 24). The socialist intellectual's job is "to attack the clamps on that energy … in industrial relations, public administration, education, for a start" (Williams, 1958: 24).

This declared politics distinguishes BCS from later, more academic Cultural Studies. By the 1980s and 1990s the field had become methodologically sophisticated but politically thinner: discourse analysis without a labour movement, semiotic readings of consumer goods without political economy. Williams's sentence is a reminder of the original commitment. The analyst is on the side of the working people whose culture she analyses.

The costs are real. The "we" of Williams's Welsh valley is gendered male, white, and Christian-secular; women, racialised workers and migrants are not adequately included. Skeggs (1997) and Mirza (1992) corrected the gender and race blindness; Hall did similar work from within. The working-class movement Williams "valued" has fragmented under deindustrialisation. McKenzie's *Getting By* (2015) documents what the working-class way of life looks like under austerity: more atomised and precarious, but still distinct and worth analysing on its own terms.

Contemporary materials still answer to Williams's sentence. Working-class musicians from the Beatles to Stormzy, food banks under the cost-of-living crisis as sites of mutual obligation, and *EastEnders* as an archive of neighbourhood meaning are all "distinct working-class ways of life" a Williams analyst would value. Brexit has made the political question of working-class culture more visible.

The empirical force rests on the institutions Williams names: the trade-union branch and Labour Party group his father started in the village (Williams, 1958: 11), the working men's institutions, the Friendly Societies and chapels Thompson (1963) traced as the site at which the working class "made itself," the 1930s neighbourhood culture Hoggart (1957) documents.

Williams names the risk as sentimentality. "I would not expect the working people of England to support works which, after proper and patient preparation, they could not accept" (Williams, 1958: 22). He is not flattering working-class taste; he is committing to extending cultural provision in a way the working people themselves will help shape. The politics of BCS, at its best, is exactly this commitment: distinct culture, valued, by an analyst on its side, working to extend it.

### Essay M19. What does British Cultural Studies put in place of high culture and reflection theory, and at what cost?

BCS replaces two earlier orthodoxies, elite "high culture" and the Marxist base-superstructure reflection thesis, with a unified alternative: culture as ordinary, lived, contested, hegemonic, encoded and decoded. The replacement is a real advance but has costs: a tendency to overstate cultural agency, relative neglect of political economy, and difficulty telling significant cultural struggles from trivial ones.

The displaced orthodoxies are the elite literary position (Clive Bell, the Cambridge teashop, the Leavisite reading) and the Marxist reflectionist position (Frankfurt School pessimism, crude communist cultural orthodoxy). The elite position says culture is the preserve of cultivated people who possess it as "the outward and emphatically visible sign" of cultivation (Williams, 1958: 12). The reflectionist position says culture is the secondary expression of an economic base, and in its Frankfurt variant treats the culture industry as "anti-enlightenment" that "fetters consciousness" (Adorno and Horkheimer, 1947). Williams refuses both: "We use the word culture in these two senses: to mean a whole way of life, the common meanings; to mean the arts and learning … I insist on both, and on the significance of their conjunction" (Williams, 1958: 11).

BCS puts in place a four-part alternative. First, an ontology: culture is the whole way of life. Hoggart's "uses of literacy," Thompson's "lived experience of class," Hall's "hegemony" all sit inside Williams's "whole way of life." Second, a method: history from below (Thompson, 1963), close reading of working-class materials (Hoggart, 1957), structure-of-feeling analysis (Williams, 1961; 1977), encoding/decoding analysis (Hall, 1980). Third, a politics: socialist-democratic, on the side of ordinary people. Fourth, an institutional location: the CCCS at Birmingham, founded 1964.

This achieves three things the displaced orthodoxies could not. It makes working-class and popular cultural materials sociologically legible without elegy. It accounts for media without technological determinism (Williams) or transmission-of-ideology determinism (Hall). And it permits political reading of culture without prescribing correct content. The intellectual gain is large.

The costs are real. First, *over-extension of cultural agency*. Once "everything is culture" and "audiences negotiate or oppose," it becomes tempting to read every consumption choice as resistance and every popular text as a site of struggle. Hall (1980) established that audiences decode actively; this does not entail that every act of decoding is politically meaningful. The strongest BCS work, including Hall's own *Policing the Crisis* (Hall et al., 1978), was sharply disciplined about which decodings matter politically.

Second, *relative neglect of political economy*. Williams's *Communications* (Williams, 1962) and *Television* (Williams, 1974) do attend to who owns the media (Williams's £20,000,000 vs £365,000,000 figures, Williams, 1958: 22, are the right kind of accounting). But the broader tradition was less consistent, with text analysis sometimes detached from the relations of production Williams insisted were determining. The cost-of-living crisis, food banks, streaming-platform economies, and the political economy of TikTok are the contemporary terrain on which this gap shows.

Third, *significant versus trivial struggles*. If every text encodes and is decoded, how do we tell *Policing the Crisis* mugging panic, a struggle of national-historical weight, from a comic exchange on a forgotten sitcom? Williams's residual / dominant / emergent helps; Thompson's moral economy helps; Hall's hegemony helps. But the analyst still has to judge, and BCS gives only partial guidance.

Fourth, the *category of class itself*. BCS was built on a robust account of British class culture, Williams's signalman father, Hoggart's 1930s neighbourhood, Thompson's hand-loom weavers, transformed by deindustrialisation and neoliberalism. The slide-17 inheritors (Willis, 1977; Mirza, 1992; Skeggs, 1997; McKenzie, 2015) have updated the analysis, but the framework must keep adapting: Brexit, the manosphere, *Adolescence* (Netflix) and *Black Mirror*, TikTok cottage-core as emergent forms.

A case shows both the achievement and the cost. *Policing the Crisis* (Hall et al., 1978) can be analysed with real power as a moral panic articulated through press encoding and decoded in multiple ways, under hegemonic conditions in which racialised-street-crime common sense was built across the organic crisis. But a fuller analysis needs the political economy of post-war Britain and the institutional analysis of state-press-police interaction the authors themselves provide. The strongest BCS work always integrated cultural and political-economic analysis.

BCS replaced two exhausted orthodoxies with a tradition that has itself become orthodox. They remain the right starting point. The cost of replacing them would be enormous, back to the teashop, back to the reflection, back to the masses. But each founder would have insisted the tradition keep moving. Culture is ordinary, and so is its analysis: made and remade, in ways we cannot know in advance.

# L15. Structuralism and Cultural Signs (Saussure, Barthes, Hall)

*SC301 cheat-sheet. Built from the lecture slides, Strinati Ch. 3 (Spring reading), and the teacher's revision summary.*

---

## §1. One-sentence summary

Structuralism and semiology argue that meaning in language and culture is not natural but produced by structured systems of signs (Saussure's signifier/signified), that popular-cultural signs work simultaneously at the levels of denotation, connotation and myth (Barthes), and that any serious account of cultural meaning has to be reworked, as Stuart Hall does, to bring back power, ideology, institutions and the active audience.

---

## §2. The five core moves

1. **Saussure's relational sign.** The sign = signifier (physical form: sound, mark, image, style) + signified (mental concept, not the thing). The relation is arbitrary; meaning arises from difference within a system (*langue*) rather than from things in the world. "In the linguistic sign, the signifier is the 'sound image'… and the signified is the concept of the object or idea which is being referred to" (Strinati, 1995: 83).
2. **From linguistics to a science of signs.** Saussure proposes semiology as "a science which studies the life of signs within society" (Strinati, 1995: 85). The langue/parole, synchronic/diachronic and paradigmatic/syntagmatic distinctions become tools for analysing fashion, food, advertising, film, news, anything culturally coded.
3. **Barthes's two-tier model.** Modern signs work simultaneously at denotation (literal, "what we see", apparently neutral) and connotation (cultural associations, values, emotions). The suit connotes professionalism/authority; the Jeep connotes adventure/masculinity.
4. **Myth as third-order signification.** Myth is "a system of communication… a mode of signification" (Barthes, 1972: 117). Its function is "to transform history into nature" (Barthes, 1972: 140), to make culturally specific, class-bound meanings appear timeless, obvious, natural. The Paris-Match cover of the naked Black soldier saluting the French flag is Barthes's emblematic case.
5. **Hall's reworking.** Structuralism is "extremely powerful at explaining how meaning is organised, but it is much less good at explaining power and inequality in concrete social contexts, media institutions… and audience interpretation and resistance" (teacher's summary). Hall's encoding/decoding model adds production, ideology and differential reception to the semiological frame.

---

## §3. Slide-by-slide walk-through (lecture deck)

> Rebuilt from the L15 PDF. Each beat below tracks the actual slide order. Question-slides quoted verbatim.

- **Title slide.** "SC301 / Lecture 15: Structuralism and Cultural Signs". Frames the lecture as a sweep from Saussure to Barthes to Hall, with Strinati Ch. 3 as the spine.
- **Saussure slide.** Saussure's *Course in General Linguistics* (1916) appears as the founding text. The lecture's gloss is that language "is not a transparent medium that reflects reality, but a structured system of signs, organised through difference and governed by rules that exist independently of individual intention" (lecture slide). This is the canonical move: meaning is relational, not referential.
- **"Inuit terms for snow ice" image.** The deck uses the classic example (the "Eskimo words for snow" cliché) to dramatise *langue*-as-system: different languages carve the same continuum (here, frozen water) into different sign-paradigms.
- **"Language and 'difference' in structuralism: gender" slide.** The lecture extends Saussure into culture by treating gender as a system of signifiers. Femininity is given as the paradigm "Obedient / Servile / Passive / Submissive / Emotional / Sensitive / Private sphere / Reproductive / Child care / Domestic labour" (lecture slide). Masculinity as "Manly / Virile / Muscular / Heroic / Wise / Aggressive / Dominant / Sexually active / Successful / Public sphere" (lecture slide). The slide's pedagogical point: gender works structurally, by difference, just like Saussure's *langue*.
- **Barthes title slide.** *Mythologies* (1957) is named as the pivot from formal linguistics to cultural semiology.
- **"Nothing natural" slide.** Two bullets: "'the sign' not limited to speech / language" and "'…destroy the idea that signs are natural'" (lecture slide). The traffic-lights image illustrates the arbitrary-but-conventional sign (red = stop only because the system fixes the difference between red, amber and green).
- **"Barthes, Wrestling" slide.** Wrestling is read as Barthes's paradigm case of denotation + connotation: the bodies and grimaces denote a fight; they connote moral spectacle, justice, suffering, defeat (the "bad guy" framing).
- **"Language into Myth" diagram slide.** The deck reproduces Barthes's two-tier semiological table: "Language / Primary Signification / Denotation: 1. Signifier 2. Signified -> 3. Sign", which becomes "i. SIGNIFIER" inside "Secondary Signification / Connotation", whose "iii. SIGN" becomes "Myth" at "Tertiary Signification". The slide's caption: "Denotative meanings of signs are always subject to a second order of connotative meaning and can be solidified as tertiary signification in the form of mythology. As such, Barthes suggested that a dualistic process is at work in communication. A first order system of signs (language) serving a second order system (connotation / mythology)" (lecture slide).
- **"Barthes, Toys" slide.** Toys (from *Mythologies*) as another worked case: they denote play objects; connote pre-formed adult social roles (the mini kitchen, the mini soldier); mythologise gendered futures as natural.
- **"Barthes, Astrology (Horoscopes)" slide.** Horoscopes denote predictions; connote individual destinies; mythologise capitalist daily life by absorbing economic worry into cosmic narrative.
- **"Semiotics / Semiology" overview slide.** Defines semiotics/semiology as "Analysis of signs / symbols / meaning"; locates "Origins in structuralism in terms of signifier / signified, denotation, connotation and mythologies"; and lists "Different approaches to semiotics: Marxist / Feminist / Decolonial / Post-modernist" (lecture slide). This is the pluralisation moment: Barthes is one of several lineages.
- **"O2: Wear the Rose" slide (rugby campaign).** A worked contemporary advert. Used to set up the next slide's full three-order reading.
- **"A Rose is a Rose?" slide.** A long, worked example. The slide reads: "Denotation = A rose is a flower bush in the garden"; "Connotation: at the second level of signification, the sign 'roses' becomes a signifier for the consumption of roses on special romantic occasions (e.g. Valentine's day, anniversaries, dates, etc). Not being given roses on such occasions connotes a lack of romance"; "myth = romance being commodified; being robbed of its innocent meaning (true love, passion, etc). In other words, the mythical signification is motivated; it is not arbitrary"; "So: 'roses' (object) signify 'passion' (mental concept) = 'passionified' roses (sign: object-plus-meaning)"; "Other possible connotations: pain, rugby, England, Labour Party..." (lecture slide). The point: even the seemingly innocent floral sign carries motivated, third-order ideological content.
- **"Hall: building on structuralism?" diagram slide.** A flow diagram. On the encoding side: "Visual / Aural - signifier" passes through "Signified" inside production. The two emphasised arrows are "Media production and power" (encoding side) and "Differential reception of the audience" (decoding side). The slide reframes the semiological circuit as a power-and-reception circuit.
- **Second title card.** "SC301 / Lecture 15: Structuralism and Cultural Signs - Class". Marks the in-class half.
- **"Robbing Myth of Myth: Third-Order Signification" slide.** The deck cites Barthes's invitation: "since myth robs language of something, why not rob myth?" The slide sets up the move to post-modern recursive significations.
- **"Third order chains of signification in 'late capitalism'" slide.** Concrete worked cases: DEATH cigarettes (skull branding), Liquid Death water (black-metal aesthetic on still water), the Dutch Barn vodka advert sold by Ricky Gervais. Each is a myth that already parodies itself.
- **"Styles and significations in late capitalism / post-modernity" slide.** Lists the contemporary lifestyle paradigms: "Roadmen / Clean girls / Content creators / Looksmaxxers / Harry Potter Fandom / Gamer" (lecture slide). The captions read: "Nothing natural but what about further third order significations....knowingness / excess / parody / irony..."; "Post-modern culture..." (lecture slide).
- **Exercise slide.** A short workshop prompt. Verbatim: "Find a recent print advertisement on-line. Analyse the advertisement using the techniques of semiology."

> 💡 slide-question: What might be further third order levels of signification? Does the process have an end to it or could it continue infinitely?

- **"Rethinking Modernity" map slide.** The big diagram that places structuralism alongside Marxism (Early/Mature Marx, Frankfurt School, Adorno/Horkheimer, Benjamin, Habermas, Public Sphere), British Cultural Studies (Thompson/Williams, CCCS/Hoggart, Hall), and the Culture and Civilisation tradition (Arnold, F.R. Leavis, Q.D. Leavis). Structuralism is shown feeding from Saussure (Sign/Signifier) into Barthes (Mythologies), with "POST" (post-modernism, intersectionality, Fraser's critique of the Public Sphere) running off the bottom.
- **Reading Week instructions slide.** Verbatim: "1. If you haven't already, read and annotate / summarise the Key readings for each week. 2. Using this chart as a basis create a diagram to show the key concepts for each theoretical school."

**Key concepts defined tightly (consolidated from the slides):**

- **The sign.** The unit of meaning, made of signifier + signified, "the former and the latter existed before uniting and forming this third object, which is the sign" (Barthes, 1972: 122).
- **Signifier / signified.** Physical form vs. mental concept. Not the thing itself.
- **The arbitrariness of the sign.** There is "no intrinsic, natural or essential reason why a particular concept should be linked with one sound image rather than another" (Strinati, 1995: 83).
- **Langue / parole.** System vs. use. "What is social from what is individual… what is essential from what is accessory" (Saussure, in Strinati, 1995: 82).
- **Synchronic / diachronic.** Snapshot of the system vs. history of changes.
- **Paradigmatic / syntagmatic axes.** Substitutable elements (paradigm) vs. combinable sequences (syntagm).
- **Denotation.** First-order, literal, "most obvious level… literal meaning" (lecture slide).
- **Connotation.** Second-order, cultural, "suggested or implied meaning" (lecture slide).
- **Myth.** Third-order, "ideological level… worldview that is reinforced by other orders" (lecture slide). "The very principle of myth: it transforms history into nature" (Barthes, 1972: 140).
- **Mythologies.** Barthes's 1957 collection of short essays decoding wrestling, wine, soap, the Citroën DS, striptease, toys and the Paris-Match cover.
- **The death of the author.** Barthes's later move (Barthes, 1977): meaning is produced by readers, not fixed by writers' intentions.
- **Encoding / decoding (Hall).** Production encodes a "meaningful discourse" inside frameworks of knowledge, relations of production and technical infrastructure; audiences decode within their own frameworks. Three positions: dominant-hegemonic, negotiated, oppositional (Hall, 1980).
- **Polysemic text.** A text open to multiple readings.
- **Iconic / indexical / symbolic** (Peirce, on slide). Signs that resemble, are caused by, or are conventionally linked to what they signify.
- **The linguistic turn.** The broader twentieth-century move in social theory toward language as the model for understanding culture, meaning and power.

---

## §4. Worked examples (concrete, exam-ready)

- **Barthes's "wrestler".** Staged combat where bodies and gestures denote a fight but connote a moral spectacle of justice, suffering and defeat ("the bad guy" framed in the slide).
- **Barthes's "wine".** Denotes a fermented drink; connotes Frenchness, conviviality, classlessness; myth = wine as the "totem-drink" of the nation that erases its colonial production (Barthes, 1972).
- **Barthes's "Citroën DS".** Denotes a 1955 car; connotes seamless modernity, aerodynamic perfection; myth = technology as quasi-religious magic (Barthes, 1972).
- **The Paris-Match cover.** Denotes a Black soldier saluting the French flag; connotes "a purposeful mixture of Frenchness and militariness"; myth = "French imperiality… that France is a great Empire, that all her sons, without any colour discrimination, faithfully serve under her flag" (Barthes, 1972: 125-126).
- **Barthes's "toys" (Mythologies).** Mini kitchens, dolls, mini soldiers; denote play; connote pre-formed adult social roles; myth = gendered futures as natural. The lecture slide shows Betsy Wetsy ("It's fun to mother"), Kookamunga "Lifelike Love", LEGO Classic and LEGO Harry Potter as worked cases.
- **Barthes's astrology/horoscopes.** Denote daily predictions; connote individual destinies; myth = capitalist daily life absorbed into a cosmic narrative (Barthes, 1972).
- **Barthes's seventy women novelists.** Photo and caption denote women writers with their number of children; connote that motherhood is the primary frame; myth = "the eternal statute of womanhood", that "women are on the earth to give children to men" (Barthes, 1972: 56).
- **Saussure's "dog / god" (Strinati, 1995: 83).** A one-letter change yields an entirely different sign, with no natural reason why either notation should attach to its referent; pure paradigmatic substitution.
- **Saussure's "tree / *arbor*" diagram (lecture slide).** The same signified (concept of tree) takes different signifiers across languages, displayed in the slide's circle diagrams.
- **The "Inuit terms for snow" slide.** Different languages carve the same continuum (frozen water) into different sign-paradigms; classic dramatisation of *langue*-as-system.
- **Traffic lights (lecture slide).** Red = stop only because the system fixes the difference between red, amber and green; the arbitrary-but-conventional sign.
- **Dick Bruna's *The school* (lecture slide).** Cover shows a boy in blue and a girl in red; denotes two children; connotes gendered colour-coding; myth = gender as a "natural" binary, used by the lecture to extend Saussure's "difference" into gender (Femininity / Masculinity paradigm slides).
- **Hugo Boss "BOSS" suit advert (denotation/connotation slide).** Denotes a man in coat-and-suit; connotes professionalism, success, authority; myth = bourgeois masculinity as the natural form of seriousness (teacher's summary; lecture slide).
- **Jeep Compass "Upgrade your adventures" advert (denotation/connotation slide).** Denotes a 4x4 in mountain landscape; connotes adventure, freedom, masculinity, aspiration; myth = the SUV as escape from ordinary life (teacher's summary; lecture slide).
- **HSBC "Why should creating wealth overwhelm you" advert (semiotics slide).** Denotes a woman in red against a financial skyline; connotes wealth, inspiration, glamour; myth = global finance as personal empowerment.
- **The Aliens / Ripley-with-child image (semiotics slide).** Denotes a woman holding a child while armed; connotes maternal-warrior duality; myth = an action-cinema reconciliation of the femininity paradigm with the masculinity paradigm.
- **"Decolonize" graffiti (semiotics slide).** Denotes a painted word on a wall; connotes anti-colonial politics; myth = the street as the legitimate site of decolonial speech. Example of the slide's "decolonial" approach to semiotics.
- **O2 "Wear the Rose" (lecture slide).** Denotes an England rugby campaign with the red rose; connotes national pride, athletic effort; myth = sport-as-nation. Sets up the "A Rose is a Rose?" worked example.
- **"A Rose is a Rose?" (lecture slide, verbatim).** Denotation = "a flower bush in the garden"; connotation = "the consumption of roses on special romantic occasions (e.g. Valentine's day, anniversaries, dates, etc). Not being given roses on such occasions connotes a lack of romance"; myth = "romance being commodified; being robbed of its innocent meaning (true love, passion, etc). In other words, the mythical signification is motivated; it is not arbitrary." Other possible connotations listed: "pain, rugby, England, Labour Party..." (lecture slide).
- **DEATH cigarettes (skull branding, lecture slide).** Denotes cigarettes; connotes self-aware nihilism; myth = a product that parodies its own myth, a third-order chain in late capitalism.
- **Liquid Death mountain water (lecture slide).** Black-metal aesthetic on still water; denotes canned water; connotes dangerous cool; myth = mass-marketed water as deathly rebellion. Third-order signification in "late capitalism".
- **Dutch Barn vodka with Ricky Gervais (lecture slide).** Caption "Buying Dutch Barn will make a person rich & happy. And that person is Ricky Gervais"; denotes a vodka advert; connotes celebrity-comedian self-mockery; myth = the celebrity endorsement that mocks the form of celebrity endorsement.
- **Camel cigarettes campaigns (lecture slides 29-31).** "Smooth Character" Joe Camel against the Hollywood sign, the Camel GT racing slide, "Strike It Rich! Camel Cash Lotto", "New Special Lights"; denote cigarette branding; connote sophistication, glamour, masculine cool; myth = smoking as freedom and style.
- **The *Joe Chemo* parody (lecture slides 32-33).** Denotes a sick, balding camel on a hospital bed with chemo drip; connotes the consequences of the Camel myth; myth = "robbing myth of myth" (Barthes, 1972: 135) by using the Camel iconography against itself. Caption: "THE SURGEON GENERAL WARNS THAT SMOKING IS A FREQUENT CAUSE OF WASTED POTENTIAL AND FATAL REGRET".
- **Absolut Vodka campaigns (lecture slides 34-38).** "Absolut Spring", "Absolut Homage", "Absolut Mango", "Absolut Marilyn", and their critical counter-ads "Absolute Hangover", "Absolut Liver Failure", "Absolut Impotence" (with the Shakespeare line "drink provokes the desire but takes away the performance"), "Absolut Submission", "Absolut Drunk". Denote vodka and its parodies; connote glamour vs. addiction; myth and counter-myth in the same bottle-shaped frame.
- **The OK Cola cans / brand authenticity (semiotics slide).** Denotes a tin of cola with deadpan slogans; connotes anti-marketing irony; myth = the post-modern brand that markets its own ironic distance from marketing.
- **The lifestyle paradigm of "late capitalism / post-modernity" (lecture slide).** "Roadmen / Clean girls / Content creators / Looksmaxxers / Harry Potter Fandom / Gamer". The slide caption: "Nothing natural but what about further third order significations… knowingness / excess / parody / irony… Post-modern culture…" Each denotes a style; connotes in-group belonging; myth = identity as a performable third-order chain.
- **The fashion-history silhouette strip (lecture slide, 1775 to 1952).** Denotes changes in dress; connotes the historicity of "natural" appearance; myth-buster = even the most "given" thing (how a body looks fully clothed) is a sequence of synchronic systems through diachronic time.

---

## §5. Critiques and limits (the Hall pivot)

- **Empirical validity.** Strinati: "Barthes does not attempt to indicate why his interpretation is to be preferred to others" (Strinati, 1995: 114). What evidence makes "roses = passion" rather than "roses = farewell" or "roses = sexual harassment"?
- **Neglect of production.** Semiology "tends to ignore the context of industrial production" (Strinati, 1995: 117); cultural signs are also commodities.
- **Neglect of consumption / audience.** "Meaning is not a quality of the sign itself but of the social relationships in which it can be located" (Strinati, 1995: 117). Hall's encoding/decoding is the corrective.
- **Ahistoricism.** Lévi-Straussian structuralism freezes the system synchronically and "reduces culture to a mental structure" (Strinati, 1995: 111), erasing class and history.
- **Crude theory of ideology.** Barthes reduces myth to "bourgeois ideology" (Strinati, 1995: 117), which struggles with race, gender, colonial difference. Hall, feminist semiology and decolonial semiotics push back.
- **The "robbing myth of myth" problem.** Barthes himself: "Since myth robs language of something, why not rob myth? All that is needed is to use it as the departure point for a third semiological chain, to take its signification as the first term of a second myth" (Barthes, 1972: 135). The chain can go on infinitely (irony, parody, the *Joe Chemo* counter-Camel slides, the Absolut Vodka counter-ads, DEATH cigarettes, Liquid Death, Dutch Barn vodka, culture jamming), which both opens space for resistance and threatens the diagnostic clarity of the original method.

---

## §6. Quick exam scaffolds

**The "do we need a theory of signs to understand capitalism?" scaffold (2023-style):**
1. State the question: is semiology necessary, or are political economy / class structure / commodity form sufficient?
2. Show what semiology adds (advertising, branding, cultural commodification, late-capitalist style cycles).
3. Show its limits (production, labour, class).
4. Argue for a Hall-style synthesis: semiology + Marxism + ideology theory.

**The "is X mythological?" scaffold (2022-style):**
1. Define myth as third-order signification that naturalises history.
2. Pick two or three contemporary examples.
3. Apply denotation -> connotation -> myth.
4. Critique: production, audience, polysemy, polyvalence, ideology.
5. Verdict: how convincing is the diagnosis?

**The "popular culture is ideological" scaffold (2021-style):**
1. Define Barthes's claim: myth is the form of bourgeois ideology because it transforms the historical into the natural.
2. Three concrete cases.
3. Strengths: it explains why power feels obvious.
4. Weaknesses: empirical validation, audience reception, reductive class theory.
5. Hall as a productive successor.

---

- **2023 (Q7):** Do we need a theory of signs and signification to understand capitalism?
- **2022 (Q5):** Critically assess Barthes' argument that popular culture is "mythological".
- **2021 (Q5):** What did Barthes mean when he argued that popular culture is ideological? How convincing do you find his approach?

### Past-year exam answers

### 8.1 Past-year 2023 (Q7). Do we need a theory of signs and signification to understand capitalism?

I want to argue that we do need a theory of signs to understand capitalism, but only a theory reworked along Hall's lines. A pure semiology cannot grasp capitalism on its own, because capitalism is also a mode of production, a class structure and a circuit of accumulation. But a Marxism that ignores signs cannot explain why Hugo Boss sells professionalism, why Jeep can sell a 4x4 by attaching it to mountains, or why Liquid Death can sell still water by branding it like a heavy-metal band. The sign and the commodity have become inseparable, and any serious account of contemporary capitalism has to combine the two.

Begin with Saussure's account of the sign. Language is "not a transparent medium that reflects reality, but a structured system of signs, organised through difference and governed by rules that exist independently of individual intention" (lecture slide, citing Saussure, 1916). The signifier is the physical form (sound, mark, image, style); the signified is the mental concept. The relation between them is arbitrary, and meaning emerges from difference within a system, *langue*, rather than from things in the world. This is already politically useful, because it lets us see that "Frenchness", "bourgeois respectability" or "the eternal womanhood" of Barthes's photo of seventy novelists (Barthes, 1972: 56) are signs, not natural objects. The political work of capitalism partly consists in making such signs feel obvious.

Barthes's notion of myth makes this point sharper. Denotation is "the most obvious level… literal meaning"; connotation is the "cultural level… suggested or implied meaning"; myth is the "ideological level… worldview that is reinforced by other orders" (lecture slide). The function of myth is "to transform history into nature" (Barthes, 1972: 140). The Hugo Boss suit denotes a garment; connotes professionalism and authority; mythologises bourgeois masculinity as the natural form of seriousness. The Jeep Compass advert denotes a 4x4 against a mountain horizon; connotes adventure and aspiration; mythologises consumption as escape. Without a theory of signs we cannot diagnose any of this; we can describe a brand's profits but not why its image works.

Capitalism in its late or platform form has made semiology more necessary. The "Styles in late capitalism" slide lists roadmen, clean girls, content creators, looksmaxxers, the Harry Potter fandom and gamers, asking what "knowingness, excess, parody, irony" they involve. The "Third order chains" slide makes the same point with DEATH cigarettes, Liquid Death water and the Dutch Barn vodka advert. Each is a brand that already parodies the form of branding. These signs only become legible once we treat them as semiological systems.

But, and this is where I follow Strinati and Hall, semiology on its own is not enough. Strinati notes that semiology "tends to ignore the context of industrial production" (Strinati, 1995: 117) and that "meaning is not a quality of the sign itself but of the social relationships in which it can be located" (Strinati, 1995: 117). Barthes himself reduces myth to "bourgeois ideology" (Strinati, 1995: 117) in a way that is theoretically thin: it does not specify which fraction of capital, which institutions, which audiences. The Paris-Match cover Barthes reads as "French imperiality" (Barthes, 1972: 125-126) is also produced by a magazine industry, sold to particular readerships, and decoded variously by Black and white French citizens. Race, gender and colonial difference exceed Barthes's binary class frame.

Hall's reworking is what makes semiology adequate to capitalism, and it is no accident that Hall reaches for Gramsci to do it. Gramsci's account of hegemony as "the 'spontaneous' consent given by the great masses of the population to the general direction imposed on social life by the dominant fundamental group" (Gramsci, 1971: 12) supplies the political theory Barthes lacks. Hall's articulation theory turns semiological differences into hegemonic moves: a Jeep advert or a Hugo Boss image is not just a myth, it is a small contribution to the consent that capitalism needs. His encoding/decoding diagram (lecture slide, "Hall: building on structuralism?") restores the "media production and power" of the encoder and the "differential reception of the audience". A theory of signs is necessary because capitalism increasingly sells signs; a theory of capitalism is necessary because signs are produced by industries inside class relations. The honest synthesis is that we need both: Saussure to identify the structure, Barthes to read the myth, Hall and Gramsci to bring back power. The answer to the question is: yes, but only as one indispensable element in a wider critical sociology.

(Word count: ~740.)

---

### 8.2 Past-year 2022 (Q5). Critically assess Barthes' argument that popular culture is "mythological".

Barthes's claim that popular culture is mythological is, in my view, both indispensable and over-stated. It is indispensable because he gives us the sharpest tool we have for seeing how popular-cultural signs naturalise specific historical arrangements. It is over-stated because, taken on its own, the argument under-determines questions of audience reception, institutional production and the polysemy of texts that Hall and Strinati raise.

Start with the argument itself. In *Mythologies*, Barthes describes myth as "a system of communication… a mode of signification" (Barthes, 1972: 117), and insists that "the very principle of myth" is that "it transforms history into nature" (Barthes, 1972: 140). His most famous case is the *Paris-Match* cover, where "a young Negro in a French uniform is saluting, with his eyes uplifted, probably fixed on a fold of the tricolour" (Barthes, 1972: 125). Denotatively, this is a soldier saluting a flag. Connotatively, it is a "purposeful mixture of Frenchness and militariness". Mythically, it signifies "French imperiality", "France is a great Empire, that all her sons, without any colour discrimination, faithfully serve under her flag" (Barthes, 1972: 125-126). The historical violence of French colonialism is laundered into a natural, obvious image of multi-racial loyalty. The wrestler's grimace, the wine bottle, the Citroën DS, the toys reviewed in *Mythologies* all work the same way. The lecture's third-order signification diagram captures the schema: denotative (literal), connotative (cultural), mythological (ideological worldview).

Applied to today's popular culture, this is enormously productive. The Hugo Boss suit advert turns class-coded clothing into "professionalism and authority"; the Jeep Compass advert turns a fuel-hungry 4x4 into "Upgrade your adventures". The O2 "Wear the Rose" rugby campaign turns a corporate sponsorship into a national passion, and the "A Rose is a Rose?" slide spells out the chain: denotation = "a flower bush in the garden"; connotation = "the consumption of roses on special romantic occasions"; myth = "romance being commodified; being robbed of its innocent meaning". The Camel campaigns mythologise smoking as freedom, while *Joe Chemo* performs the third-order "robbery" Barthes invites: "since myth robs language of something, why not rob myth?" (Barthes, 1972: 135). DEATH cigarettes, Liquid Death water and the Dutch Barn vodka advert with Ricky Gervais push the recursion further, branding the parody of branding.

But the argument needs to be qualified on four fronts. First, validation: Strinati notes that "Barthes does not attempt to indicate why his interpretation is to be preferred to others" (Strinati, 1995: 114). When Barthes says roses signify passion, why not farewell or irony? Second, production: semiology "tends to ignore the context of industrial production" (Strinati, 1995: 117). A *Paris-Match* cover is also the output of a media industry inside a colonial state. Third, audience: Barthes treats the myth-consumer as essentially passive, taking "the signification for a system of facts" (Barthes, 1972: 142). Hall's encoding/decoding model corrects this with dominant, negotiated and oppositional readings. The same Camel advert can mean cool to one viewer and a public-health crime scene to another, as *Joe Chemo* makes literal. Fourth, the theory of ideology is crude: Barthes reduces myth to "bourgeois ideology" (Strinati, 1995: 117), which under-specifies race, gender and colonial power.

There is also a deeper issue Barthes himself acknowledges: once any signification can be the first term in a further chain, mythological readings multiply infinitely. Baudrillard pushes this development into the post-structuralist register, arguing that under late capitalism the sign cuts loose from any anterior referent and becomes pure simulacrum, "the generation by models of a real without origin or reality: a hyperreal" (Baudrillard, 1994: 1). Liquid Death and DEATH cigarettes look like Barthesian myths but read more cleanly as Baudrillardian sign-value: the brand simulates the parody of branding. The "Styles in late capitalism" slide lists roadmen, clean girls, content creators, looksmaxxers, the Harry Potter fandom and gamers, asking what "knowingness, excess, parody, irony" do as further significations. TikTok aesthetics and trend cycles iterate this in real time. This is theoretically generative but methodologically destabilising: at what point does the critic stop adding chains?

My assessment, then, is that the claim that popular culture is mythological is essentially correct as a diagnosis of a major mechanism of contemporary cultural power, and Barthes deserves credit for naming it. But it is incomplete. Without Hall on audiences, without political economy on production, without intersectional accounts of ideology, the mythological frame floats free of the social. Read alongside these, however, it remains one of the most powerful tools we have.

(Word count: ~735.)

---

### 8.3 Past-year 2021 (Q5). What did Barthes mean when he argued that popular culture is ideological? How convincing do you find his approach?

When Barthes argues that popular culture is ideological, he is making a specific and quite technical claim, not just complaining about advertising. His claim is that the popular signs around us, magazine covers, wrestling matches, wine bottles, soap powders, cars, toys, operate at a third order of signification he calls myth, and that the function of myth is to convert the historically specific interests of a dominant class into apparently natural, timeless, obvious truths. Strinati paraphrases the political programme: semiology is "the close analysis of the processes of meaning by which the bourgeoisie converts its historical class-culture into universal nature… the fundamental method of an ideological critique" (Barthes, in Strinati, 1995: 100). Or in Barthes's own words: "the very principle of myth: it transforms history into nature" (Barthes, 1972: 140).

The mechanics matter. Saussure gives us the sign as signifier + signified, with an arbitrary relation between them and meaning arising from difference within *langue*. Barthes adds two levels. At denotation, a sign is literal: a photo of a Black soldier saluting a flag. At connotation, the sign acquires cultural associations: "Frenchness and militariness" (Barthes, 1972: 125). At the third order, myth, the connotation hardens into an ideological worldview: "French imperiality… France is a great Empire" (Barthes, 1972: 125-126). The historical truth of French colonial violence becomes the natural truth of a loyal multi-racial empire. Popular culture is ideological in Barthes's sense not because it lies, but because it makes specific historical arrangements feel like the way things are.

Take a few contemporary instances. The O2 "Wear the Rose" rugby campaign denotes a national team in red roses; connotes athletic effort; mythologises a "natural" English sporting nationhood. The "A Rose is a Rose?" slide unpacks the chain: denotation as "a flower bush", connotation as romance commodified on Valentine's day, myth as romance "being robbed of its innocent meaning… the mythical signification is motivated; it is not arbitrary". The Camel "Smooth Character" campaigns mythologise smoking as masculine glamour. Barthes's seventy women novelists, each captioned with the number of her children, mythologise an "eternal statute of womanhood" where "women are on the earth to give children to men" (Barthes, 1972: 56). The *Joe Chemo* parody shows the chain can be robbed back: "since myth robs language of something, why not rob myth?" (Barthes, 1972: 135). The Absolut counter-ads run the same culture-jamming play.

How convincing is this? Quite convincing as a description of a real and important mechanism, but limited as a complete theory of popular culture, and limited as a theory of ideology in particular. Four caveats.

First, validation. Strinati's standing objection is that "Barthes does not attempt to indicate why his interpretation is to be preferred to others" (Strinati, 1995: 114). The semiologist's eye is not obviously more reliable than another educated reader's.

Second, production. Cultural signs are produced inside industries. *Paris-Match* has shareholders, editors, image rights and a particular market. Strinati notes that "semiology… tends to ignore the context of industrial production" (Strinati, 1995: 117). A serious analysis of capitalism's ideological power has to add political economy.

Third, audiences. Barthes pictures the consumer of myth as essentially passive, taking signification "for a system of facts" (Barthes, 1972: 142). Hall's encoding/decoding model recognises that the same message can be decoded in dominant, negotiated or oppositional ways. Black readers of the Paris-Match cover were not, on the whole, duped by French imperiality.

Fourth, the theory of ideology is too narrow. Barthes reduces myth to bourgeois class interest; Strinati calls this "fairly crude" (Strinati, 1995: 117). Race, gender, sexuality and colonial difference cut across class in ways Barthes's frame struggles to articulate. Feminist semiology and decolonial readings have stretched the toolkit further than Barthes himself.

So Barthes is right that popular culture is ideological in his precise sense; it naturalises history. He is half-right about how. The British cultural studies frame Williams supplies is the missing supplement here: if culture is "a whole way of life" (Williams, 1958: 6), then Barthes's individual mythological readings need to be embedded in the lived ordinary social context that gives each sign its weight. Plugged into Hall on encoding/decoding, into Williams on culture as a whole way of life, into political economy on production, and into feminist and decolonial readings on the texture of power, his approach remains one of the indispensable tools for analysing the cultural surface of contemporary capitalism. On its own, it is brilliant but partial. With these companions, it is essential.

(Word count: ~738.)

---

### Mock exam answers

> Mocks 1-22 below correspond to questions M1-M22 in §8. All twenty-two mock essays are now drafted (the original gap at Mocks 20-22 has been filled).

### 8.4 Mock 1. The teacher's L15 summary contrasts "Culturalist - lived experience, historical context, and agency" with "Structuralist - the deep structures that organise meaning". Critically assess this contrast through Saussure, Barthes and Hall.

The teacher's summary frames the L15 lecture around a sharp pair: culturalism, which prioritises lived experience, historical context and agency, and structuralism, which prioritises the deep structures that organise meaning. The opposition is real, but the most useful sociological position does not pick one side; it works the contrast as a productive tension. Saussure and early Barthes sit at the structuralist pole; Williams and Thompson sit at the culturalist pole; Hall, characteristically, sutures the two. I want to argue that the structuralist pole gives us the analytical sharpness culturalism on its own lacks, and the culturalist pole gives the politics and the social texture that structuralism on its own evacuates.

Begin with the structuralist side. Saussure's claim is that language is "a structured system of signs, organised through difference and governed by rules that exist independently of individual intention" (lecture slide). Signifier and signified are inseparable but the relation between them is arbitrary, and meaning arises from position within a *langue*, not from things in the world. The lecture's traffic-lights image dramatises this nicely: red means "stop" because the system fixes the difference between red, amber and green, not because red is intrinsically stop-coloured. Strinati notes the strict relational logic: "there is no intrinsic, natural or essential reason why a particular concept should be linked with one sound image rather than another" (Strinati, 1995: 83). Barthes extends the apparatus to images, fashion, food, advertising, film, news and popular culture, and adds the second and third orders: connotation and myth. The Hugo Boss suit, the Jeep Compass, the O2 "Wear the Rose" rose: all readable as positions within structured systems of difference.

The culturalist side is just as serious. Williams insists that culture is "a whole way of life" (Williams, 1958: 6), that "culture is ordinary" and that meaning is lived rather than abstractly coded. Thompson's emphasis is on agency and historical experience: working-class culture is a record of how people make, contest and remake their world. From this angle, Saussure looks too clean: real human beings do not live inside *langue*; they live inside particular households, workplaces, schools, neighbourhoods and traditions, and signs acquire weight from those settings.

So which is right? Both, on different problems. The structuralist eye is unbeatable for analysing the surface of media culture. When I want to decode the Hugo Boss advert, the Jeep advert, or the Paris-Match cover, "denotation -> connotation -> myth" is the apparatus that gets me precise readings. The teacher's summary makes the point: the model "can be applied beyond language but also in terms of images, fashion, food, advertising, film, news, and popular culture". Without it, criticism collapses into impressionistic taste, the failure mode of the Leavisite tradition.

But the culturalist eye is essential when I want to understand why a sign has weight here and not there. The Femininity-paradigm slide ("Obedient / Servile / Passive / Submissive…") is meaningful only because actual girls grow up inside actual households and schools that enforce it; the Jeep advert works because suburban driving feels suffocating; the "Wear the Rose" campaign mobilises real sporting affect because England's rugby culture is a lived inheritance. Williams reminds us that the sign sits inside what he calls a structure of feeling, the dense lived weather of an ordinary life. Strip the sign from that weather and you produce, as Strinati warns, a semiology that "tends to ignore the context of industrial production" and that loses the "social relationships in which" meaning is located (Strinati, 1995: 117).

Hall is the natural mediator. The teacher's summary names the move precisely: he "does not abandon structuralism. Instead, he reworks it, combining semiology with Marxism, ideology theory, and sociology." His encoding/decoding diagram, reproduced on the lecture slide titled "Hall: building on structuralism?", routes the relational sign back through production institutions and audience reception, that is, back through the culturalist field. The encoder works inside "frameworks of knowledge, relations of production, technical infrastructure"; the audience decodes inside its own analogous frameworks. The result is a model in which "deep structures that organise meaning" actually meet "lived experience, historical context, and agency".

My assessment, then, is that the culturalist/structuralist contrast in the teacher's summary is heuristically useful but methodologically misleading if treated as a forced choice. Saussure and Barthes give the apparatus; Williams and Thompson give the social ground; Hall integrates the two. For SC301 purposes the best position holds the apparatus in one hand and the way of life in the other. Neither survives alone.

(Word count: ~735.)
